#2828. NBA scouts missed Yaxel Lendeborg’s greatness with an easy mistake

The high school class of 2020 produced one of the most hyped collections of top-ranked prospects in recent memory. Jalen Green, Terrence Clarke, and Josh Christopher were household names from early in their teenage years for mixtape compilations that drew comparisons to Kobe Bryant and other star scorers. Jalen Suggs was a two-sport stud who bypassed an Ohio State football scholarship because he was better at basketball. Scottie Barnes and Evan Mobley were portable, long-limbed defensive prodigies, and Cade Cunningham shot up to the top of the class after a stirring EYBL run that had him looking like American Luka Doncic.

Yaxel Lendeborg was also in the class of 2020, but while his peers were gracing the cover of SLAM and winning international gold medals, he had yet to play organized basketball. Lendeborg's grades weren't good enough to get on the court back in his hometown of Pennsauken, New Jersey, and he was more interested in playing video games than applying himself to anything that would better his future. It's possible his enormous talent would have slipped through the cracks entirely if not for a junior college on the other side of the country taking a chance on him with its last scholarship in a Covid-shortened season following an impressive weekend at an exposure camp for Dominican players.

Nearly six years later, Lendeborg already looks like something close to an NBA star as a 24-year-old rookie with the Golden State Warriors. His winding journey from Arizona Western College to UAB to Michigan to now playing alongside Stephen Curry has no real analog, but it still offers some valuable insight into how prospect evaluation is changing in a rapidly evolving landscape for young players. Lendeborg is an exception to just about every rule in the sport, but his ascent is no accident, and it could inform similar success stories in the coming years for teams looking hard enough.

What Lendeborg is doing to open this season is nothing short of amazing. He's averaging 22.3 points, 7.3 rebounds, and 3.7 assists on pristine 64.5% true shooting through his first seven games. His 37-point explosion against the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday showed the full extent of his skill set. When he was guarded by the skinnier Derrick Jones Jr., Lendeborg wielded body blows in the paint for easy scoring chances. When Brook Lopez tried to corral him in drop coverage off a pick-and-roll, Lendeborg calmly drained a pull-up three-pointer. He showed impressive body control when attacking downhill, and relentless aggression in punishing a small guard in Darius Garland on switches. With a like-sized defender in Kobe Sanders on him, he ripped mid-range shots like a seasoned pro.

No rookie should be capable of this type of immediate excellence. Then again, Lendeborg is anything but a typical rookie.

The Warriors drafted Lendeborg at No. 11 overall this year, but even they weren't fully convinced he was the player they needed. Golden State reportedly coveted Brayden Burries, who went one pick ahead of them to the Milwaukee Bucks, and they were prepared to select him over Lendeborg. Yaxel's own college coach passed on him for one of his Michigan teammates when the Dallas Mavericks chose Morez Johnson at No. 9 overall days after hiring Dusty May.

It was easy to see the track record of older first round draft picks and immediately write off Lendeborg as a low-ceiling prospect. I never bought that argument. When I ranked Yaxel at No. 5 overall on my final draft board, I wrote "I typically balk at the idea that older prospects are more 'NBA ready' than younger ones who reach the league sooner, but it feels true in Yaxel's case." In reality, he was never that difficult of an evaluation if you could get past his age.

What sold me on Lendeborg was that he was improving in the exact ways you want someone his age to improve, albeit at a lower level than the NBA. When he entered UAB from junior college, he was mostly a rebounding big who provided value by generating extra possessions and protecting the paint. In his second season at UAB, he started to show off his playmaking chops, showing that he could run offense with the ball in his hands by using his own scoring gravity to set up his teammates. He also doubled his three-point makes from the previous season. As his offense was starting to develop, Lendeborg was named AAC Defensive Player of the Year while mostly playing center.

Lendeborg was good enough to get drafted in the first round in 2025 out of UAB. After testing the process at the combine, though, he decided to take a massive NIL bag from Michigan as the top-rated player in the transfer portal. As I was covering the Wolverines during March Madness, I asked Yaxel what he heard from NBA scouts that convinced him to go back to college. His answer showed the self-awareness required to go from good to great on your own timeline.

"(The NBA) wanted to see a lot more three-pointers and a lot more versatility in my defense," Lendeborg told SB Nation. "I tried to be more of three, because in the NBA, I'm not gonna be the superstar. I'm gonna be playing next to somebody like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, and he doesn't need me to score for him. He needs me to get stops. I just tried to figure out my role and do whatever I can do to get there."

Michigan's unique team-building strategy forced Lendeborg into the exact role NBA evaluators wanted to see him in. May started three nominal college centers next to each other who were each good enough to have a team built around them on their own. Lendeborg's malleability was the biggest reason it all worked. Forced out to the perimeter full-time for the first time in his brief career, Yaxel showed he could shoot threes with volume, defend away from the paint, and grease the offense with connective passing all without losing his physicality at both ends.

Lendeborg proved he was willing to sacrifice for team success, and he never needed to put up the biggest numbers to answer the NBA's questions. Here was a player with the size to play NBA center after measuring at 6'8.5 without shoes, 235 pounds with a 7'4 wingspan who already showed he could play alongside other bigs while contributing to winning at a high level. He could do the role player stuff of rebounding, setting screens, spacing the floor, and moving the ball as a passer, and he still had an extra gear as an isolation scorer who could leverage his size into more efficient chances. All the while, he kept getting more confident and more accurate as an outside shooter.

The scary thing about Lendeborg is his most impressive flashes haven't translated to sustainable success … yet. Through seven games, he's only making 25% of his pull-up threes on 3.4 attempts per game. If those start falling even at a clip in the low 30s, there's no real cap on his ceiling.

So many young forwards get drafted high in the NBA just because they have the frame, athleticism, and pedigree the league looks for. In the best case scenarios, these players will develop as passers and shooters without losing their physicality in their age-21, age-22, and age-23 seasons. This is exactly what Lendeborg did first at UAB and then at Michigan, and his development curve is made even more impressive by his late start in the sport.

His progression as a player is even more satisfying when juxtaposed against another former Warriors lottery pick who graduated high school in 2020: Jonathan Kuminga. Kuminga was never asked to play a winning role with physicality early in his career when evaluators saw a potential star scorer. He never developed the ball skills or shooting that Lendeborg is showing now. Yaxel's progression shouldn't have been discounted just because it happened in college, not the NBA. In every other way, he was giving scouts everything they wanted.

The two best players in college basketball last year were Yaxel and Cameron Boozer, and no one else was close to him. This is what made Boozer the obvious No. 1 overall pick in my eyes: he was the only player in the country close to Lendeborg's level, and he did it while being five years younger than him. While there's plenty of season left to go, it's no surprise that Lendeborg and Boozer have been the two best rookies to start this season.

Lendeborg checked every box for a role player, and in the NBA, the best role players are truly more valuable than many who get blessed as stars. Yaxel is a premium example of that. The NIL is going to keep good players in school longer before, and don't be surprised if some of the top prospects in the next draft are also multi-year college veterans, if not 24-year-old rookies. It's easy to say progress isn't linear when watching young basketball players, but it's harder to act like it when the chips are on the table. Lendeborg was always running his own race. Right now, he's showing he can still finish first even with a late start.

#2827. Star LeBron James gives thoughts on Sixers president Mike Gansey

PHILADELPHIA -- Philadelphia 76ers President of Basketball Operations Mike Gansey is a popular man in the City of Brotherly Love. The new head man of Philadelphia's front office was able to first land Jaylen Brown in a big trade and then landed LeBron James in the offseason as he built a legitimate championship contender in his first offseason.

Gansey, a native of Olmstead, OH, is very familiar with James. Not only did Gansey spend time with him during his 15 years in Cleveland's front office, but the two also go way back to high school as a certain photo of James and Gansey was floating around Twitter throughout Philadelphia's chase of James.

"Yeah, I remember that day," James laughed after Monday's win over the Chicago Bulls. "One, I didn't have no recollection of, like, why was I there as a freshman. I've seen all those guys, all those seniors there. Maverick (Carter), now my business partner, but a brother of mine, he was there. Mike Gansey was there, obviously, and so many other like seniors."

The above photo was taken by the Cleveland Plain Dealer as the best high school basketball players in Ohio were highlighted. James, a freshman at the time, was shocked he was even in that same category.

"I watched a lot of those guys in the tournaments and AAU tournaments, and then through the high school ranking, so it was so surreal for me being a freshman, being part of that whole that—I think it was a Plain Dealer, I don't know what, the Plain Dealer something, but yeah, and I knew of Mike Gansey," James continued. "I knew how much he could hoop. We all knew about him in Akron, so that was pretty cool."

Now the President of Basketball Operations in Philadelphia, James is happy to see Gansey thriving. He and the other Cavaliers knew it was only a matter of time, but to see it happen is a sense of happiness for him as he and the Sixers move forward.

"He's deserving," James finished. "Very deserving. Very deserving, and we always knew, you know, players, people running the organization in Cleveland knew that he had the makeup of that, you know? So, it's pretty cool to be able to work with him now again, and just got like a long history. I was a freshman in high school. I was 14 years old. I'll be 42, so a long history. Long history."

Gansey, James, and the Sixers will look to keep things moving in the right direction as they head into the rest of the season.

#2825. Hawks edge narrow victory against six-man Pacers

The Atlanta Hawks continued their mini road-trip on Monday night, picking up a 108-104 victory against the Indiana Pacers. Nickeil Alexander-Walker scored 34 points, tying a career-best nine three-pointers in the process. Lu Dort added 14 points for Atlanta. For the Pacers, Jay Huff led with 22 points with Quenton Jackson adding 20 points.

The big story of this game could only be the injuries/absences. The following players were either injured or rested last night for the Pacers (who were on the second night of a back-to-back): Tyrese Haliburton, Paskal Siakam, Ivica Zubac, Aaron Nesmith, Andrew Nembhard, Obi Toppin, Kelly Oubre, and TJ McConnell, to name but a few, leaving the Pacers with just six available bodies.

NBA dot com's summary of this game paints quite a picture when it comes to the Pacers absences and who was available:

"The players who sat out have a combined salary of about $193 million, while those on the court make about $15 million."

For the Hawks, Jalen Johnson was sidelined in this game after the ankle tweak in New Orleans, while Jock Landale also missed out. In Johnson's place, Lu Dort would start. Kingston Flemings was also absent due to a one game league suspension following an elbow in New Orleans.

If one is to be realistic about the situation that presented itself for Atlanta last night, it's hard to conceive any situation where the Hawks should have work excessively hard or be in any position where this game is realistic doubt. But that's exactly where the Hawks found themselves when it came to clutch time.

At several points in this game the Hawks established secure double-digit leads — 14 points, 15 points — in the second and third quarters. And in both instances, the Pacers pegged them back. A lack of size inside meant that when the Pacers found Huff, they also found a recipe that worked inside and led to consecutive baskets which wiped the lead in the second quarter for a spell.

In the third quarter, the Hawks shot 28% from the field, and then went on a nearly four minute field goal drought in the fourth quarter down the stretch, with Onyeka Okongwu's hook fortunate to drop to give the Hawks a secure four-point lead with 10 seconds remaining.

With a second left and a good contest, it was pretty desperate stuff for the Hawks but they finally got their much needed field goal, and the Pacers' juice finally ran out.

This Okongwu basket was also a rare example of the Hawks getting a basket in the paint, scoring just 26 points in the paint, only 10 of which came in the second half.

The Hawks found success early shooting the three, and fell flat shooting inside the arc, and decided the strategy was to just hoist threes where possible as players such as Alexander-Walker (nine threes), Corey Kispert (four threes in the first half) and Lu Dort (4-of-6 from three) found fortune outside. In the end, the Hawks shot 23-of-51 from three, and it's the only reason they won this game. Atlanta shot 45% from three and 38% from the field.

Hawks head coach Quin Snyder praised the quality of the win despite acknowledging the Hawks were not at their best at the rim while missing players themselves

"It's a really good win," said Snyder postgame. "We knew we were going to be in a dogfight kind of game. Huff gives him size and rim protection. We weren't very good at the rim, and they made plays. We got a 10/12-point lead at one point, that's when you hopefully have a chance to break the game open and we were never able to do that. At this point in the year, the way every team is kind of growing, hopefully, the Pacers can get healthy. That's really hard. We had a little bit of that tonight with not having Jalen, Jock, and Kingston. We missed a lot of layups, and some of that was because we were playing against a team who had size. Good to get out of here with a win, all wins are good. These are the type of games, close games, that help you get better."

I couldn't disagree more with the general sentiment here that this was a 'good win'. While all wins ultimately add to the Hawks' record, so from that point of view they're 'equal' in that they all add a '+1,' not all victories are equal in how they're made, and not all victories are 'good.'

For example, how would you compare the recent victory against the Cleveland Cavaliers with this victory? Or the absolute drumming of Charlotte earlier in the season? Yes, they all added one win to the Hawks' record, but the perception around them and how the Hawks performed are completely different.

Adding to that, while the loss of Johnson, Flemings, and Landale in this game are note worthy, Snyder has no leg to stand on by mentioning that the Hawks missed these players while Indiana was missing all who they were missing.

With respect to the 'Super 6' as they were dubbed by the Indiana broadcast (and there's lots of good things to say about those six players), the Hawks — even without those three players — have so much more quality on paper of those who were available that this should never have been a close game. Not to mention depth; the Hawks ran out — almost on purpose, it felt — a deeper rotation than normal. Some of that accounts for injuries/absences, so there were minutes for Asa Newell and Zuby Ejiofor in the front-court, but the likes of Kispert and RayJ Dennis also got real rotation minutes.

Just to add further insult to the embarrassment of riches that were in Atlanta's favor, five of those six Pacers players played real rotation minutes against Brooklyn on Sunday, and were tasked with playing — in most cases — 40-plus minutes with little time to rest.

The Pacers deserve a lot of credit for how close they brought this game, because they had absolutely no right to be anywhere close to winning this game. Everything that was stacked against them should have resulted in a double-digit loss at the bare minimum.

But plays from Huff on both ends of the floor, energy from Kobe Brown coming off the bench, the tenacity of Braden Smith (who I thought was excellent) kept the Pacers close enough at times to make a run and keep the Hawks within striking distance of a run, which they made multiple runs to get back into the game.

From the Hawks' perspective, it was clearly not working at the rim so they dialled in from the perimeter. Against New Orleans, the three-point shooting was deplorable, but was excellent last night and was Atlanta's saving grace. So, in that regard, that's a positive the Hawks can build on that they can bounce back from an extremely cold performance to an extremely high volume performance, led by Alexander-Walker's nine threes leading to 34 points on 12-of-25 shooting and 9-of-15 from three:

Postgame, Snyder praised Alexander-Walker's ability to defend while also continuing to hit shots, also crediting the role of CJ McCollum in Alexander-Walker's performance.

"The thing about Nickeil is he's still playing on the defensive end too," said Snyder postgame. "He seems to make plays on both ends of the floor. He's playing with so much confidence. I thought CJ did a really good job of finding him late. I liked the shots that CJ was getting too, you just have certain nights that the ball won't cooperate. Nickeil hit big shots for us, it seemed like, the whole game."

With Johnson and Flemings out — in addition to Alexander-Walker's hot hand — McCollum took more of a playmaking role in this game, dishing out 12 assists in total and the first time McCollum has registered 10 or more assists in a game in over three years.

While McCollum finished 4-of-17 from the field, his contributions in the playmaking department do help make up for the volume of misses.

Elsewhere across the roster, Lu Dort put in a fine performance in the starting lineup, shooting 5-of-10 from the field and 4-of-6 from three. Dort hit what I thought was a huge three in the third quarter to stop the bleeding and prevent Indiana from getting too close:

This was, arguably, one of the most important swings in the game. Had Huff hit that three, the Pacers would have cut the lead down to two points. Dort's three really punished that miss, taking the lead up to eight points and buying the Hawks some immediate relief. If there was a spot when the Hawks sorely needed a good night shooting the three from Dort, this was the one and he delivered.

While everyone will forget the nature of this victory soon enough, the overarching takeaway, again, is that the Hawks were easily beaten inside the paint (conceding 54 points). This is Snyder's biggest concern from this game, spotting the trend that has occurred in several games now (but not before doubling down on his belief that this was a good win).

"Every win is a good one, and people say that because it's true," said Snyder. "Tonight was one of those nights. I thought when they did make the late run, we didn't get rattled. We didn't do everything right. The Pacers made some plays. We had a stretch where we put them on the foul line and that makes it hard because we can't get any force offensively, or thrust. didn't get any offensive thrust. The paint is something that we've got to shore up one way or the other. That's probably the biggest thing for us right now defensively is just not doing a better job protecting the paint because it's going to be real difficult to win when teams score on the paint like these guys did, and some other teams have too."

The Hawks (4-4) are back in action on Wednesday for the first of two meetings against the Washington Wizards (4-3), the first of which wraps up their three game road-trip.

#2823. Carson Hocevar Suspended From Homestead Race by Spire Motorsports

Carson Hocevar will not cap off his breakout 2026 NASCAR Cup Series campaign with a run around the 1.5-mile Homestead-Miami Speedway this weekend, as the driver has been suspended for the NASCAR Cup Series Championship Race.

The suspension, which stems from Hocevar brake-checking Austin Cindric multiple times, including on the straightaways, last weekend at Martinsville, comes internally from Hocevar's Spire Motorsports team, which felt the need to make the decision rather than forcing NASCAR to make the decision for them.

"A decision like this has a lot of variables and a cascading effect across an organization like ours," Jeff Dickerson, the team's co-owner, said in a prepared statement. "The easy thing would have been to leave this in NASCAR's hands and let them decide what any penalty should be. To us, however, this isn't about money or points. We believe in respect. Our integrity matters. This is the right decision for Spire Motorsports."

While Dickerson expressed his disappointment in Hocevar's actions at Martinsville, which resulted in Cindric exiting the race early due to the damage sustained, the co-owner of the organization reaffirmed his team's belief in its 23-year-old driver.

"Everyone here loves working with Carson, and we've enjoyed watching him thrive alongside our team," Dickerson explained. "Sometimes the right decision for someone you care about hurts in the short term. The way Carson conducted himself at Martinsville doesn't meet the standard we set for our drivers, team members, or employees, and there are consequences for that. That doesn't mean we don't love him and support him."

Dickerson finished his statement off with, "Racing at the Cup level is a privilege, and it comes with an expected level of professionalism from everyone who represents Spire Motorsports. We'll go to Homestead united and compete as an organization. After that, we can get ready for Daytona in February with the right mindset to contend for a championship."

Following the announcement of Hocevar's suspension, the driver of the No. 77 Chevrolet issued a statement of his own on what he calls an embarrassing day.

"This is an embarrassing day for me," Hocevar said. "I let the people down that gave me the opportunity of a lifetime to drive a Cup car. I also let down my team, sponsors, and fans. I crossed the line with my on-track actions and gave Jeff and Spire Motorsports no option but to put someone else in the 77 car this weekend at Homestead. I'll be rooting for the entire organization this weekend and look forward to coming back in 2027 as a better driver, competitor, and teammate."

Hocevar, who scored the first victory of his NASCAR Cup Series career earlier this season at Talladega Superspeedway, has reached career-best totals in every major statistical category this year. In addition to the one win, Hocevar has set career-highs in top-fives (6), top-10s (12), poles (2), laps led (198), average start (13.3), average finish (15.9), and by being locked into the top-16, he'll have his career-best points ranking (previous best was 21st in 2024).

Unfortunately, for Hocevar, he won't have a chance to add to those totals this weekend at Homestead. Fortunately, for Hocevar, this one-race absence will give him the opportunity to grow as a person and driver, and possibly prevent future suspensions.

#2820. Luka Dončić's offense is carrying Lakers. Is LA too dependent on its 'showman'?

LOS ANGELES — Luka Dončić earned a standing ovation from the Los Angeles Lakers fans before going on to beat the Miami Heat 138-117 at Crypto.com Arena on Monday, Nov. 2.

Dončić has beocme the early favorite for regular season MVP as the NBA's leader in scoring average (38.3) and 3-pointers made per game (5.9).

The Slovenian point guard is known for his offensive prowess and his ability to score. It's also what makes the Lakers a threat in the Western Conference.

He finished with 42 points, 13 assists and seven rebounds against the Heat on Nov. 2.

More: Heat defense under scrutiny after Lakers rout

Lakers coch JJ Redick praised Dončić's offensive dominance on several occasions in recent weeks, referring to him as a "showman" and a "supernova" while also comparing his rhythm on the court to a theatrical stage.

"He's just making tough shots; averaging 38 points is not easy in this league," Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo said. "He's making tough shots and you just tip your hat off to him."

The two-time scoring champion is averaging 29.3 points per game for his career, which places him third all-time behind Michael Jordan and Wilt Chamberlain. Both players averaged 30.1 ppg for their respective careers.

Dončić has propelled the Lakers to a fast start this season, and his play on Monday was no different. He scored 16 points as Los Angeles led Miami 37-30 in the first quarter.

Dončić is averaging 15 points in the opening quarter, and has scored at least 13 in all but one game this season.

When the six-time All-NBA player is hot, so are the Lakers.

The Lakers have outscored opponents by 113 points when Dončić is on the court during the seven games he's played this season, according to StatMuse.

When Dončić isn't on the floor, things can get tricky for Redick.

Los Angeles' bench nearly blew a 16-point lead with 1:43 left in the fourth quarter on Sunday against the Toronto Raptors.

The Raptors cut the Lakers' lead to make it a five-point game. Toronto scored 11 points in 40 seconds and forced Redick to put Dončić and Austin Reaves back into the game and help secure the victory.

On Monday, Dončić and the Lakers produced 111 points, the team's highest-scoring point total through three quarters this season. This time, the Lakers left very little room for mistakes and refused to give up the lead in the final frame.

Dončić's ability to score isn't the only benefit of having him on the court.

Even if Dončić had a low-scoring night, he will always remain a threat that will keep defenses focused on him. It does free up his teammates for opportunities, who can also benefit from his playmaking and his ability to draw a double team.

That was the case Monday, as the Heat applied double-team looks on Dončić.

"I think at the beginning of the season we didn't execute well with the double team, but today I think we improved a lot," Dončić said. "Everybody was in the right spots, so it's not just me.

"It's everybody, just to be in the right spot and being aggressive and shooting with confidence."

Lakers forward Ziaire Williams has been able to benefit from some of the open looks that come with sharing the floor with Dončić.

"Very easy looks," Williams said. "Way easier than they've been in the past. They're sending two (players) to Luka and two at (Reaves) every time."

Reaves has proven he can be a high-efficiency volume scorer, but he is less likely to thrive without Dončić on the court.

If Dončić were unavailable, opposing game plans would focus on Reaves and he would be challenged by teams' toughest defenders.

Beyond Reaves (23.1 ppg), the Lakers would have to rely on center Walker Kessler (14.3) as a third-scoring option.

Williams (11.3) and Collin Sexton (10.3) could also be options, but neither would be able to guarantee similar production to Dončić on a nightly basis.

#2819. Fabregas: ‘Como will face wild atmosphere in Lens, quality of Thauvin’

Cesc Fabregas warns Como that there will be a 'wild atmosphere' against RC Lens in the Champions League tomorrow and he is keeping a close eye on Florian Thauvin.

It kicks off at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis in Lens on Wednesday at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

The Lariani are in their first ever Champions League campaign and doing remarkably well, winning both home matches with four goals scored against RB Leipzig and Manchester United, but losing away to Feyenoord.

While RC Lens might not seem to be on paper as big as those sides, Fabregas warns they are not to be underestimated on home turf.

TURIN, ITALY – OCTOBER 27: Cesc Fabregas, Manager of Como 1907, celebrates after the Serie A match between Torino FC and Como 1907 at Stadio Olimpico Grande Torino on October 27, 2026 in Turin, Italy. (Photo by Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images)

"It's a wild atmosphere, I played here two or three times for Monaco, I love nights like this, because you can feel the passion even during the warm-up," Fabregas told Sky Sport Italia.

"It will be interesting and a marvellous experience for our players. We wanted these nights, so if you are not motivated to play these, then you're in the wrong job."

There is a familiar face to Italian football, as former Udinese man Florian Thauvin has flourished since his return to France.

"Thauvin is an incredible player, he was at Marseille, then we faced him for Udinese. He makes the difference, has huge quality, scores a lot of goals, so he is the reference point for this team, and we need to keep a close eye on him."

COMO, ITALY – SEPTEMBER 10: Cesc Fabregas, Manager of Como 1907, celebrates after the UEFA Champions League 2026/27 League Phase MD1 match between Como 1907 and RB Leipzig at Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on September 10, 2026 in Como, Italy. (Photo by Claudio Villa/Getty Images)

Como are perhaps no longer a surprise outfit at this stage, so what will their ambitions be if they win here tomorrow?

"We will try to win and then see what happens, but this season is a whole new experience for Como, our world is opening up. If we get a good result, then we'll see how to go into the final four games, but we have to keep taking it one game at a time," added Fabregas.

"There's no point thinking about what might happen, we just need to enjoy these nights."

NAPLES, ITALY – AUGUST 30: Cesc Fabregas, Manager of Como, reacts during the Serie A match between SSC Napoli and Como 1907 at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona on August 30, 2026 in Naples, Italy. (Photo by Francesco Pecoraro/Getty Images)

While Como would in the past need to score lots of goals to win fixtures, they seem to have found different ways of approaching tests now.

"We need to be able to handle different situations. We played 39 games the first season, 43 the second, this year it'll be at least 47-48, it might be over 50, so that means we need to balance out the energy.

"There are moments where we need to control the situation, because I remember last season we were great for the first 60 minutes and then fell away at the end. We cannot do that this term, so we're more alert about that."

COMO, ITALY – SEPTEMBER 10: Cesc Fabregas, Manager of Como 1907, celebrates after the UEFA Champions League 2026/27 League Phase MD1 match between Como 1907 and RB Leipzig at Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on September 10, 2026 in Como, Italy. (Photo by Claudio Villa/Getty Images)

Como also have a huge game coming up in Serie A against Inter this weekend, but they have limited players available, with Trevoh Chalobah, Moise Kean, Jesus Rodriguez, Assane Diao and Jayden Addai out of action.

"Chalobah isn't ready for this game, we'll see on Sunday. We are a little penalised in the Champions League because of the list, so we've got only 15 players tomorrow. That makes preserving energy tougher in this tournament, but Serie A remains the most important competition."

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died as a result of a freak accident during the Spanish second division match against FC Andorra, so Fabregas wanted to send a message.

"In such a wonderful sport as football, it is honestly hard to deal with things like this. I send my heart to his father and mother, I am a parent, and the idea of going to see your son playing in a match and life can end in a moment, it makes you think.

"It was a huge blow, I cannot imagine the pain they are feeling, so I send an embrace to his family, to his teammates who experienced that, it can never be forgotten."

#2817. 'It was all right': LeBron James takes a sip of fan's wine during Sixers' win over Bulls

Like many very rich people, 40-somethings and very rich 40-somethings, LeBron James loves himself some wine.

The all-time leading scorer in NBA history has long been nose-deep in the wine game, raising glasses with longtime pals-turned-oenophiles like Carmelo Anthony and Chris Paul for more than a decade. His Instagram posts about which wines he and his teammates were enjoying on any given night could drive consumption trends. He's appeared on the cover of Wine Enthusiast magazine; he once pulled up to a Los Angeles Lakers game with a glass of wine. When he and eventual Lakers head coach JJ Redick launched their basketball strategy podcast, "Mind the Game," every discussion of coverages and tactics was punctuated by no small number of swirls and sips; no less a source than r/wine has proclaimed the King "no wine slouch." (And Reddit would never steer you wrong.)

"I've heard it's good for the heart," James told ESPN's Baxter Holmes for a story on the NBA's "secret wine society" published in 2020. "Listen, I'm playing the best basketball of my life, and I'm drinking some wine pretty much every day. Whatever it is, I'll take it."

James isn't quite playing the best basketball of his life anymore, near the start of his 24th professional season and his first as a member of the Philadelphia 76ers. He's still pretty damn good, though, and he's still taking it, whatever it is … even if "it" is in a fan's cup during a game.

With the Sixers holding an 11-point lead on the visiting Chicago Bulls in Philadelphia on Monday night, James leaked out in transition after a missed 3-pointer by Bulls swingman Isaac Okoro. After corralling the long rebound, Philly point guard Tyrese Maxey looked up and tossed a hit-ahead pass for the streaking James … that was just a bit too ambitious for the about-to-be-42-year-old to haul in.

As the ball went out of bounds, so too did James. As he did, he bumped into a fan seated several rows back behind the Sixers' basket. Rather than sprinting back onto the floor to get back on defense, though, LeBron lingered for a moment — long enough, in fact, for the referees to prevent the Bulls from inbounding the ball without him, and for Maxey to run after his new teammate to get him back into the game.

Soon afterward, the replays showed us why. LeBron didn't just take a moment to say hi to a fan; he also took a little swig of what the fan was sipping on, too.

"LeBron crashed into me," the fan, Troy Clemons, told ESPN's Kris Rhim. "He grabbed me, he said, 'My bad.' My drink spilled everywhere. He took my drink from me, and he basically just took a sip of it, gave it back and ran back on the field."

"I wanted to see if it was worth it on my arm, how good it was," a smiling James said in the locker room after the game, according to Rhim. "It was all right."

This isn't the first time that James has considered engaging in a bit of mid-game imbibing with fans. Back in 2017, with his Cleveland Cavaliers holding a lead over the Toronto Raptors in the first game of the second round of the playoffs, James found himself frustrated after smoking a layup that would've given him a chance for a three-point play … and expressed his emotions by skipping over to a courtside vendor and grabbing a bottle of beer out of her hand:

That time, though, James didn't actually slug it down.

"Not much of a beer guy," he said at the time. "If she had had some red wine, I probably would have definitely took a sip."

LeBron James (right) is pretty clearly having a lot of fun in the early stages of his first season in Philadelphia. (AP/Chris Szagola)

Even with how expensive drinks are at arenas these days, Clemons didn't much mind the spill — or sharing a little bit of his spirit with Philly's newest superstar.

"I'm just glad for him to be here," Clemons said. "I'm not worried about the wine getting on me."

Nor, for that matter, were the 76ers too worried about the Bulls. Philly controlled the action for the bulk of the contest, leading by as many as 22 points in what ended as a 126-107 win. Maxey led all scorers with 26 points and 11 rebounds in the win, which improved the Sixers to 7-1, good for first place in the Eastern Conference — a strong, and very enjoyable, start to the voyage for this new-look superteam.

"Listen, it's a long marathon," James said after the game. "If you don't find ways to have fun throughout it — even though you're working, even though you're locked in — then it could wear on you. So for me, especially at this point in my career too, being able to just appreciate the moments, the small moments."

Clemons enjoyed the moment, too — although, somewhat shockingly, he didn't decide to commemorate it with what would've been a 1-of-1 collectible.

"At the end of the day he's another man like me," Clemons said, according to NBC Sports Philadelphia. "I mean, he's LeBron, but at the end of the day, I threw that cup in the trash. And it's nothing up with him — I just got a fresh drink, though."

Domestically, Udinese were seen off 5-2 at the weekend, with top scorer Donyell Malen again among the goals.

You have to go back to May of 2021, in the Europa League semi-finals. It finished 3-2 to Roma, with Edinson Cavani grabbing both of our goals.

United however, progressed through to the final by winning 8-5 on aggregate.

That was due to a brilliant 6-2 first-leg triumph at Old Trafford. Bruno Fernandes and Cavani both bagged braces but there were no fans there to see it due to Covid restrictions.

Everyone else, head on over to LiveSoccerTV to find your viewing options.

#2809. Knicks Bulletin: ‘It’s a matter of time in my opinion’

As everyone already knew before the game, the Knicks beat the Nets.

Here's the latest from the only people that play meaningful basketball in New York's five boroughs.

On the Knicks' bench performance against Brooklyn:

"Our bench was fantastic. I thought Landry came off and gave us a big lift on both ends of the floor. Jordan as well. And then Tyler — I thought Tyler's minutes were tremendous. He did a fantastic job running the team, getting us some easy looks, and then he was solid defensively."

On searching for a lineup combination to stop Brooklyn's momentum:

"When we went into a little funk was at the beginning of the second. Us not scoring gave [Brooklyn] a little hope because they were able to shrink that lead and tie it up, even take the lead. When you give a young team confidence, now it's hard to turn the water off … So I just started searching at that point and went to Tyler, went to Landry, tried JC, and then we found a group that caught a little groove and helped us take the lead back and create separation."

On Jordan Clarkson accepting a reduced role and being an exceptional teammate:

"You have a veteran that's been there, done that. and he's willing to accept the role that most guys wouldn't accept – even guys younger that haven't proved as much as he's proven in this league. And he's willing to accept it. So, in my opinion, if he's willing to accept it, which is what he did last year, and still try to uplift everybody, connect everybody while he's going through what he's going through, then everybody else should. That's that's the ultimate team player, I will say this about JC. I've been around some good teammates. He's got to be the best. He is the definition of ultimate pro."

"A lot of (his minutes) are based on the feel."

On Mikal Bridges' early-season struggles and what he needs to do to regain his form:

"Yeah, he's just got to keep playing. Everybody goes through those ups and downs throughout the course of the season, and obviously, it's the beginning of the season right now, so he's got to find his way. Not just with him but with everybody, when you're in a funk you gotta find one or two things to hold your hat on. Mikal is one of the best runners in the NBA.

"In both directions – offensively and defensively. So he's just got to try to hang his hat on that as well as his cutting and trying to do the other little things – rebounding and driving and touching the paint and spraying it. Then this shot will come eventually."

On his confidence that Bridges will eventually rediscover his shooting touch:

"It's a matter of time in my opinion, before Mikal gets going."

On not penalizing players, including Alavarado, for missing games because of injuries:

"I try not to take a guy out [of his rotation spot] due to injury and the reality is Jose got hurt."

On his conversation with Jose Alvarado and Tyler Kolek about the backup point guard rotation:

"Jose got hurt, and Tyler gave us some good minutes. But at the end of the day, I sat them both down and I told them, 'Hey, Jose, you're our backup because you ended the season as our backup.'

"Both you guys helped us win last year. Jose in the finals, and Tyler in the Cup final. Both you guys got to be ready because a change can happen anytime."

On Karl-Anthony Towns' increased playmaking responsibilities and turnovers:

"KAT's touches are going up, but his turnovers have gone up. KAT is a load making plays with the basketball. He's just gotta finish the play. And not get it deflected or turn it over."

On the Knicks attempting too many risky passes and Towns' offensive fouls:

"Obviously, they have to do better [with the turnovers] and we talked about it. We will continue to talk about it. We've tried to make the home run pass. That's happened a few times. And obviously some turnovers from KAT are offensive fouls. He's got to be better in that area. But for the most part, we have to keep trying to hit singles as opposed to triples and home runs."

On preferring dead-ball turnovers to mistakes that lead to fast breaks:

"Obviously, you don't want your opponent to have the opportunity to get out on the break, so if it's a situation where we have a chance to get back or the ball is dead, I'd prefer that. We've had some turnovers, like [with] Philly in the first half, it felt like we paid the price for it. So to try to just control that a little better at times will help us. But we'd rather have our defense set up than not."

On making better use of his increased touches and playmaking responsibilities:

"I just care about wins. So I gotta do better, making sure with that time [holding onto the ball] and translating it to more wins."

On the need for keeping the Knicks' offense moving:

"I think we just all gotta be together, figure it out. Things just can't get stagnant, and just gotta keep moving."

On Jordan Clarkson accepting a smaller role to help the Knicks win:

"I think it shows his character more than anything else. He's someone that if he was on a different team, he could play 20, 25 minutes every night. He could score double digits. He could be that spark, that microwave off the bench. And he's here. He was willing to sacrifice and take a smaller role, be a part of something bigger than himself. So it shows its character.

"It shows his professionalism. To be able to go out and do those things. And when he's not doing it, he's out there coaching, not on the court, he's coaching guys up, talking to them, letting them know what he sees. So he's the ultimate professional. He's someone that you want on your team. And whenever he's given an opportunity, he'll go out and play well."

On the Knicks finally increasing their pace in the fourth quarter against Brooklyn:

"We finally played fast, got stops. We've been playing very slow, very stagnant. We finally got out, we ran and we got good looks."

On why the Knicks' strong fourth quarter against Brooklyn did not erase their earlier problems:

"No. No, the issues are still there. That [fourth quarter] doesn't erase the problem or erase the issue. So you gotta figure that out and get better."

On the Knicks' offensive struggles persisting despite their victory over the Nets:

"The issues are still there. I think defensively, we were solid. I think this year, for the most part, our defense has been pretty good. Obviously there have been some lapses. … But our offense has to get in a better flow, and that's kind of what's holding us back right now. So a win doesn't erase the problem or erase the issues. We got to figure those out and get better."

On the contributions of the Knicks' reserves against Brooklyn:

"We talked about [Clarkson] earlier, Landry (Shamet), I mean, he had big threes. That third quarter kept us in it. Jose (Alvarado) played well. Ty (Kolek) played well. [Andre Drummond], I think he had to win like nine rebounds, ten rebounds in, like, 11 or 12 minutes. It shows you the depth that we have, that it could be anybody's night on any given night."

On Mike Brown's confidence in him and his willingness to use different players:

"I think it shows his (Brown's) confidence in me. I think he has confidence in every game on the roster. As he's shown, he'll throw any guy in at any time, to do the spark."

On Mike Brown's willingness to confront the Knicks' problems directly:

"We have to be real with ourselves, and Mike's great with that, assessing things in film, calls it as it is. Our group's great with that. We all understand that by no means — we're not taking this as any potential fool's gold. Like I said, the whole goal right now is to continue to get better, and we want to do that. So that's the thought process."

On his early experiences playing against Jordan Clarkson:

"When I was younger, my only thought of him was that he was really hard to guard and it felt like he always went at me. I used to hate it. He'd score and talk a little s—."

On Clarkson's team-first attitude and willingness to accept substitutions:

"Knowing him now, knowing who he is, it's not crazy. The guy just wants to win. He wants to do whatever he can for this group, his teammates. He'll play a stint out there for two minutes and get subbed out. A lot of guys in the NBA, the reality is, if they get subbed, they're pissed. The whole thing. He never has any of those moments."

On the physical toll of the Knicks' championship run:

"We definitely played until June last season and I think everyone still feels it."

"When I got to Utah, I was trying to think of a number. The only player I remembered as a kid who played for the Jazz (whose number wasn't retired) was Greg Ostertag. So, when I got to New York, I kept it."

#2807. Bengals travel plans for game vs. Falcons in Madrid

The Cincinnati Bengals have some interesting travel plans this week.

Zac Taylor's Bengals will grab a flight overseas for next Sunday's game in Madrid, Spain, after practice on Tuesday.

That means an off day Wednesday for the Bengals, then practice Thursday and Friday at the Spanish National Team Training Facility.

"The week shapes up different," Taylor said, according to Joe Reedy of the Associated Press. "It speeds up the coaches a bit so that the comfort of being here in our office is different than on the road. As much as you can get done here before you get on the plane, you'd prefer to do that. Clean things up as you go. You treat it like a six-day week."

So, expect to see plenty of updates from the team and players post-practice on Tuesday and as they journey to Madrid. Maybe plenty from an off day on Wednesday, too.

The goal, of course, is to get the players overseas and acclimated to a normal lifestyle there as quickly as possible before they play the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday (9:30 a.m. ET kickoff time).

This article originally appeared on Bengals Wire: Bengals travel plans for game vs. Falcons in Madrid

Former Florida State Seminoles shortstop Taylor Walls is putting together quite the start to his offseason.

Less than 24 hours after earning the first Gold Glove Award of his major-league career, Walls received another vote of confidence from the Tampa Bay Rays. The organization exercised his $3.1 million club option for the 2027 season, ensuring the former Seminole will remain in Tampa Bay for at least another year.

The timing was fitting. Walls has built much of his major-league reputation on elite defense, and the Gold Glove finally rewarded him after previous finalist appearances. Tampa Bay's decision to keep him around a day later further reinforced the value the Rays place on what he provides at shortstop.

The 30-year-old also produced his best offensive season in several years, batting .222 with a .309 on-base percentage, two home runs, 36 RBIs and 21 stolen bases across 433 plate appearances. He helped Tampa Bay reach the World Series while establishing a career high in wins above replacement.

Before reaching the majors, Walls spent three seasons at Florida State from 2015-17. He started 196 games for the Seminoles, finished his career with a .284 batting average, and helped FSU reach the 2017 College World Series before Tampa Bay selected him in the third round of that year's MLB Draft. Walls was also a first-team All-American as a sophomore in 2016.

Walls has been with the Rays since making his MLB debut in 2021. Now, fresh off the biggest individual honor of his professional career, Tampa Bay has ensured the former Seminole will remain part of its plans for at least one more season.

#2796. Jeffery Simmons: Felt great to get my first sack as a Chicago Bear

It didn’t take long for Jeffery Simmons to get his first sack as a Bear.

Simmons took Sam Darnold down on the Seahawks’ fourth offensive play on Monday night, and he said afterward that as soon as he saw that they were blocking him one-on-one, he knew a big play was coming.

“If you block me one-on-one, I need to win the one-on-one. If I don’t win a one-on-one, the coaches should be on me. I hold myself to a high standard,” Simmons said. “It felt great to get my first sack as a Chicago Bear in my first game.”

Simmons always drew a lot of double teams during his All-Pro seasons with the Titans, and he drew plenty on Monday night in his first game since the Titans traded him to the Bears as well. He said he challenged his fellow Bears defensive linemen to take advantage of it when he was getting double teamed.

“If I’m getting a double team, I expect them to win their single block,” Simmons said. “We don’t need to blitz. I feel like if we can win at the line of scrimmage without the blitzes, that makes the guys’ jobs on the back end that much easier.”

Simmons played 55 defensive snaps, by far the most of any Bear in the game. He played 87 percent of the Bears’ defensive plays, which was exactly his snap count percentage for the Titans this season before he was traded. The Bears made a big investment in Simmons, trading two first-round draft picks for him, and they got a big return immediately.

In the moments before kickoff, Simmons said he was trying to keep his emotions in check by reminding himself, “It’s just football.” But it was hard not to be emotional.

“The emotions, especially during the national anthem, the emotions were coming and coming,” Simmons said.

Simmons said after the game that it means a lot to him to be playing meaningful football. The Titans are 1-7 and the Bears are 6-2 and Simmons knows the blockbuster trade was an opportunity for him to compete for a Super Bowl.

#2794. 2 injured All-NBA teammates invoke Shai Gilgeous-Alexander to go full '05/06' Kobe mode

Huffing and puffing for air, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander was absolutely exhausted. The usually-stoic NBA superstar provided the world a glimpse of the workload he'll have to shoulder for the next two months. This is the new grim reality that the Oklahoma City Thunder are living in.

Gilgeous-Alexander absolutely carried the Thunder to a 117-102 win over the Cleveland Cavaliers. He finished with 43 points on 14-of-35 shooting. That included an eye-popping 13 shot attempts in the fourth quarter as he carried them across the finish line for the much-needed morale boost.

It wasn't pretty and the selfish style of basketball goes against Gilgeous-Alexander's nature of playing within the flow of the offense, but the Thunder are in a dire situation. As most know by now, they're going to be without three of their four best players for the foreseeable future.

The Thunder became the first NBA team in 50 years to lose three starters on the same night for 20-plus games in a row. A costly win over the LA Clippers on Oct 25 has completely junked up their championship ambitions. Now, it's about pure survival mode.

Jalen Williams is out for most — if not all — of the 2026-27 season with a fractured fibula and a dislocated ankle. Same for Cason Wallace with a torn labrum. Both required surgery. Chet Holmgren also sustained a torn patellar tendon. He's out for two-plus months and opted for a biological treatment to return sooner.

Considering the circumstances, the Thunder are scrambling to salvage the 2026-27 season. Punting a couple of games due to shock, they've reached the acceptance stage of their grief. It looks like OKC has made the conscious decision to fully lean on Gilgeous-Alexander's scoring superpowers until help arrives.

Count Holmgren and Williams as two supporters of OKC's desperate, but just, new strategy. Gilgeous-Alexander left it all on the floor in Cleveland. His 35 shot attempts were a career high. Expect more video-game-esque numbers like that until New Year's arrives and OKC is gifted one of its All-NBA talents back.

Holmgren wrote on his Instagram story: "Dump that clip 2. Reload and dump it again." Williams expressed a similar message in his social media story by simply saying: "05/06." — referring to Kobe Bryant's legendary season that year where he averaged 35.4 points on 27 shot attempts a night.

I guess we'll see if Gilgeous-Alexander can handle the Herculean workload for the next two months. It's not something the Thunder want to do — the plan before D.C.C. (Dub, Chet, Caso) happened was to phase in an off-ball role to save his legs for the NBA playoffs — but now, it's a necessity for pure survival mode.

Entering Monday's game with a better mindset, Gilgeous-Alexander left it all on the floor. Let's see if he can do it again on Wednesday against Cleveland, and then on Friday against Memphis, and then so forth and so on until Holmgren and Alex Caruso provide some help.

#2793. Mike Macdonald: We lost in all three phases

Monday night’s game in Seattle featured a pair of 2025 NFC playoff teams who would like to be back in the postseason this year and it ended with the Bears celebrating a 34-17 win over the defending Super Bowl champions.

The Seahawks had made it a three-point game early in the fourth quarter, but a 39-yard screen pass to Kalif Raymond converted a key Bears third down on the next drive and the roof caved in on the Seahawks from there. The Bears ended the night with 111 more offensive yards than the Seahawks and their defense thwarted Seattle on 10 of their 11 third down attempts over the course of the night, which led Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald to say after the game that “there’s no other way to sugarcoat” the way his team got beat.

Seahawks kicker Jason Myers missed an extra point and had a field goal blocked and the Seahawks committed several personal fouls to add to their woes on a night when the Bears were clearly better across the board.

“They made it happen, and we didn’t,” Macdonald said, via the team’s website. “It’s a team effort; we lost as a team. The Seahawks overwhelmed the Chiefs in a Week 7 win, but Monday night was the kind of step back that explains why they’re 4-4 on the season. Having it happen against another NFC contender at home makes the blow more painful and Macdonald said the Seahawks “have some work to do” if they’re going to position themselves for another run at the end of this season.

#2789. 5 Reasons For The Jazz To Consider A Lauri Markkanen/Domantas Sabonis Swap

The Jazz have been disappointing to start the year, and you know what that means; it is time to completely alter the foundation of the team, purely for the sake of it. Will Trade A or Trade B actually make the team better? No one can say, but nevertheless, they must be completed – SOMETHING must be done, anything!

There are the obvious, small-potatoes that Jazz fans are proposing. Kris Dunn would be nice; he would immediately be our only positive defender who can also dribble and pass. Tre Jones, maybe? He can run a clean offense off of the bench. Maybe we give Nikola Topic a shot! I wonder if there's a reason our minds are all immediately going to back-up point guard options.

However, one report (potentially not based in reality) out of Sacramento really got people thinking:

(EDITORS NOTE: Since writing, this report has gained a bit more credibility, via Tim McMahon)

Before I elucidate the 5 reasons I think a trade for Domantas Sabonis makes basketball-sense, let me give the lay of the land:

The trade that I am defending is a one-for-one Lauri Markkanen and Domantas Sabonis swap, which works financially.

I do not know who has more value. Markkanen's contract is longer, but seemingly more desired across the league. Thus, due to my confusion, I am assuming no picks are exchanged.

Maybe this is a three-team trade, with Markkanen sent elsewhere. That doesn't impact my thinking in this article. I do not care where Markkanen lands, and am operating under the assumption that this deal nets us Sabonis and costs us Markkanen.

With that in mind, please indulge me as I arrogantly, ignorantly, and prematurely attempt to fix the Utah Jazz.

Will Hardy loves his top-of-the-key, dribble-handoff offenses. He gave Kelly Olynyk his last strong full season showing, he got lots of run out of Kyle Anderson, and he built an entire offense around Jusuf Nurkic after premature claims that Father Time had conquered the Bosnian Beast. A big man at the top of the key and 4 swarming, cutting teammates is Hardy's idea of a good time. I mean, look at how every set from Nurkic's 3rd triple double of last year was organized:

Jusuf has still yet to play a game in the 2026-2027 season as he deals with injury, and his absence is obvious. Hardy has attempted to run some of the sets with Jaxson Hayes, but Hayes simply doesn't have the feathery touch or sense of timing that makes Nurkic so deadly from these spots. Because of this, the offense has stalled. The Jazz are last in the league in rim attempts per game, and in the bottom 10 in three point attempts. These are the shots that get prioritized in offenses built off of ball movement and motion, but with Nurkic out, many possessions end with Keyonte George or Isaiah Collier dribbling for 18 seconds before taking a contested mid-range jump shot.

Domantas Sabonis was born for the Will Hardy offense. In 2023, the Kings had the best offense in the association, and it was built almost entirely on the back of Domantas Sabonis and his top-of-the-key decision making. He is, indisputably, the 2nd best big-man passer in the league, and around the top when it comes to screen-setting as well. Hardy has turned players that the league had given up on into the centerpieces of offenses, and Sabonis, being a player still in the thick of his prime, would actualize Hardy's offensive dreams to an extent not yet before seen. Sabonis would potentially average a triple double on this team, and the offense would have a structure in a way that has been heretofore, absent.

When Sabonis is being derided, it is fairly easy to anticipate the reasoning of the deriders. He isn't a vertical, shot-blocking presence around the rim. He isn't the quickest when switched out onto the perimeter. And he isn't necessarily the most intimidating shooting threat. Domantas Sabonis, for all his skills, is a known commodity – what he can't do now, he likely won't be able to do later.

Similarly, people seem to generally understand what Jaren Jackson Jr. struggles with. He struggles as a rebounder and with physicality in general, and thus isn't really cut out to play consistent center minutes. He often falls victim to tunnel vision, and seems to have made the decision to pass or shoot before he begins his offensive process. On paper, Jaren seems like the versatile big man option that every contender craves, but once you peel back some of the layers, you can see that he quite dependent on a context that caters to his flaws.

I struggle to think of a more synergistic front court pairing than these two.

JJJ can struggle on the boards as much as he wants, and the Jazz would still be carried to a respectable mark by 3 time rebounding champion Domantas Sabonis. There's a limit to the level of defense Jaren can anchor on his own due to his poor rebounding, but Sabonis, who is not a good individual defender, would boost Jaren by, at the very least, consistently being able to end plays with rebounds. Domantas can continue to struggle blocking shots (his highest per-game mark is 0.6), but as long as he can be large down low, he allows Jaren Jackson Jr. to play to his strengths as a help-side roamer. Jaren provides spacing for Domantas to both hit cutters up top and bang down low, and Sabonis can set the bruising screens that Jaren never really could. Together, these two former all-stars can amplify strengths and mitigate weaknesses. We would not just be trading for Domantas Sabonis; in this deal would be included a superior version of JJJ.

I hope to make one thing clear; I am not a Lauri Markkanen "hater". In fact, I have strongly advocated for keeping him throughout the rebuild, and my opinion of him has not really changed after his slow start to the year (although I do have a theory that his transformation into a body builder has hurt his flexibility and, in turn, his impact). Today, Markkanen is still an all-world level off-ball shooter and scorer who, in most contexts, can add to a team's attack without taking anything away. However, I am beginning to wonder that Utah is not one of those contexts. This team is facing a severe drought of dribblers and passers – everyone is attempting to do their work off-ball. Without players with gravity to work off of, Lauri Markkanen is taken out of his ideal role.

Normally, I wouldn't mind this too much. Even playing out-of-role, Markkanen is still clearly a positive offensive player. However, with the rapid development of Ace Bailey, one must now consider the opportunity cost of every Lauri Markkanen minute played and action ran. This season, Ace has made huge strides defensively (making him an even better fit next to a guy like Sabonis), and has continued to improve his efficiency in all the same sets that Hardy runs for Markkanen. Both are big forwards who move and shoot like smaller, quicker players, but who aren't necessarily the most capable creating their own shot. Considering that (a) Markkanen is significantly more expensive and (b) he is significantly older, it has been clear to me that, eventually, he would be the odd-man out and the first of the core to be traded. With Ace taking a leap and Jaren filling the other forward possession, now is as good a time as any to start looking into Markkanen trades (although I would feel a twinge of guilt if he did spend the heart of his prime in Utah, waiting for a playoff run, and then we trade him to Sacramento). If that trade can net a former all-star who is a perfect fit in Hardy's offense, that should cause some real consideration on the part of the Jazz brass.

As discussed in Reason #1, the Jazz are currently outlierishly bad at interior scoring, making 5 less shots in the paint per game compared to the #29 team in that stat. Sabonis will help in one aforementioned regard; his top-of-the-key passing will open up rim attempts for cutters. However, that isn't the only mechanism Sabonis will utilize to put consistent pressure on the paint; he himself would be the most intimidating rim presence on the roster. Sabonis consistently shoots near half of his shots within 3 feet of the basket, and shoots those shots at a career 72% clip. Many of these shots are assisted, but not all of them – Sabonis has shown the ability to post-up on his own and collapse the defense. Even the assisted shots from Domantas have more value than any of the same plays from the current interior players the Jazz employ. Sabonis has a combination of fluidity, strength, and touch that no one of the team can match, which makes him a more intimidating presence rolling to the rim than any of Hayes, Markkanen, Bamba, or whoever. Currently, the Jazz attack is centered entirely from the outside – rim attempts feel more lucky than strategic. An inside-out attack would strain opposing defenses in a way the current roster simply cannot.

I hope my sarcasm was evident in that subheading. In reality, I have 4 reasons and an anti-reason. I think each of the prior 4 are strong enough on their own, but they also operate under a base assumption that might not be true: that something must be done. In doing so, they disregard the most likely scenario. To me, that scenario still is that the Jazz are not a bad team. Maybe they're not the level of a 6 seed, as I saw some hoping, but likely they are closer to the average projection of quality than how they are currently performing. Would it be nice for the Jazz to have performed better than they have? Sure, but in that same vein, it would be nice if Jaren Jackson Jr. did not immediately get injured. I would be nice if we could see Jusuf Nurkic hitting cutters like he did last season. It would be nice if we weren't missing a disproportionate amount of our three pointers. Yes, it would be nice if we were winning, but this losing is not something that we can yet draw meaningful data from.

So, a proposition; let us continue to watch the games with caution, and a critical eye, but with a mind not yet predisposed to make changes at the first sign of trouble. Make careful notes of where the team is struggling, and pay close attention to how those areas develop throughout the remainder of the season, and even keep potential trade targets in your mind, but to this point? There is limited need for any of these changes to be made reality. This team has disappointed me too, Lauri Markkanen included, but I think it is important to maintain a sense of confidence in the player evaluations we have crafted for years, instead of tossing them out the window and calling the Kings at the first sign of trouble. Sabonis would be a good fit on this roster, but he'd be a good fit at the February trade deadline too; at this point, there should be no rush for transactions.

What are your thoughts on Sabonis's fit on the team? Markkanen's? When is the right time to start discussing trades? Sound off below!

#2785. Carson Hocevar Suspended for NASCAR Season Finale After Martinsville Controversy

Carson Hocevar's NASCAR season is ending one race early.

Spire Motorsports has suspended the 23-year-old driver for Sunday's Cup Series season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway following his controversial run-in with Austin Cindric at Martinsville Speedway.

The decision, reported Tuesday by The Athletic, means Hocevar will not compete in the final race of the 2026 season. Justin Haley will take over the No. 77 Chevrolet at Homestead.

The punishment is particularly significant because it came from Hocevar's own team, rather than NASCAR. The sanctioning body could still impose additional penalties.

The trouble began during Sunday's Xfinity 500 at Martinsville, where Hocevar and Cindric were battling for position just past the 200-lap mark.

Hocevar repeatedly slowed in front of Cindric, leaving the Team Penske driver with little room to avoid contact. Cindric struck the back of Hocevar's Chevrolet multiple times, sustaining substantial damage to the front of his No. 2 Ford.

Cindric eventually retired from the race and finished 36th. Hocevar continued and finished 21st.

"At some point, I mean, NASCAR, what are we doing?" he said. "Like, we're just weaponizing cars here. I stack on entry with the guy and he has a mental breakdown."

Hocevar offered a considerably different assessment afterward.

"No, I don't know, I got lost there for a second," he told NBC when initially asked about the incident.

When pressed about whether his actions were intentional, Hocevar denied deliberately targeting Cindric and characterized the contact as typical Martinsville racing.

"I just think that's just Martinsville and I think we were just having fun," he said.

That explanation did little to quiet the controversy. Two days later, Spire made the decision to keep Hocevar out of its car for the season finale.

Haley will step into the No. 77 Chevrolet for Sunday's race, giving Spire a replacement with extensive Cup Series experience.

The suspension also adds another chapter to Hocevar's complicated season. His aggressive driving has drawn criticism from competitors, and the Martinsville race brought renewed scrutiny after another incident in which he spun while battling near the front of the field. Hocevar denied spinning intentionally.

Spire has disciplined Hocevar before, including a suspension and fine in 2025 following inappropriate comments about Mexico City.

This time, however, the consequences extend directly to the racetrack.

Rather than closing out the season behind the wheel, Hocevar will watch another driver compete in his Chevrolet. Whether NASCAR adds its own punishment remains to be seen.

#2784. The Dallas Mavericks need to grow up

The NBA regular season is filled with numerous peaks and valley's. 4 game winning streaks can become 6-game losing skids, dominant wins can be followed by embarrassing losses.

You will find no better example of this phenomenon than the Dallas Mavericks in their two-game stretch against the Houston Rockets and Sacramento Kings. The Rockets game was an announcement to the rest of the NBA.

Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Iriving have brought the Mavericks back, and they will no longer be a punchline in NBA culture.

Losing to the Kings by 15 points is a reminder that this team won 26 games in the 2026-2027 season, and that their superstar is still only 19-years-old.

The feeling among the fanbase was already negative hours before tip-off when the Mavericks ruled Irving out with left-knee injury management. This left many (myself included) very confused, seeing as the Mavericks had not played since Friday.

But Irving's absence is not the reason for their performance, nor should it excuse the frankly embarrassing effort the Mavericks showcased Monday night. Flagg had, in my estimation, the worst game of his NBA career, shooting 3-19 from the field with 6 turnovers. But the stats don't illuminate just how poor Flagg was. He was lazy in transition, didn't show any interest in boxing out, and struggled to generate any advantages for his teammates.

Flagg was not alone in his lack of intensity, as the rest of the Mavericks roster (save for Walter Clayton Jr. and Morez Johnson Jr.) played like they had forgotten what a three-pointer was. The Mavericks shot 7-33 from three, and were 3-28 outside of Clayton Jr.'s shooting. They struggled to execute any sort of offensive set, nor could they effectively space the floor at any point. The Kings, of all teams, exposed many of the flaws this team possesses, all of which were amplified by the lack of Irving.

But the players weren't the only ones at fault.

For the first time this season, Dusty May showed that he is a first-time NBA coach. The starting lineup was a baffling decision. Starting Flagg alongside no other ball-handlers or shooters is a proven terrible strategy, and yet, May fell into the same trap that Jason Kidd fell into last season. Flagg is simply much better when he can play off of another ball handler, and not when he is next to Caleb Martin and P.J. Washington.

Losing games like this is reminiscent of last year's team, which triggers dark memories for all Mavericks fans.

Now, this game could simply be a mirage. An off-night where your best player simply played terrible. But the Mavericks have to break their bad habits of years previous. These losses are unacceptable for a team that should have playoff aspirations. And this isn't simply a one-year focus point. Good habits are the things that lead to championships in the future, and those good habits need to be built as early as possible.

Hopefully the Mavericks use this game as a learning experience, because if they don't, the season could turn ugly before the blink of an eye.

#2782. The Vikings should explore a trade for Daniel Jones

At a time when the Vikings are believed to be talking to the Colts about a potential trade for running back Jonathan Taylor, they should adjust their focal point, just a bit.

The Vikings should be talking to the Colts about a potential trade for quarterback Daniel Jones.

When the thought first popped into my somewhat relaxed brain on Sunday, I was mostly kidding. After reflecting on Sunday’s 19-15 loss to the Lions — and revisiting the rare displays of frustration from receiver Justin Jefferson late in the game and, even more significantly, from coach Kevin O’Connell when talking to quarterback Kyler Murray after an ugly interception late in the first half — it’s not a joke.

They should immediately pivot from Taylor to Jones.

The Vikings had Jones in the building two years ago, after he was released by the Giants. They wanted to keep him for 2025, more (by all appearances) than they wanted to keep Sam Darnold. (Indeed, there were whispers of a potential benching of Darnold for Jones in the 2024 postseason.)

Now that the Colts are in full-blown pre-rebuild mode, trading Jones should be part of the effort to clear the decks (and stockpile picks) for the next G.M. And while the Colts have a window to avoid more than $10 million of Jones’s $38 million compensation package for 2027 via a trade in the early days of the new league year in March, they could get more now from a contender that envisions Jones as an immediate upgrade.

Jones obviously won’t be the long-term answer in Indianapolis. And he would undoubtedly welcome the chance to move on from a team that prematurely threw in the towel last week by trading guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.

In Minnesota, Jones would be an immediate upgrade over Kyler Murray. The difference between Jones vs. Murray could be more significant than the difference between Jonathan Taylor and Aaron Jones/Jordan Mason. Which, if accurate, would result in a bigger overall bump to the offense.

The Vikings have a championship-caliber defense, thanks in large part to the work of defensive coordinator Brian Flores. The grind-it-out-and-get-a-win formula had been working — until it didn’t.

Here’s the inescapable reality. When they win with quarterback play that is inconsistent and, in turn, frustrating to people like Jefferson and O’Connell, it’s easy to overlook the flaws and keep pushing forward. When they lose, the frustrations of that moment become compounded by the lingering frustrations regarding plays and points left on the field in the wins that were salvaged by the defense.

Whether it’s Jones or someone else (including a possible pivot to Carson Wentz), O’Connell and G.M. Nolan Teasley need to conduct a frank, candid, and objective assessment of the quarterback play under Murray. The fact that they picked Murray over J.J. McCarthy shouldn’t be a factor. That’s the kind of pride/ego consideration that keeps dysfunctional teams dysfunctional by doubling down on a mistake instead of admitting it and moving on.

The Vikings need to realize that: (1) the defense is great; (2) the running game is good enough; and (3) the passing game is too spotty to be expected to make a big play in a big spot.

Consider the decision that O’Connell made with 3:01 to play on Sunday, when the Vikings faced fourth and five from their own 33. Down four points after the Detroit running game had hot-knife-through-buttered their way to the go-ahead touchdown, why give the ball back to the Lions and let them close out the game by continuing to lean on Jahmyr Gibbs?

In that moment, O’Connell thought the chances of winning were enhanced by punting — not by asking the offense to gain five yards in a gotta-have-it situation.

While the choice showed unwarranted confidence in the defense, it showed NO confidence in the quarterback.

Frankly, that one specific decision from O’Connell leads naturally to the next, more consequential decision that the organization must make. If O’Connell doesn’t trust the offense under Murray to gain five yards with the game on the line, the Vikings should no longer entrust the offense to Murray.

It’s that simple. And, if the Vikings hope to avoid an outcome to the season that will result in an every-other-year playoff appearance and another one-and-done postseason, they’ll make the decision that someone other than Murray should be playing quarterback.

At a time when politics have become a major national focal point, this would be a so-called 80-20 issue among Vikings fans. They’ve seen the “just good enough is just good enough” movie for decades. With the defense the Vikings currently have, the offense needs more. If they’re serious about having a snowball’s chance in San Diego to get back to the Super Bowl for the first time in 50 years, they’ll send Kyler to Belize and make a play for Jones.

Or someone else. See if the Raiders are willing to part with Kirk Cousins (they shouldn’t be, but why not make the call?) Call the Chargers about Justin Herbert. Scour every depth chart and start doing the due diligence.

When Cousins suffered a season-ending torn Achilles tendon just before the trade deadline in 2023, the Vikings mobilized instantly to find a replacement. Based on the full body of work from Murray to date in 2026, they should be doing the same thing now — if they want to parlay their 6-0 start into the best possible finish.
