#2778. Which offseason narratives were wrong (and right) about the Sixers

It hasn't always been pretty, but nearly two weeks into the season, the Sixers have the best record in the Eastern Conference at 7-1. They've already toppled three other East title hopefuls in the New York Knicks (twice!), Cleveland Cavaliers and Indiana Pacers, although the Pacers were without both Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring) and Ivica Zubac (ankle), which takes some of the shine off that win.

There's still plenty of meat left on the bone for the Sixers, who are nowhere close to a finished product yet. But they easily could have been below .500 right now, which would have inevitably led to questions about Nick Nurse's job security and whether they would be the next would-be superteam that went up in smoke.

Given the scope of the Sixers' roster changes this past offseason, plenty of people had plenty of questions about them coming into the year. Some of them have proven valid. Others looked hilariously off base in real time and have proven to be exactly that. (The local media has a far better batting percentage than the national media in that regard.)

Let's go through which offseason Sixers takes are aging like spoiled milk and which are proving to be hauntingly prescient.

What do you get when you combine two former MVPs, four former All-NBA selections and a high-upside, second-year high-lottery pick in your starting lineup? Would they form a cohesive unit, or would they devolve into the "your-turn, my-turn" style of play that's common when stars link up?

The offense is still very much a work in progress, especially in the half court, but sharing the ball has not been a problem thus far. The Sixers are just outside of the top 10 leaguewide in total passes made per game, and all four of LeBron James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown are averaging at least four assists per game.

As it turns out, putting together a team of extremely talented, high-IQ basketball players is actually a good idea. Who knew?

Given their collection of high-end talent, the Sixers figured to be elite offensively. One of the main questions about them coming into the season was what they'd look like on the other end of the floor.

Hilariously, they've been far better on defense than on offense thus far.

With the usual small-sample-size caveat at this time of year, the Sixers currently have the NBA's third-best defensive rating. When they aren't turning the ball over and allowing easy runouts, they've shown far more cohesion in half-court settings than expected this early in the year.

After the season-opening win over the Knicks, Embiid told reporters that he's hoping to earn an All-Defense nod this season, because playing defense at that level "changes everything" for our team. Brown said "defense is what we're going to have to continue to hang our hat on," and it's "non-negotiable."

The Sixers figured to have a high defensive ceiling in the playoffs once they were exerting maximum effort and had individually tailored, opponent-specific game plans. The regular season was the bigger question. So far, they're acing that test.

Joe Vardon of The Athletic asked that question to Brown on media day—and promptly got shut down—but he was hardly the only one who was curious about that. After all, the Sixers were importing two strong personalities into their core, both of whom have been the best player on their respective teams before.

After the first two weeks, there's little question who the Sixers' alpha is, though. It's Tyrese Maxey.

Because the Sixers' starting five is so stacked, the have the luxury of mismatch-hunting whenever one of their starters has a clear matchup advantage. But against the Pacers last Wednesday, the Sixers' entire late-game offense effectively boiled down to "Tyrese, make something happen." The same goes for their shorthanded win over the Charlotte Hornets on Halloween, when Maxey erupted for a season-high 38 points.

Back in training camp, Brown talked about how Maxey took it upon himself to welcome the newcomers and help them acclimate. He's clearly taken the leadership mantle upon himself both on and off the floor, and the rest of the Sixers appear content to let him roll with it.

With that said, should we start a nightly Alpha Tracker just in case?

Shout-out to Draymond Green for this galaxy-brained take.

"If I'm VJ Edgecombe's agent, I'm not sure I'm happy with the summer that the 76ers have had," Green said on his podcast this offseason. "If I'm just VJ Edgecombe's agent, because this could affect a lot for VJ Edgecombe. Like you go from being sometimes the second option when Embiid was out to sometimes being the fifth option. It's a big, big, big difference. I don't know if y'all understand how big of a difference that is."

Edgecombe's production has dipped relative to his rookie year—he's averaging only 12.7 points, 7.1 rebounds and 3.0 assists per game thus far—but that hardly means his development is being stunted by his new superstar teammates. Look no further than his 17-point, 13-rebound game against the Milwaukee Bucks or his 11-point, seven-rebound, six-assist outing against the Cavaliers.

Edgecombe might not put up monster stats this year, but his willingness to play whatever role the Sixers ask of him and play it well should only further endear him to his teammates and coaching staff. That's the type of player who you want—and should pay to have—in your locker room.

Even before Ariel Hukporti went down with a torn Achilles in the Sixers' preseason opener, backup center looked like a potential weak spot. Now, it's arguably their biggest issue, particularly given Embiid's injury history and ongoing load management.

Adem Bona has largely been invisible to start the year other than the one game that Embiid missed against Detroit. Tacko Fall (hip) and Dominick Barlow (back) have yet to play, while Jabari Walker (knee) missed two games. That's left them relying on LeBron and Dean Wade as small-ball 5s at times, which is not a sustainable solution.

As Maxey astutely noted after the Pistons loss, "It would be great to get some of our tall guys to come back." External reinforcements do not appear to be on the way, at least for another month, which means they'll have to look inside for ways to solve this problem for now.

The Sixers have largely been a dismal rebounding team under Nick Nurse. That didn't figure to change this year given their personnel, and through five games, those concerns have played out as expected.

While the small-sample-size caveat very much applies at this time of year, the Sixers are currently 24th in rebounding percentage. They were 22nd in 2023-24 and 21st last season, so their early-season output is right in line with how they've fared in recent seasons (at least ones when their entire roster doesn't get injured).

With Andre Drummond now in New York and Hukporti out for the year, the backup center situation plays into these struggles to some extent. However, this is a teamwide issue that they need to improve upon.

"We've got to be better at rebounding the basketball, and we have to do it by committee," head coach Nick Nurse recently told reporters. "I mean, I think if you're missing some of your size and all that kind of stuff, obviously it becomes a problem. And, all five guys have to rebound. I just look at the numbers there, and the defensive rebounding from just across the board, no matter the position, just hasn't been good enough.

"So, everybody's got to chip in with a few more. That has to be the answer."

Maxey is the only plus three-point shooter in the Sixers' starting lineup. They have Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope as snipers off their bench, but long-range shooting always figured to be an issue for this group. Lo and behold, the Sixers are 24th in three-point makes, 26th in three-point attempts and 18th in three-point percentage.

They're due for some positive regression to the mean in the coming weeks. Maxey is shooting only 33.9 percent from deep, which would be the third-worst mark of his career. He figures to bounce back up into the high 30s (if not the 40s) in due time. After all, Simons started 5-of-21 from distance over his first four games and then went on a three-games heater, going 16-of-27 from deep. He's now over 40% on the season on high volume.

With that said, Brown is shooting 41.9 percent from deep, which would be his career high if he keeps shooting that well across this entire season. In other words, he's due for negative regression moving forward.

The bigger-picture bottom line: Unless Embiid and/or Edgecombe become more reliable from three, this issue might plague their starting five all year.

Given their compilation of talent, the Sixers figure to have one of the league's most lethal offenses this year. However, the players have spent the past month warning that it'll be a work in progress early in the season given how many new pieces they're incorporating.

As it turns out, they weren't kidding. The Sixers are 19th in overall offensive rating and 20th in half-court offense.

That's bound to normalize as the starters develop more chemistry with one another. It's hard to imagine this group finishing in the bottom 10 of the NBA in half-court offensive efficiency. Until then, they at least need to cut down on their turnovers to avoid generating run-out opportunities for opponents.

Unless otherwise noted, all stats via NBA.com, PBPStats, Cleaning the Glass or Basketball Reference. All salary information via Spotrac and salary-cap information via RealGM.

#2774. Jerry Jones claims (incorrectly) that there's "no correlation" between coaching pay and winning

Jerry Jones has said that the size of the check he would write to guarantee another Super Bowl win would be "embarrassing."

Jones, when it comes to the resources he is willing to invest in the team, is cheap. He won't fire coaches who have buyouts. And he won't pay top dollar for new coaches.

The owner and G.M. of the Cowboys defended his approach during his latest visit to 105.3 The Fan in Dallas by making the nonsensical claim that there's no connection between coaching pay and winning.

"In the NFL, this is after years of looking at all the teams and all the coaches, there is no — there is zero correlation between how much you pay a coach, or how many coaches you have, as to winning," Jones said. "There is no correlation. And that's a random sample of years and all 32 teams involved.  So put that in your hopper and smoke it."

He's just wrong. Hiring a proven coach, and paying him accordingly, can change everything. We've seen it, time and again.

Andy Reid instantly turned the Chiefs into consistent contenders, and three-time Super Bowl winners. Sean Payton has made the Broncos into an annual contender, positioning him to become the first coach to win a Super Bowl for two different teams. Most recently, John Harbaugh has immediately changed everything for the Giants.

Harbaugh's success will result in his former rival, Mike Tomlin, fending off teams willing to pay him upwards of $30 million per year to swap out his earpiece and microphone on the NBC sideline set for the Sony headset along the white stripe.

Jones prefers to speculate, when it comes to coaches. In lieu of paying for a coach who has proven that he can win, Jones wants to roll the dice on an unproven commodity in the hopes of maximizing the return on his investment.

"You can be pretty creative in hiring your coaches," Jones said. "You can be creative sometime when you don't even know you're hiring the coaches.  And so I've had some good experience of hiring people who have never been in the NFL. I've had some experience of hiring young coaches, older coaches, and so, of course, you constantly remind me, as you should, of what my record is. And I understand that.  But I also know that the next time you throw the pick, if you were the old California gold miner, you may hit the Comstock Lode. And then it is gloryhole."

"Creative" is another way of saying "cheap." Buy low, and reap the benefit when the less expensive option yields results. And stick with him until his contract expires, to avoid having to pay two coaches at the same time.

It would be different if there truly was no correlation between quality (and cost) of coach and winning. But there ABSOLUTELY is a connection.

Still, Jerry prefers to dig through the bargain bin in search of an abandoned Botticelli. His own twist on "if you have to ask you can't afford it" is "if you have to ask I don't want it."

It's no surprise. In the early days of the salary cap, members of the media often pointed out that there's no cap on coaching pay. In time, the NFL realized, "Oh shit, there's no cap on coaching pay."

That has led to what some believe is an effort to collectively keep coaching pay from growing at the rate that it should. And some in league circles are convinced that Jerry Jones is the ringleader of what is, as a practical matter, an effort to collude.

Even if he's not going to pay top-of-market money for a coach, the higher the market goes, the more expensive it gets across the board. The rising tide, in other words, raises all dinghies. And Jerry would much rather spend his money on his aircraft carrier that has been retrofitted into a luxury hotel.

That's his prerogative. But Cowboys fans — who fork over their money and who devote their time and attention to watching games on TV and consuming Cowboys content — should understand what's going on. Jerry Jones is pinching pennies when it comes to paying coaches. As a result, he's often getting what he isn't paying for.

His mindset is highly relevant to the looming wreckage of the 2026 season. If coach Brian Schottenheimer has guaranteed money left on his contract for 2027, he will not be fired. And if Jones can avoid owing Schottenheimer a buyout, Jones will resist joining the pursuit of Tomlin, who admitted on the most recent edition of Football Night in America that he grew up a fan of the Cowboys.

Actually, that could make Jerry think that deep-seated rooting interest will give him a chance at hiring Tomlin on the cheap. Because cheap does as cheap is. And, when it comes to his team (and specifically to his coaches), Jerry Jones is cheap.

#2771. Warriors ‘loved’ Draymond Green’s ejection: ‘Lit a fire in all of us’

SAN FRANCISCO — The first time Draymond Green and longtime nemesis Dillon Brooks shared the floor this season, only one of them was still left by the end.

In that battle, consider Brooks the winner.

In the one that actually matters in terms of wins and losses, point to Green and the Warriors.

Green's ejection 2 minutes into the second half Monday night awakened the sleep-walking Warriors, who erased a 17-point deficit in his absence to pull out a 116-113 win.

"He lit a fire in all of us," said Stephen Curry, "and we had to respond. So I'm glad we did."

Golden State Warriors' Draymond Green (23) and Phoenix Suns' Jalen Bridges (15) are separated by security in San Francisco on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. JOSE CARLOS FAJARDO/Bay Area News Group via AP

While the double technical ended Green's night and put him two closer to the 16-tech threshold that automatically merits a one-game suspension, the Warriors had no problem with it.

"I loved it," said fourth-year guard Brandin Podziemski, who had six points in the first half but finished with 20. "It fueled our team. We didn't have that edge to start the game. …

"Maybe he sensed it. Maybe he didn't. But it helped."

Green wrapped both arms around Khaman Maluach as Phoenix's 7-foot center tried to finish at the rim shortly into the third quarter and threw him to the ground. Almost as soon as Maluach hit the floor, Brooks was in Green's face, a familiar juxtaposition for two of the NBA's most fiery players. Green responded by grabbing Brooks' jersey with both hands, close to his neck.

Golden State Warriors' Draymond Green throws down Phoenix Suns' Khaman Maluach during an NBA game at Chase Center in San Francisco, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. JOSE CARLOS FAJARDO/Bay Area News Group via AP

Upon review, the incident resulted in technical fouls for Green and Brooks, and a second on Green for his "throwdown" of Maluach. That earned Green an early trip to the showers.

And almost instantaneously, the game flipped in the Warriors' favor.

They were trailing 68-57 when Green was tossed at the 10-minute mark. Not even four minutes later, the Warriors had rallied to tie the score at 73 and never trailed by more than six again.

The Suns responded to Green's absence by going small, subbing out Oso Ighodaro with 6-foot-7 forward Ryan Dunn at center. Coach Steve Kerr didn't care to weigh in on Green's testy back-and-forth with Brooks but said the Suns' adjustment "opened up the game."

"I think they played maybe 12 minutes of super small with [6-foot-7 forward Ryan] Dunn at the five," Kerr said. "It kind of opened up the game a little bit. Our crowd got into it and our guys just did a great job of finding energy on a back-to-back."

Stephen Curry (30) and Draymond Green (23) of the Golden State Warriors smile on the bench against the Denver Nuggets on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in Denver. NBAE via Getty Images

While the Warriors were on the back end of their second back-to-back of the season, the Suns were well-rested having played Friday. When they squared off Monday night, it was the Warriors' eighth game of the season to only the Suns' fifth.

So even though Green and Curry sat out against the Clippers the night before, it was understandable for the Warriors to come out sluggish.

The fact that they were able to rally and finish stronger, well, maybe some credit belongs to the guy who spent most of the second half in the locker room.

"We've got to have our brother's back when he defends us," Curry said. "But it's also one of those games, most of the guys on the back to back, Phoenix had been off for a couple days, they started 1-3 and [we] knew they were gonna come out playing desperate. …

"We just tried to weather the storm, execute, give ourselves a chance, and that third quarter was the run that we needed to get back into it."

The Jets’ loss to the Raiders in Week 8 dropped them to 2-6 and it left their record since hiring head coach Aaron Glenn at an unimpressive 5-20.

That opportunity starts in Kansas City this week and missing out on it will only turn the heat under Glenn’s seat higher.

#2764. Caleb Williams has arrived as a top-tier quarterback

In recent weeks, Simms and I have raised once or twice the question of whether Bears quarterback Caleb Williams belongs in the top tier of NFL franchise quarterbacks.

Based on Monday night’s 34-point performance against a Seahawks defense that held the Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes to three points a week earlier, it’s time to render a verdict.

The new top four, in our view, are (in no particular order), Josh Allen, Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow, and Caleb Williams.

Lamar Jackson previously had been the fourth. A lost season due to multiple injuries puts him at No. 5, until he reestablishes himself in 2027. (And there’s no reason to believe he won’t, if he can get and stay healthy.)

In Week 7 at Seattle, Mahomes completed 19 of 33 passes for 165 yards, no touchdowns, and one interception. His passer rating for the game was 58.9. In Week 8 at Seattle, Williams went 24 for 34 for 247 yards, one touchdown, and no picks. Williams also sparked a 39-yard gain on a key third-down backward pass to receiver Khalif Raymond, which set up the score that turned a 20-17 margin into a 27-17 clincher.

And before anyone says Mahomes didn’t have any support in the running game, Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III and Bears running back D’Andre Swift averaged an identical 2.6 yards per carry against the Seahawks’ defense.

So, yes, Caleb is a top-level NFL quarterback. Despite missing three games with a hamstring injury, his odds to win the NFL MVP award are down to 5-1, behind only Allen, Brock Purdy, and Burrow.

If the Bears keep doing what they did on Monday night — and if they finish the season with the No. 1 seed in the NFC — Williams will get plenty of votes. And he has a real chance to win it.

Even if he’d much rather win the MVP award not for the regular season, but for the Super Bowl.

The spirit of Dolly Parton will be with the Nashville Predators this season.

The NHL revealed all 32 Hometown Remix jerseys on Nov. 2, including the Predators' all-navy look. The jerseys include gold trim and design elements symbolizing "heritage rodeo-tailoring flair" and "a modern take on country roots, showmanship, and Preds pride."

#2750. Andy Reid: Chris Jones is giving his all, doing everything he can do

The Chiefs have lost their last two games.

Coincidentally or not, defensive tackle Chris Jones has been blanked on the official stat sheet in each one.

Jones, who turned 32 in July, has just 13 total tackles with one tackle for loss, three QB hits, and a half-sack through seven games in 2026.

On the whole, the Chiefs have just eight sacks this season, averaging just over one per game. Only Philadelphia has a lower sack rate than Kansas City, which has been getting one on just 3.69 percent of opponent dropbacks. By contrast, Minnesota leads the league with a 12.32 percent sack rate. Chicago is No. 2 at 9.65 percent.

What’s up with the Chiefs’ pass rush? How can the team get things going, particularly with Jones?

“[W]hen you rush four, you want to get somebody home, obviously. That’s what [defensive line coach] Joe [Cullen] strives for, and the guys strive for, and we’ve been doing a good job with getting pressure on,” head coach Andy Reid said in his Monday news conference, via transcript from the team. “You’ve just got to get to the quarterback. We had a lot of blocked balls, which was great, you’ve got to be relatively close to get those. Especially if they’re intermediate throws, the trajectory of the ball is one that you’ve got to be relatively close [to] get a hand up to be able to block.

“But going back to Chris, I mean, Chris is giving his all. He’s doing everything he can do. He gets doubled from various angles. He’s going to draw a lot of attention, and so that’s [an] advantage to the other guys to have a chance to get themselves home. So, as much emphasis is put on Chris, let’s take advantage of that and get ourselves on the quarterback. So, not just to the quarterback, but on the quarterback.”

The Chiefs will be back at home to face the Jets in Week 9. New York ranks No. 26, allowing a sack on 9.62 percent of passing attempts. We’ll see if that can get Kansas City’s pass rush going on Sunday.

#2749. Alexis Mac Allister reveals Liverpool told him they had no plans to renew his contract in a 'painful' blow

Alexis Mac Allister has revealed that Liverpool told him last season they had no plans to renew his contract, admitting the news was painful and unpleasant. The Argentina midfielder, whose deal runs until the summer of 2028, insists staying at Anfield is what he wants most and believes the recent changes behind the scenes mean anything can happen now.

Mac Allister has been one of Andoni Iraola's key men this season, scoring four goals, three of them in three Champions League matches, and providing one assist. However, his long-term future remains uncertain, with his current contract expiring in the summer of 2028 and no progress made towards a new deal.

Speaking to Argentine journalist Gastón Edul at his home, Mac Allister said: "First of all, obviously, I feel that affection from the fans, and that's something incredible for me. It's not easy at a club like Liverpool to be appreciated the way I am."

Reflecting on his time at Anfield before turning to his contract, he added: "I enjoy it a lot, and obviously winning a Premier League title with this club is something very special, something the fans don't forget. Obviously, we're in a situation where I have a year and a half left on my contract.

"Last season I was told that the club's idea was not to renew it, at least for now. And obviously, that was a painful, unpleasant situation." Mac Allister joined the Reds from Brighton in the summer of 2023 for around £45 million.

Asked whether the saga has left him stressed or despondent, Mac Allister said: "Not that much, because at the end of the day, I still had, and still have, time left at this club, which is what I want most – to stay here.

"The reality is that the manager has now changed, the sporting director has changed, and new investors are coming into the club. So I think I'm now in a position where anything can happen. We'll see what happens in the future. I've always said that I'm very happy here, that I really enjoy it, and we'll see."

Liverpool have already tied down Ryan Gravenberch until 2032 after he signed a new deal in March, while Dominik Szoboszlai has committed until 2031. Mac Allister has also been linked with Real Madrid.

For now, his focus turns to tomorrow's Champions League trip to Fenerbahce, as the Reds look to bounce back from Sunday's defeat to Arsenal.

#2747. The Christmas Day schedule is shaping up to be massive

When the schedule is released every May, plenty of standalone games that look good at the time morph into something not quite as appetizing as the season unfolds. Some standalone games get better with time.

This year, there’s a trio of massive games lurking on Christmas Day.

At 1:00 p.m. ET, it’s the Packers at the Bears. At 4:30 p.m. ET, it’s the Bills at the Broncos. At 8:15 p.m., it’s the Rams at the Seahawks.

With the Bears emerging as a threat to win the NFC North and the No. 1 seed in the conference, the rematch with their biggest rivals (who beat them 31-7 in Week 5) becomes must-see TV. Bills at Broncos, a rematch of a postseason overtime classic that got Buffalo coach Sean McDermott fired, should have direct implications on two division races and the chase for the lone bye in the AFC.

The nightcap shapes up to be not a battle for the NFC West title and/or the top seed but a potential elimination game, given that both Seattle and L.A. are currently 4-4.

Regardless, all three games should be significant. Impactful. Consequential.

And they’ll more than make up for the Christmas Eve game, which has the 2-5 Texans at the 2-6 Eagles.

#2746. The Point Guard Problem

"What If" Wolves Volume 6: "Khan, you bloodsucker!" – Captain James T. Kirk or JetAllen

When the Minnesota Timberwolves acquired LaMelo Ball this offseason, I found myself asking a simple question: did the Wolves finally solve their point guard problem? Early returns are optimistic at this point. Some good games, some not so. But based on history, what else should we expect from this franchise?

The Timberwolves have been through point guard after point guard. None of them seem to last long, if at all. This team has been going through PGs like Spinal Tap goes through drummers. RIP Peter James Bond.

The Timberwolves started off by taking what they thought was a franchise cornerstone in Pooh Richardson, their first-ever draft pick. We have previously discussed why that didn't work out in the first "What If" Wolves article. Since picking Pooh, the Wolves have struggled to find a franchise player at the one. There have been some solid players, even All-Stars, but they were always short stints. The point guard problem should have been solved by now, and hopefully it finally is with Ball, but repeated mistakes have left this position in a constant state of flux.

I had originally planned to write an article focusing only on the reign of terror brought to this franchise by former General Manager David Kahn. But my liquor cabinet was only half-stocked at the time, and I would need copious amounts of booze to relive that whole ordeal. Instead, we will focus on one issue. One teeny, tiny issue that I consider the biggest mistake in franchise history.

David Kahn was on the job for exactly 33 days (trust me, I counted) when he made quite possibly the greatest trade in Timberwolves history.

Kahn traded former Rookie of the Year Mike Miller and guard Randy Foye to the Washington Wizards for Etan Thomas, Darius Songaila, Oleksiy Pecherov, and the fifth pick in the upcoming 2009 NBA Draft. Only Pecherov would ever play for the Wolves (44 games), but the prize of the trade was the pick. With the addition of the fifth overall pick, MN would now draft back-to-back with the fifth and sixth picks.

With the fifth overall pick in the 2009 NBA Draft, the Timberwolves selected my (and Leo's) favorite player of all time, Ricky Rubio.

NEW YORK – JUNE 25: Ricky Rubio, selected number five overall by the Minnesota Timberwolves poses for a portrait during the 2009 NBA Draft on June 25, 2009 at the WaMu Theatre in New York, New York. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2009 NBAE (Photo by Jennifer Pottheiser/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Rubio was a dynamic PG from Spain. His list of accomplishments overseas was incredible: he turned pro at 14 years old, won the Rising Star Award, FIBA Young Player of the Year Award, was named Spanish ACB League's best point guard, Defensive Player of the Year, and won a EuroLeague Championship. Quite the trophy room.

But I believe what put Ricky at the top of the draft class was his final performance of the 2006 Europe Under-16 Championship, where he scored 51 points, grabbed 24 rebounds, had 12 assists, and stole the ball 7 times. One of the greatest games ever played. Rubio also held his own in the 2008 Olympic Finals against the USA, where Ricky went up against the likes of Jason Kidd, Dwyane Wade, Chris Paul, and Kobe Bryant.

To me, Rubio was a lock with the 5th pick in the draft. But man, did Kahn ever mess up the next pick. This is where the "What If" Wolves will take over, fire Kahn immediately, and take the player that I was begging the Timberwolves to take.

I remember the draft like it was yesterday. I was sitting on the couch at my in-laws' house. My son was born a few months prior, so we were at the grandparents' house to get some baby relief. And I was yelling at the television.

David Kahn was on the job for exactly 34 days (trust me, I counted again) when he made the biggest mistake in Timberwolves history.

With Ricky Rubio in the fold, my thoughts were to get him a lights out shooter that can pair with him in the backcourt. Rubio had already proven that he could lock down defensively (yes, bigger guards would have been a problem, but only a few teams had elite big guards that operated out of the post), so the other guard could take on the smaller matchup. So who was the best shooter in the draft? Not Jonny Flynn, I can tell you that.

With the 6th overall pick in the 2009 NBA Draft, the "What If" Wolves selected Wardell Stephen Curry II from Davidson College.

NEW YORK – JUNE 25: Stephen Curry, selected seventh overall by the Golden State Warriors speaks to Mark Jones of ESPN during the 2009 NBA Draft on June 25, 2009 at The WaMu Theatre at Madison Square Garden in New York City, New York. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2009 NBAE (Photo by David Dow/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Steph Curry was the best story coming out of the 2008 NCAA Tournament. Curry owned March Madness that year by beating larger schools Gonzaga (40 points), Georgetown (30 points), and Wisconsin (32 points) before eventually losing in the Elite Eight to Kansas (25 points). Curry would leave tiny Davidson College the following year after being named to the All-American First Team, leading the nation in scoring (28.6 ppg), and shooting 41% on three-pointers for his college career. In my eyes, Curry was the perfect complement to Ricky Rubio (Watch how effortless Curry's game is in the video below).

David Kahn compared Flynn and Rubio to Hall of Famers Earl Monroe and Walt Frazier of the New York Knicks. I can sort of see the familiarities with the flash of Rubio and Monroe along with the defense of Flynn and Frazier. But both Pearl and Clyde could score. Flynn couldn't shoot a lick, finishing his career shooting 33% from three and 40% overall from the field. Don't get me wrong, Rubio shot just as bad for his career, but he found a way to average double digits in scoring for his career, plus he was an elite set-up man.

According to NBC Sports' Kurt Helin, even the Wolves players and coaches were baffled by the draft. This is why Curry was the right pick from the get-go.

There were also some issues with good ol' dad when it came to drafting Steph Curry. Dell Curry was a great shooter with the Charlotte Hornets in the 90s (40% career three-point shooter) and taught his boys how to let it fly. He also was trying to force his eldest son to get drafted by the Knicks, who owned the 8th overall pick.

That's right. Dell didn't want his kid to go to the Golden State Warriors either. So why did they not listen to the father's threats? Well, they didn't have David Kahn as a GM, and since the "What If" Wolves fired Kahn, neither do we. We ignore Dell's wishes and take Curry right after Rubio.

David Kahn looking over his shoulder as he is about to be fired. | NBAE via Getty Images

Now, if this fantasy scenario plays out according to my plan, the Timberwolves don't have to wait two years for Rubio's arrival like in reality. Ricky comes over as an 18-year-old PG prodigy with impervious knees. Steph plays at the shooting guard position offensively. Being off-ball saves his ankles a bit, and his career trajectory starts on a more positive note. Rubio and Curry switch defensively, and both play the passing lanes for easy steals. Rubio now has a more open lane to finish at the rim due to the actual threat of a Curry three-pointer (Wolves shot 34% as a team in 2009-10).

The pace of play is quickened after great outlet passes from Kevin Love. And the "What If" Wolves become a playoff contender for the first time since Kevin Garnett was traded to Boston. Hell, KG might even come back earlier if he gets to play with Rubio and Curry. Rubio may still eventually be traded, or he retires to go back home to Spain, but Curry would then slide over to the point, and all would be right in the world. Curry would go on to possibly beat out KG as the best Timberwolf of all time. As a consolation, he would at least go down as the best point guard. Unless Melo gets us a chip.

Just for fun, here is a top ten list of the most games started at the point guard position for the Timberwolves.

Ricky Rubio – 384 games started (two separate stints)

Bonus: Jonny Flynn – 89 games started for the Timberwolves (only a three year NBA career)

Bonus Bonus: Stephen Curry – 1065 regular season games started for the Golden State Warriors, 149 playoff games started.

Bonus Bonus Bonus: Steph would've been too miserable to start any games with his prized golf courses covered in snow.

#2742. Mark Davis: "Absolutely no pressure whatsoever" from me to start Fernando Mendoza

The Raiders have gotten good play out of quarterback Kirk Cousins through the first eight games of the season, with the team sitting at 4-4 after Sunday’s victory over the Jets.

With Cousins keeping the team in contention, it’s unclear when No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza might make his first career start.

That’s just fine with team owner Mark Davis, who talked about the young QB in a Monday interview with CNBC.

“From me, there’s absolutely no pressure whatsoever,” Davis said, via Adam Hill of the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

“Today, there’s a lot of pressure put on teams when they draft a guy No. 1 that you have to play him right away,” Davis added. “That’s why I think we were so fortunate to get Kirk Cousins as someone who could bridge the gap and let this young man learn a lot about what football is in the pros, the speed of the game, and the things that have to be done. … And he’s picking it up great, but I think we’re fortunate he doesn’t have to go out and play.”

Davis doesn’t want Mendoza to feel like he has to feel any kind of pressure to perform, because that could end up hindering his growth.

“I’ve seen quarterbacks get fast-tracked onto the field and they may do well, but they don’t learn all the intricacies of footwork and everything else it takes,” Davis said. “So they’re limited in their development, maybe throughout their career.

“I’m really happy with the way it is with Fernando right now, and we’ll see what happens.”

Much of Davis’ happiness with Mendoza has to do with how the QB has handled everything off the field.

“I tell people jokingly that if he can play football, he’s going to be amazing,” Davis said. “Because he’s got every other intangible you could want in a person. He’s a hard worker. He’s a sponge.

“[And] he’s working with Mr. [Tom] Brady on a lot of things.”

Mendoza has made one appearance so far this season, completing 6-of-8 passes for 48 yards in mop-up duty during the Week 5 loss to the Patriots.

#2738. TWG Motorsports reportedly not shopping other teams amid potential sale of Cadillac F1

TWG Motorsports is not up for grabs, per The Athletic, despite the fact that TWG Global CEO Mark Walter is reportedly shopping his stake in Cadillac F1.

Created in 2024 after TWG Global acquired multiple motorsports teams, TWG Motorsports holds ownership in Cadillac F1 (Formula One), Andretti Global (IndyCar), Spire Motorsports (NASCAR), Wayne Taylor Racing (IMSA) and Walkinshaw TWG Racing (Supercars). According to The Athletic, only Cadillac F1 is being shopped.

"At this stage, TWG Motorsport is not seeking out buyers for its other properties — NASCAR's Spire Motorsports, IndyCar and Formula E's Andretti Global, IMSA's Wayne Taylor Racing and Supercars' Walkinshaw Andretti United," The Athletic reported.

Cadillac F1 became F1's first new team in a decade this year. The team, which has a base in Fishers, is co-owned by TWG Motorsports and General Motors, Cadillac's parent company. When asked by IndyStar for comment Monday regarding Walter potentially selling his stake, General Motors declined to comment and TWG Motorsports did not respond.

The potential sale of Cadillac F1 after just one season comes with the backdrop that Walter's TWG Global company is under investigation by the U.S. Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission. The DOJ and SEC are looking into whether TWG Global, through subsidiaries Delaware Life and Clear Spring Life and Annuity, illegally disclosed affiliated assets.

More: Fishers-based Cadillac F1 reportedly for sale as TWG Global faces federal probe and lawsuit

Since the investigation became public in July, Walter has sold his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers and his 13% share of the Premier League's Chelsea FC. Reports now believe that Cadillac F1 and the Los Angeles Sparks could be next. TWG Global denied any wrongdoing by its insurance companies in August.

#2736. Jerry Jones claims (incorrectly) that there's "no correlation" between coaching pay and winning

Jerry Jones has said that the size of the check he would write to guarantee another Super Bowl win would be “embarrassing.”

Jones, when it comes to the resources he is willing to invest in the team, is cheap. He won’t fire coaches who have buyouts. And he won’t pay top dollar for new coaches.

The owner and G.M. of the Cowboys defended his approach during his latest visit to 105.3 The Fan in Dallas by making the nonsensical claim that there’s no connection between coaching pay and winning.

“In the NFL, this is after years of looking at all the teams and all the coaches, there is no — there is zero correlation between how much you pay a coach, or how many coaches you have, as to winning,” Jones said. “There is no correlation. And that’s a random sample of years and all 32 teams involved.  So put that in your hopper and smoke it.”

He’s just wrong. Hiring a proven coach, and paying him accordingly, can change everything. We’ve seen it, time and again.

Andy Reid instantly turned the Chiefs into consistent contenders, and three-time Super Bowl winners. Sean Payton has made the Broncos into an annual contender, positioning him to become the first coach to win a Super Bowl for two different teams. Most recently, John Harbaugh has immediately changed everything for the Giants.

Harbaugh’s success will result in his former rival, Mike Tomlin, fending off teams willing to pay him upwards of $30 million per year to swap out his earpiece and microphone on the NBC sideline set for the Sony headset along the white stripe.

Jones prefers to speculate, when it comes to coaches. In lieu of paying for a coach who has proven that he can win, Jones wants to roll the dice on an unproven commodity in the hopes of maximizing the return on his investment.

“You can be pretty creative in hiring your coaches,” Jones said. “You can be creative sometime when you don’t even know you’re hiring the coaches.  And so I’ve had some good experience of hiring people who have never been in the NFL. I’ve had some experience of hiring young coaches, older coaches, and so, of course, you constantly remind me, as you should, of what my record is. And I understand that.  But I also know that the next time you throw the pick, if you were the old California gold miner, you may hit the Comstock Lode. And then it is gloryhole.”

“Creative” is another way of saying “cheap.” Buy low, and reap the benefit when the less expensive option yields results. And stick with him until his contract expires, to avoid having to pay two coaches at the same time.

It would be different if there truly was no correlation between quality (and cost) of coach and winning. But there ABSOLUTELY is a connection.

Still, Jerry prefers to dig through the bargain bin in search of an abandoned Botticelli. His own twist on “if you have to ask you can’t afford it” is “if you have to ask I don’t want it.”

It’s no surprise. In the early days of the salary cap, members of the media often pointed out that there’s no cap on coaching pay. In time, the NFL realized, “Oh shit, there’s no cap on coaching pay.”

That has led to what some believe is an effort to collectively keep coaching pay from growing at the rate that it should. And some in league circles are convinced that Jerry Jones is the ringleader of what is, as a practical matter, an effort to collude.

Even if he’s not going to pay top-of-market money for a coach, the higher the market goes, the more expensive it gets across the board. The rising tide, in other words, raises all dinghies. And Jerry would much rather spend his money on his aircraft carrier that has been retrofitted into a luxury hotel.

That’s his prerogative. But Cowboys fans — who fork over their money and who devote their time and attention to watching games on TV and consuming Cowboys content — should understand what’s going on. Jerry Jones is pinching pennies when it comes to paying coaches. As a result, he’s often getting what he isn’t paying for.

His mindset is highly relevant to the looming wreckage of the 2026 season. If coach Brian Schottenheimer has guaranteed money left on his contract for 2027, he will not be fired. And if Jones can avoid owing Schottenheimer a buyout, Jones will resist joining the pursuit of Tomlin, who admitted on the most recent edition of Football Night in America that he grew up a fan of the Cowboys.

Actually, that could make Jerry think that deep-seated rooting interest will give him a chance at hiring Tomlin on the cheap. Because cheap does as cheap is. And, when it comes to his team (and specifically to his coaches), Jerry Jones is cheap.

#2734. Cardinals RB Jeremiyah Love reportedly headed to injured reserve with high-ankle sprain

Arizona Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love is headed to injured reserve with a right high-ankle sprain, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reports.

The injury and IR designation will sideline Love for a minimum of four games. The Cardinals have upcoming games against the Seahawks, Rams, Chiefs and Commanders.

Love injured his ankle in Sunday's win over the Dallas Cowboys when his ankle got rolled underneath his body on a tackle. He was able to get up to walk to the sideline, but he did not return to the game as the Cardinals rallied from a 14-3 halftime deficit for a 33-30 overtime win.

The ankle injury is the third and most serious for Love since the Cardinals selected him with the No. 3 pick in April's NFL Draft.

Love previously sprained his right ankle in the preseason, causing him to miss multiple preseason games. He was ready to play in Arizona's Week 1 game against the Chargers.

The Cardinals revealed after a Week 4 loss to the Giants that Love was dealing with a left ankle injury. That injury sidelined him for games against the Rams and Broncos in Weeks 6 and 7. He returned from that injury to face the Cowboys before injuring his right ankle again before halftime.

Now Love is looking at an extended absence with the third ankle injury of his rookie season.

Love was the No. 3 pick in April's NFL Draft and is a big piece of Arizona's long-term plans. But injuries have limited his ability to gain traction during his rookie season.

Love was a star at Notre Dame who earned first-team All-America honors and the Doak Walker Award as college football's best running back as a junior. He tallied 1,652 yards from scrimmage and 21 total touchdowns in 2025 while averaging 6.9 yards per carry.

#2729. It’s fun to be a Sixer right now

Typically, he enjoys drinking it when he's not playing, but apparently exceptions can be made.

On Monday night, James went into the crowd going after a loose ball in the third quarter of the Sixers' 126-107 win over the Chicago Bulls. There was a brief stir from the fans. We later found out it was because James had taken a sip from a spectator's cup.

"I crashed into him, spilled some of his wine," James said. "So I wanted to see if it was worth it on my arm, man. How good it was."

Spoiled by California wines, no doubt, but James is profiling well with his new team.

When James' agent Rich Paul did his media blitz during his client's free agency, he mentioned happiness as the biggest factor for the King's decision.

In the fourth quarter, as the Sixers began to pull away, James found himself guarded by the 6-foot-1, 190-pound Tre Jones. LeBron easily bullied Jones into the post. Jones bit on a fake and Leonard Miller came over to help. James pump-faked again, this time getting Miller in the air, absorbing the contact and burying a short fadeaway.

And on the next offensive possession, it was Tyrese Maxey's turn to get into the lane and convert a crazy finish while getting fouled.

Safe to say, this group is having a good time.

"Listen, it's a long marathon," James said, "and if you don't find ways to have fun throughout it — even though you're working, even though you're locked in — it could wear on you. So for me, especially at this point in my career, too, being able to just appreciate the moments, the small moments. These fans are great to us. We try to be great to them as well by playing the game the right way, playing the game hard, and then also just being showmen as well."

James finished the night with 15 points, nine assists and seven rebounds. Maxey with 26 points and 11 assists. Jaylen Brown had 25 points, 11 rebounds and five assists. Joel Embiid, who was on a minutes restriction while managing plantar fasciitis, recorded 15 points, eight rebounds and three assists. The Sixers as a team had 36 assists on 48 makes.

Tough night for the "there's only one ball!" crowd.

And let's not forget about VJ Edgecombe — you know, the guy whose growth was going to be stunted because the Sixers have too many good players. The second-year guard scored a season-high 21 points, his first 20-plus point game on the young season, and dished out five assists.

It was a rewarding scoring night for a guy who's done all the dirty work for the Sixers' starting group. Edgecombe said his lower usage rate isn't his concern, though.

"I don't get antsy or impatient or anything," he said. "We're 7-1 and that's the most important thing. … And like tonight, I was able to get going a little bit, but once you just find that joy out there, just playing basketball … I was just kind of hard on myself early [this season] because I was missing shots I [usually] make and that's not on nobody else but me. And like I say, it's fun when you're winning. I don't want to be a cancer because I ain't getting the shots that I want to get. I'm still learning. I'm in year two."

The chemistry between the starting group is growing. A 7-1 start is a big help, but there seems to be an eagerness for all of them to learn each other. It's something that's been going on since training camp. In fact, a lesson from camp made its way onto the game floor.

James hit Edgecombe with not one but two absurdly accurate bounce passes in transition, but the pair needed to build trust to execute them when it counted.

"There's a couple times in training camp that he kind of slowed up and didn't think I'd get the pass there to him," James said. "And I told him all he has to do is just run, and I'll try to put it on time, on target as much as I can."

After the game, Edgecombe described it as a teaching moment. He was rewarded for that diligence.

Against the Bulls, Edgecombe was ready, flushing down multiple transition opportunities.

"If you're open, he's going to pass it to you," Edgecombe said. "The main thing is just being ready. Tonight, I had to run to go get them."

And this team is still in the fermentation process.

"It's a lot of talent, man," Brown said. "And we like each other and we're just kind of like building that chemistry of how we can get this thing to a well-oiled machine. So I think we're taking steps forward every single day. I think we still got a long way to go to be a really, really solid, great team. But we've been able to win some games. We started out the season 7-1 and you haven't seen our best version yet. So that's a good sign."

#2725. Jets star goalie Connor Hellebuyck requests trade: Where three-time Vezina Trophy winner could land

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After months of speculation about his future in Winnipeg, Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck has confirmed his trade request publicly.

Hellebuyck's name has come up in trade rumors since the 2025-26 season ended, and the rumor mill will only pick back up now that he's gone public with his request. NHL training camps will open soon, and Hellebuyck wanted to provide more clarity on the situation.

"Winnipeg has been home for my entire NHL career, and I will always be grateful for my time there.

"I have never forgotten June 23, 2012. That's the day Winnipeg took a chance on a goalie playing in Odessa, Texas. I gave everything I had from that moment to prove the Jets made the right decision.

"Several months ago, I privately requested a trade. I have tried to handle the situation quietly and respectfully while giving the organization time to explore its options.

"With training camp approaching, I felt it was important to publicly confirm my request. My position has not changed, and I believe moving on is the best path forward for me and my family.

"I appreciate everything Winnipeg Jets fans have meant to me throughout my career and hope a resolution can be reached soon."

In what would become one of the biggest steals in NHL Draft history, the Jets used the No. 130 overall pick to select Hellebucyk in 2012. Just seven years later, Hellebuyck established himself as one of the best goalies in the lea, and he's maintained that level of play for nearly a decade.

A three-time Vezina Trophy winner, Hellebuyck has a legitimate claim as the best goaltender in the world. Over the last three seasons, Hellebucyk has totaled 73.4 goals saved above average, per Natural Stat Trick. That's 20 more than the next closest goaltender -- Andrei Vasilevskiy -- and includes a rather underwhelming 2025-26 campaign.

There have been plenty of years in which Hellebuyck carried mediocre Jets teams, but 2025-26 was not one of them. He actually allowed 0.35 goals above average with a pedestrian 0.895 save percentage. Normally, it would be fair to worry about a 33-year-old goalie with those numbers, but not in Hellebucyk's case.

Hellebuyck backstopped Team USA to its first men's ice hockey gold medal in 46 years at the 2026 Olympics while allowing a total of six goals and boasting a .956 save percentage. He was exceptional in the final against Canada, where he turned away 41 of the 42 shots he faced and made one of the most iconic saves in hockey history.

THAT WAS ONE HELLE-BUYCK OF A STOP. 😳 pic.twitter.com/N3wCimdBGw

The biggest obstacle in a trade might be Hellebucyk's contract. He has five years remaining on his current deal at $8.5 million per season -- and while that may be a lot of term for a goalie his age -- Hellebucyk is worth a lot more than that at his best. The real issue is that he owns a full no-movement clause, which means Hellebuyck controls his fate, and the trade request going public certainly won't improve the team's leverage.

So, where does Hellebucyk land? Without knowing his preferred destinations, it's probably safe to assume that he wants the opportunity to win a Stanley Cup, and the team that acquires him will need the requisite cap space and resources to do so.

With those parameters in mind, here are five teams that could make sense as Hellebuyck trade suitors.

The Sabres were one of two teams frequently connected to Hellebuyck earlier in the offseason, and that makes sense. Buffalo is an ascending team with room to upgrade in the crease. Not to denigrate Alex Lyon and Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen, who were a formidable tandem in 2025-26, but I'm not sure Buffalo can bet on similar performances this upcoming season. Adding Hellebuyck would eliminate that question mark immediately and make the Sabres a favorite to win the Atlantic Division.

In fact, one of Luukkonen or Lyon could go back to Winnipeg to help provide stability in the post-Hellebuyck era. The Sabres also own all their first-round picks for the foreseeable future, and it would probably take at least two of those to pry Hellebuyck from the Jets. Just a year ago, it would be hard to believe that Hellebuyck would waive his no-movement clause to go to Buffalo, but it seems very plausible now.

When the Devils traded Jacob Markstrom to the Florida Panthers in July, I assumed it would only be a matter of time until Hellebuyck was in Newark. To this point, nothing has come to fruition, but New Jersey absolutely needs an NHL-caliber starter. Jake Allen, David Rittich and Nico Daws are on the roster right now, and that won't get the job done.

The Devils were undone by poor goaltending -- and subpar defense -- too much last year. Markstrom allowed 13.7 goals above average, per Natural Stat Trick, and even a diminished version of Hellebuyck would provide a significant upgrade over those numbers. New Jersey has the draft capital to get something done, but it also needs to clear cap space, possibly with a Dougie Hamilton salary dump.

They just won the Stanley Cup with Brandon Bussi in net, so the Hurricanes have proven they don't need elite goaltending to go all the way. Regardless, running it back with Bussi wouldn't be a very safe bet, and adding Hellebuyck would only reinforce Carolina's biggest strength. As we saw in the playoffs, the Hurricanes are already one of the best defensive teams in the league. Put Hellebuyck behind that lineup, and scoring on Carolina becomes a Herculean task.

Thanks to savvy cap management by GM Eric Tulsky, Carolina has the room to add Hellebuyck without jettisoning a current player. Oh, and Carolina has three first-round picks over the next two years. If Tulsky wants to pursue Hellebuyck, he has the resources to do it.

This is more of a longshot, but it would be fun to see the Sharks take a swing if this, assuming Hellebuyck would sign off on a trade to San Jose. Despite the fact that they overpaid for it, the Sharks blue line is better, and there is a wealth of young talent at forward. Another factor here is the current state of the Pacific Division, which is abhorrent. The third playoff spot is up for grabs, and the Sharks could secure it with Hellebuyck in goal.

Superstar Macklin Celebrini is on the final year of his entry-level deal before his $18.8 million salary kicks in next year, so San Jose needs to push the chips in here and figure out the finances next summer. Would the team be willing to trade blue-chip goaltending prospect Yaroslav Askarov to the Jets? San Jose may also need to sweeten a trade package -- or involve a third team -- in order to get Winnipeg to take on Logan Couture's contract.

Yes, Vegas is currently $8.6 million over the salary cap, so there would need to be some impressive maneuvering in order to acquire Hellebuyck. But the Golden Knights have already proven to be cutthroat if a player they covet hits the trade market. Besides, goaltending was optional in Sin City last season. Four goalies combined to allow 23.2 goals above average. Only five teams had a worse save percentage than the Golden Knights.

So, how could the Golden Knights pull off a Hellebuyck blockbuster? Trading an injured Alex Pietrangelo and his contract would help, but that may be costly. Veteran defenseman Brayden McNabb only has a modified no-trade clause, and the same is true for forwards Tomas Hertl, William Karlsson and Ivan Barbashev. Like I said, this would be tough, but the Golden Knights are one team willing to drop the entire egg carton on the floor to make a few omelettes.

#2724. Avalanche sign star Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This has been the summer of spending in the NHL, and the Colorado Avalanche just broke the bank for star defenseman Cale Makar. On Friday, the team announced that Makar signed an eight-year extension worth $163.2 million.

The contract is the richest in league history -- both in total value and annual value at $20.4 million per year. Makar is the first player in NHL history to cross the $20 million salary threshold.

At 27-years old, Makar is arguably the best defensemen in the NHL, and he will remain in that conversation for quite a while. Makar has already won the Norris Trophy twice, and he was a key factor in Colorado's Stanley Cup run, which ended with him winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

This past season, Makar posted monster numbers from the blue line yet again as he tallied 20 goals and 59 assists in 75 games. Since entering the NHL in 2019, Makar leads all defensemen in goals (20) and points (507).

"I am so excited and humbled to continue to wear the Avalanche sweater and represent this incredible organization and community," Makar said in a statement. "I would like to thank the Kroenke family, Joe Sakic and the entire Avalanche organization for their commitment, trust and belief in me. I would also like to thank my wife and family for their constant support, as well as Scott, Brian and Steve Bartlett for their guidance and assistance.

"To the Avalanche fans, thank you for your continued support and for welcoming us to Colorado years ago. Colorado has truly become a second home to us, and we are so grateful to be here. I look forward to getting back on the ice with my teammates and continuing to work toward our goal of bringing the Stanley Cup back to the Mile High City."

Over the last three seasons, Makar's impact has been immense in all three zones. He's posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 54.5%, per Natural Stat Trick. With Makar on the ice in those situations, Colorado has outscored its opponents 220-157. In two of the last three seasons, Makar has hit the 90-point mark, and he has 100-point potential at his best.

Makar's $11.4 million raise kicks in in at the start of the 2026-27 season, and it will make things significantly tighter for the Avalanche as they navigate the salary cap. The bright side for Colorado -- and the key in getting this deal done -- is that the team now has each of its core players signed through at least 2031.

There may be some sticker shock upon seeing the $20.4 million average annual value, but that's the new reality in the NHL as the cap rises exponentially. The previous record for highest salary in NHL history was just set earlier this offseason when the Anaheim Ducks signed center Leo Carlsson to a contract worth $18 million per year, and the Chicago Blackhawks announced a $75 million extension for Connor Bedard.

The next domino to fall will be an extension for Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes, who is neck-and-neck with Makar as the best defensemen in the world. Waiting until after the Makar deal was announced to sign Hughes could prove to be a mistake for Wild general manager Bill Guerin.

#2720. Lexington, Louisville top list of best college basketball cities

The Kentucky Wildcats and Louisville Cardinals have one of the fiercest rivalries in college sports, and new data shows that the Battle of the Bluegrass also features the two most devoted college basketball fan bases.

Lexington, Kentucky ranked as the No. 1 market in the country for men's and women's basketball programs, according to the "Nielsen Scarborough Fandom Index" released on Tuesday, Nov. 3 by media audience research firm Nielsen. The index was created by analyzing data across seven metrics: apparel purchases, event attendance, streaming, social media following, TV viewership, radio listening, and overall interest level.

On Nielsen's list of the top 20 college hoops markets in America, Lexington's index score of 289 took the top spot, followed by Louisville's score of 277. Nielsen noted in its news release that both Kentucky markets dominated in every metric.

The No. 3 spot belongs to Des Moines/Ames, home to Iowa State and Iowa fans. Raleigh/Durham (Duke, UNC and NC State) came in at No. 4, while Indianapolis (Butler, Indiana and Purdue) rounded out the top five.

Surprisingly, last season's NCAA men's and women's champions – the Michigan Wolverines and UCLA Bruins – didn't crack the top 20 fanbases. While larger media hubs like Los Angeles, Houston and Atlanta didn't make the list, smaller markets such as Birmingham and Knoxville did because their merchandise sales outpaced TV viewership.

Columbus, home to Michigan's rival Ohio State, ranked 17th on the list. While Columbus had lower overall TV viewership, it ranked No. 1 in apparel purchases, according to Nielsen. On the flip side, Des Moines/Ames leads in social media, radio listening and streaming but lags in apparel sales.

Des Moines/Ames (Iowa State Cyclones, Iowa Hawkeyes): 256

#2719. 2026 NHL free agent tracker: Patrick Kane returns to Blackhawks on two-year contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NHL free agency has slowed down in late July, but some notable names are still coming off the board. Most notably, Patrick Kane is returning to the Chicago Blackhawks on a two-year contract worth $16 million, the team announced on Thursday.

Already a Chicago legend and future Hall of Famer, Kane won three Stanley Cups and a slew of individual awards with the franchise that selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in 2007. Kane's first stint with the Blackhawks lasted 16 seasons, and he piled up 446 goals and 779 assists in 1,161 games. Kane ranks inside the top five of just about every statistical category in franchise history, and he will get the chance to keep climbing those lists over the next two years.

The Blackhawks sent Kane to the New York Rangers at the 2023 NHL trade deadline, and he played just 19 regular season games there before hitting free agency the next summer. Hip surgery delayed Kane's decision until November of that year, but he ultimately landed with the Detroit Red Wings, where he's spent the last three seasons.

Last season was Kane's best with Detroit, and it proved that he still had some gas left in the tank, at least offensively. Kane posted 16 goals and 41 assists in 67 games -- with 19 of those points coming on the power play.

In his second stint with the Blackhawks, Kane will add another level of playmaking to the power play, and he should strengthen a top six forward group that's bereft of proven talent. Kane will also be an excellent mentor and sounding board for fellow No. 1 overall pick, Connor Bedard, who is set to miss the first month of the season after undergoing shoulder surgery.

Kane isn't the player he once was, but he'll give Chicago a bit more pop at the top of the lineup, and his first game back in a Blackhawks jersey will be a huge night for the city.

#2718. Tuesday Tape: How close is the Chiefs’ pass rush?

In the Kansas City Chiefs' most recent loss, a 28-24 defeat to the Denver Broncos, the pass rush may have had its least impactful performance of the year.

After the game, we wrote about the Chiefs' pass rush that generated just two pressures over 34 dropbacks by Broncos quarterback Bo Nix, according to ESPN analytics. That comes roughly two months after Kansas City harassed Nix in a season-opening win with four sacks and two additional quarterback hits.

The defense executed the game plan well without pressure through three quarters, but let's take a closer look at the Chiefs' pass rush overall from Week 8:

When watching the game back, the Chiefs' rush looked its best when defensive tackle Chris Jones lined up where he should most of the time: inside over the guard in a 3-technique or 4i alignment.

On third-and-2 early on, linebacker Drue Tranquill blitzes and occupies the only player that can help right guard Quinn Meinerz on Jones. Getting a one-on-one, Jones flies off the line and through Meinerz's outside shoulder to quickly enter the pocket. A quick pass negates the win by Jones, who ends up with hands on Nix.

Jones lined up in the B-gap on 24 of the 48 plays he was on the field in Denver (50%). He typically lines up there on neutral downs (1st and 2nd down) or third-and-short.

Needing four yards to convert this third down, Nix's dropback is a little more drawn out than the previous third-and-short pass. This time, Jones and defensive end George Karlaftis bull rush the two right-side linemen and force Nix to feel them in the pocket — and Karlaftis finishes the rush by getting a hand on the pass.

After the game, Chiefs Communications noted that Karlaftis took sole possession of the NFL lead in batted passes (7). He also earned the team's only sack of the afternoon, although it came on a drawn-out play action where Denver left a tight end to block him on the back side.

One of Jones' biggest assets as a rusher is his size; he's hard to see over when a quarterback is trying to scan the field, and his 6-foot-6 frame, even when blocked, can disrupt a dropback from the front of the pocket.

When second and third downs get longer, Jones typically moves to line up either over or outside of the offensive tackle. Defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah becomes a key rusher from the inside in those scenarios; he blew up one screen pass in Denver by knifing in and getting to Nix quickly from an interior spot.

However, I believe Jones is most impactful when rushing from the front of the pocket.

After the game, Jones said the Chiefs needed to "win on one-on-ones." He mentioned it being a big emphasis. He is included in that, but the pass rushers around him need to take advantage of Jones's gravity.

On this second-and-18, the Chiefs' pass rush seems to run a stunt that invites Nix to move forward and to the right of the pocket. Jones flies down off the ball and occupies the right guard and center, setting up defensive end Ashton Gillotte to loop around behind him and meet Nix in the open space.

However, Gillotte is either late to loop or simply forgot that was his assignment until Jones was in front of him. Suddenly, Nix had a wide-open platform to confidently fire a rocket over the middle. It's hard to ask much more from the coverage on this one.

On this third-and-10, Jones draws heavy attention from the three interior linemen of Denver after rushing over the center. The left guard helps and spins around before coming back to help the fullback — a key to the Broncos' pass protection against blitzes — on linebacker Nick Bolton, who gets no penetration.

However, look at the space Karlaftis gives left tackle Garrett Bolles to work into the pocket. Instead of gearing up for an inside move based on how the line came out, the Chiefs' lead edge rusher takes himself out of the play by rushing upfield.

On the other side, a sloppily executed stunt leaves Gillote and rookie R Mason Thomas useless. This gives Nix a platform to deliver a calm strike to move the chains that he simply misses.

As the game wore on, the lack of wins from pass rushers not named Chris Jones became more evident. On this first-down play, up two scores in the fourth quarter, Nix buys himself enough time to eventually find a target over the middle for a huge gain (although Bolton slipped on his way to likely breaking up the pass).

Jones draws two blockers, and most notably, Gillotte can't get past the right tackle, leaving Nix the space to throw. With nose tackle Khyiris Tonga on the field, the team wasn't built to get after the quarterback, so is it worth criticizing the coaching staff for not using edge rusher R Mason Thomas more in a full-time role once the Chiefs build such a late-game lead?

Kansas City's pass rush wasn't the biggest factor in blowing the game in Denver, but a few more splash plays would have gone a long way in a game the Chiefs led in the second half until the final minutes.

One tweak is to keep Jones on the inside at all times when getting after the quarterback and give Thomas more run on the field; he only played 17 snaps against the Broncos, less than 30% of the snaps.

However, the main critique is of the players around Jones. He isn't making plays himself this season, but he is still drawing a lot of attention; his teammates need to sharpen their pass-rush moves to take advantage of it more often.

#2717. Thunder sign Dalen Terry out of G League to provide depth at forward

Needing perimeter depth after a series of injuries, the Oklahoma City Thunder reached into the G League and signed Dalen Terry of the Santa Cruz Warriors to a standard two-year contract, although the second year is non-guaranteed, a story broken by ESPN's Shams Charania and confirmed by other reports.

Terry, a 6'6" defense-first wing, was the No. 18 pick in the 2022 NBA Draft out of Arizona. He played three-and-a-half seasons with Chicago before being traded at last February's deadline to New York, which flipped him to New Orleans, and then the Pelicans waived him. Terry then signed a two-way deal with the 76ers and was promoted to a standard contract at the end of last season, but was waived to make room on the roster so the team could acquire LeBron James. Terry was in training camp with the Golden State Warriors and was set to report to their G League affiliate when the Thunder called.

Across 218 NBA games, Terry has averaged 3.5 points per game. The positive spin for Thunder fans, and why the team took a chance on him, is that he is a plus defender on the wing whose 3-point shooting has improved each season, hitting 36.4% overall last season.

Bringing in Terry helps the Thunder with depth in two ways. First, while he is not going to play a significant role, Terry can give them some wing minutes. Plus, by filling the 15th spot on the roster, the Thunder can use their two-way players without the restrictions of the "under-15" rule.

The Thunder are without three starters due to significant injuries. All-NBA wing Jalen Williams is out with a fractured fibula and dislocated ankle, while All-Defense guard Cason Wallace is dealing with a torn labrum. There is no timetable for either player, but if they return at all this season, it will be late in the campaign. The Thunder also are without All-NBA big man Chet Holmgren due to a right knee patellar tear, but he is expected to return sometime after Christmas (likely in early 2027).

The Thunder calmed the waters around them last night with a 117-112 win over the Cavaliers behind a big night from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander.

#2715. Dynasty Basketball Stock Watch: Ajay Mitchell, Ace Bailey climb the rankings

Another week of the NBA season is in the rearview, which has led to more storylines. The Grizzlies are 6-0 with their young squad led by Cameron Boozer and Ty Jerome. The Kings are 0-6 despite Darius Acuff Jr. putting up monster numbers as a rookie.

With these storylines, more dynasty risers and fallers have presented themselves. Let's break down two risers and two fallers from this past week.

Fantasy Basketball Waiver Wire Week 3: Aday Mara is ready to shine

Rookie big man Aday Mara headlines our top fantasy basketball adds ahead of Week 3.

The Thunder have sustained injuries to Jalen Williams (leg), Cason Wallace (labrum), and Chet Holmgren (patellar tendon), which has cleared the way for Ajay Mitchell to be a high-usage player. The 24-year-old is averaging 17 PPG, 3.6 REB, 3.4 AST, shooting 50 percent from the field, 19 percent from three, and 95.5 percent from the free throw line in 26.9 minutes per game.

With Williams sidelined, Mitchell has averaged 15.2 FGA per game compared to the 9.5 he got in the two games before the injury and 10.4 he got last season. His ability to get into the paint, take on usage with defensive attention, and play good defense will keep him on the court.

Mitchell's elite skill is his ability to finish around the rim, which is at 66.7% this season. The next step is the three-point shot. At UC Santa Barbara, he shot 33.2% on 2.3 attempts per game. In the NBA, his career average is 34.2% on 2.6 attempts per game. He's shot 87.2% from the free throw line for his NBA career, which would indicate that he has touch.

If the three-point volume increases and Mitchell returns to his career average for making them, teams will start to respect the shot more, which will open up the floor even more for him.

Mitchell signed a three-year deal with the Thunder with a team option for the 2027-28 season. The Thunder have historically taken care of their players, so it wouldn't be surprising to see them decline the team option and sign him to a longer extension like they did with Jaylin Williams.

Mitchell began the season near the backend of the top 100 in dynasty rankings, but he's climbed to No. 63 in Rotoworld's latest update. If Mitchell ever gets to a new team where he's the guard running the show, the fantasy upside would take another jump. I'd only entertain selling Mitchell if I got a young established starter back, like Stephon Castle or Keyonte George.

As a prospect coming out of Rutgers, Bailey was a scoring wing who relied on his athleticism and size to make up for questionable shot selection and inconsistent decision-making. When Bailey came to the Jazz, they minimized his role on offense and used him as a spot shooter and not someone who would put the ball on the deck. This summer, he worked on refining more of the non-scoring aspects of his game, and the results have been tremendous.

With Bailey's athleticism and size, he's able to cover so much ground and take on different assignments. His rebounds have increased from 4.2 to 7.6; his blocks have increased from 0.7 to 1.6. He still misses defensive rotations, and his handle could use work, but it's been a great showing to begin year two.

Bailey was likely around the back end of the top 100 in dynasty rankings at the beginning of the season, but he's climbed to No. 64 in Rotoworld's latest update.

Since Bailey was a top draft pick, he's likely rostered by managers who are looking to the future. Unless I'm getting an overpay like a Deni Avdija or his teammate Darryn Peterson, I'd keep him and not entertain offers. He's only 20 years old and will likely continue to improve.

Gobert is currently averaging 7.4 PPG, 12 REB, and .6 BLK, shooting 42.5 % from the field and 43.9% from the line. The main reason why the field goal percentage has dropped is that he went from averaging 77.3 percent at the rim in the 2025-26 season to 57.7 percent at the rim this season. On the defensive end, he's still been exactly as advertised. The Minnesota Timberwolves are second in defensive rating at 104.1, and Gobert is the main defensive anchor on that end.

The rim finishing will likely improve given that we have plenty of evidence that Gobert is not this bad of a rim finisher. However, he is 34 years old, and the Timberwolves drafted Joan Beringer No. 17 overall in the 2025 NBA Draft. If Gobert continues to struggle around the rim, it will be detrimental to their offense to the point where Minnesota could begin to reduce his minutes. Especially when we see instances like this:

On Rotoworld's dynasty rankings, Gobert is currently sitting at No. 142. I would not be panic selling him because of the bad shooting. He's still too impactful of a defensive player to not play. I would wait until the rim finishing improves before making a move.

Green is currently averaging 3.2 PPG, 5 REB, 6.3 AST, shooting 38.9 percent from the field, 28.6 percent from three, and 75 percent from the free throw line. In the past, he's been so good with his timing and his brain that he could play as a small-ball five and help lead a great defense.

While Green's basketball IQ is off the charts, his body is starting to show signs of regression. He doesn't have the athletic pop that he used to have, which is affecting his ability to play center. While the offense has never been a strong suit for Green, his usage has gone from 16.1 percent to 10.2 percent, which decreases his shot attempts across the board. Fortunately for the Warriors, he processes the game at a high enough level to where he can run as a point guard on offense and likely not have it affect the team as much.

In Rotoworld's latest dynasty rankings update, Green checks in at No. 232. Selling Green is a bit harder because his categorical skillset is very reliant on rebounds and assists at the big man position. If you're a competing team and are looking for a boost in those categories, Green might be the best option for the current dynasty ranking price if you can live with the bad shooting. If you're looking to sell, I would be paying attention to the other good teams in your league and see who could use what Green provides and then look for someone who fits your timeline or draft capital.

Tyran Stokes made his Kansas debut against Fordham on Monday. In 25 minutes, the 19-year-old put up 15 points (5-of-7 FGs, 4-of-7 FTs), seven rebounds, an assist, a block, and four turnovers. He looked exactly how a potential No. 1 pick should look. Stokes had some good reads in the pick-and-roll and he also made an impact defensively. Ideally, he'd get more than seven shot attempts, but he's shown that he can be more aggressive against good teams.
