#2714. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2713. Miami Dolphins: Deux et Machina, not for us!

The Miami Dolphins have played two "one-half" games the last two weeks. A "half-game" was good enough against the hapless New York Jets but a "half-game" was NOWHERE near good enough against the unspectacular New England Patriots. How they reached the Super Bowl last year just shows that lady luck and buffoonery still reign supreme in the NFL.

Zebras gone wild – Courtesy of Greek and Latin writers:

And let us not forget how the Patriots are the recipient of every close call, especially against us. I literally think that on EVERY single non-procedural penalty, the refs call up to Goodell and Satan to ask permission to charge the Patriots with a penalty. I am not joking. A bunch of blind shamans from Mongolia would do a better job officiating. How in the name of God do the field refs rule the NE dude short and then go to commercial and then when we get back from the commercial we have a "Deux et Machina" moment where NE is GIVEN a first down AND Steve Ross is kicked in the groin to boot. For those of you who may not know "Deux et Machina" ….it is a Latin phrase written into plays/stories thousands of years ago to explain how a character can be in the Aegean Sea one moment and the very next scene the character is sitting on top of Mount Vesuvius. The term translates to God and Machine. It takes God and Machine to stop the Miami Dolphins.

And the networks and the NFL trot out Gene Steratore (remember he is the Phins major Zerba enemy) to say how stupid Dolphins' fans are for even questioning the infinite wisdom of the NFL. In the offseason, I will rack my own brain and re-watch games where the Fins were completely ruined by the refs. I will try to write a treatise on this.

I HATE having to sound whiny about the officiating, but IT IS A NATIONWIDE STORY. Armando Salguero et al have discussed the garbage that masquerades as officiating.

Like D'Attaglia in the Godfather, NE is not our real enemy; just an annoyance. Buffalo is our Barzini!

On to the game itself: NE is NOT very much better than us. Don't forget that. The announcers were fawning over the overrated Drake Maye. He isn't that good. He throws a decent long ball but remember NE got the matchups they wanted. Not hard throws. He isn't 1/100th the QB that Tom Brady was. Know this: it is 10,000 times harder to thread a 3rd and 18-yard deep-square-in under a withering pass rush (one of the routes that put Aikman and Irvin in the HOF) versus throwing a deep ball when he has 5 seconds to throw with very little pressure. Generally speaking, those throws aren't there in the playoffs when it is freezing in Buffalo, Pittsburgh and Kansas City. This is one reason why the Phins haven't won a playoff game, much less a road playoff game in 10,000 years since a dome playoff game against Seattle (going from memory). Yes, Seattle used to be in the AFC. Chuck Knox, Jim Zorn, Davie Krieg all come to mind.

Moving on, I want to give out a simple sign if your team is good or not good. What I am about to say doesn't guarantee a Super Bowl or a playoff win but it tells you if you have a chance.

The sign is simply this: if you can run the ball for 2 yards when the opposing KNOWS it is coming, you have a chance to be good. The reverse: can you stop a team from getting 2 yards when everyone knows they are going to run. That is the sign. If you remember with all those McDaniel teams, we would pop 30, 40 and 50 yards runs BUT when we tried to run a for two yards with Ollie Gordon, he was BLOWN UP in the back field. Pathetic! We could not get the two yards when the other team KNOWS it is coming.

I see improvement in this field with our OLINE. I see improvement in this team. There are so many good signs. EXCEPT special teams. Our kicker gets 1 pass. He used it up on the doink. He killed us on the bad miss. It didn't cost us the game but imagine if it was close. Don't forget, Borregales missed too and he kicked in the stadium for YEARS. Are we able to get a punt block or a kick return? And someone needs to look up Carlos Huerta (kicker for the Canes about 30 years ago). Huerta was/is the GREATEST ON-SIDE KICKER EVER. The Canes were losing to Univ of Michigan by 15 in the 4th qtr in 1988. After a Canes score, he drove the ball straight into the ground and the ball shot up very high and then it was a free-for-all ( I passed up a Ted Nugent reference here, so there! )……the Canes recovered and Huerta kicked the FG to win 31-30. But no, the Dolphins tried the dribble and it failed. Special teams COULD be to our advantage BUT NO, Sullivan and Hafley are settling for mediocrity.

Back to improvements: Before we jump down the Phins throat let's remember there were many games against Pats where we led in the first half and Belichick made his half-time improvements and we lost. This happened while Jacoby was their QB.

The way we lost to them yesterday is nothing new. Vrabel learned a lot from Belichick.

Did you notice that on first down, many of Ollie's runs went for 0 or 1 yard? Then on second down he would get 6-8 yards, still good, but we did not wear them down. This is good news, NE actively had to respect our run game but they didn't wear down. We had some manageable 3rd downs. On the flip side, we wore down while on defense. They found a weakness where the RB would seemingly head for the initial run read but then almost invariably cut back BEHIND the line and way from the initial run read. I haven't looked at the film yet but that tells me the DEs and/or LBs (away from the ball) aren't getting through and/or they are overcommitting aka racing to the ball but behind their own DL ( where the LBs are )not in the backfield (easier said than done). This will sound ludicrous based on our talent but back in the day, believe it or not, teams would run at Lawrence Taylor (LB Goat) so that they could try to get hats on him. If they ran away from him, he would simply run down the back from behind. He was virtually unblockable. We need to get that edge (who plays away from the ball to penetrate) A LITTLE( in the Goldilocks zone ) to take away the cutbacks that we saw yesterday. We don't have that talent. Yet. Uche and Chop played decently but they have their limits. We all know TALENT always wins out. We are heading in the right direction, EXCEPT for special teams.

Malik played well: he made two really bad throws and if he only makes two bad throws every game, I can live with that. Who is out there in college (outside of Mestemaker who gives you a thrill? All those current QB dudes(Chambliss, Leavitt, etc. are system QBs from the sissy 7-on-7 schools…just like Maye).

The Pats made an obvious choice yesterday: funnel everything to the inside and set their DEs to keep outside to prevent the Malik runs. They dare us to run straight ahead and to throw. Their first half, we did. I have to watch the film but NE went to 9 on the intensity level and we simply didn't match. Those little Malik runs weren't there and we didn't exploit the middle of the field like we should have.

In closing, NE is a good team, not great. We need to set the organizational sights on surpassing NE and eventually Buffalo and to be able to fight against a fully charged Baltimore(with Lamar?) and KC(I fear 10 more years of Mahomes). And then to be able to fight the LA Rams, Seattle, San Francisco and the Bears(this is the team that scares me long term because Williams is young and they are improving).

#2712. Cardinals get brutal Jeremiyah Love news as No. 3 overall pick heads to IR

Cardinals get brutal Jeremiyah Love news as No. 3 overall pick heads to IR originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Arizona Cardinals beat the Dallas Cowboys in an incredible comeback win that went to overtime and saw Gardner Minshew come in and take the starting quarterback job.

But he wasn't the only one to take over in this one. Tyler Allgeier also turned into a weapon for the Cardinals, putting together a monster performance in the OT win. That only happened because Jeremiyah Love left the game early due to an ankle injury.

According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, the news for Love isn't good. The star running back selected No. 3 overall is headed to injured reserve due to this ankle injury.

"Sources: #AZCardinals RB Jeremiyah Love is headed to Injured Reserve because of a high-ankle sprain that knocks him out for 4-5 weeks," Rapoport reports. "Arizona's first-round pick has previously been dealing with a different ankle sprain."

This is some horrible news for the Cardinals and their No. 3 overall pick. Love, who has been in and out of the lineup due to injury, is now on injured reserve.

He had avoided landing on IR this season as he nursed ankle injuries, though he did miss some time earlier this year. He finally came back for Week 8, but suffered another ankle injury that is now known as a high-ankle sprain that requires an IR stint.

The Cardinals have lost their rookie RB for the next four games, meaning Love will miss Weeks 9, 10, 11, and 12. With a 4-5 week timeline for a return from injury, Love could come back for Week 13.

MORE: Jerry Jones defends Brian Schottenheimer after Cowboys collapse vs. Cardinals

But considering they have a Week 14 bye, it might make sense for the Cardinals to sit Love out for that matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles, and then try to bring him back for Week 15 to close out the regular season.

The Cardinals have a soft schedule to end the year, facing the New York Jets, New Orleans Saints, Las Vegas Raiders, and San Francisco 49ers from Weeks 15 through 18.

Love is going to miss at least four weeks, potentially five, with the bye week giving him a chance to miss six weeks and hopefully recover from a high ankle sprain and come back to end the season.

If he can return to action for those final four weeks of the year, Love could provide something positive to take away from his injury-riddled rookie season.

But, for now, the Cardinals are set to lose Love for around a month, as he's going to land on injured reserve, forcing him to miss at least the next four games for Arizona as they deal with a lot of injury issues on offense this season.

#2710. Wolverines in the NFL: Blake Corum scores again, Josh Metellus makes 13 tackles

Blake Corum scored for the second straight week, and two other former Michigan Wolverines helped the Rams keep the Chargers out of the end zone. Six Michigan alumni took the field at Ford Field as the Lions handed the Vikings their first loss of the season. And on Monday night, two former Michigan tight ends faced off in Seattle.

Here's how the Wolverines fared in Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season.

The Rams had just 10 rushing yards at halftime against the Chargers. Corum more than doubled that on one play in the third quarter, breaking free for a 23-yard touchdown that turned a one-point lead into a 17-9 advantage. He finished with a team-high 73 yards on 11 carries, averaging 6.6 yards per attempt in the 24-9 win.

The Rams had two more former Wolverines making plays on defense. Edge rusher Josaiah Stewart finished with six tackles and a sack, while cornerback Josh Wallace made four tackles, including three solo stops.

Metellus finished with 13 tackles and a pass breakup in Minnesota's 19-15 loss at Ford Field. On the other side, Aidan Hutchinson made four solo tackles and forced a fumble. He played 50 of Detroit's 53 defensive snaps, as the Lions held Minnesota to 266 total yards.

Rookies Derrick Moore and Jimmy Rolder also saw time on defense and special teams. Moore played 22 defensive snaps, and Rolder played 17 on defense and another 13 on special teams. Unfortunately, Rolder will miss the rest of the season due to a hamstring injury he suffered in this game.

For Minnesota, fullback Max Bredeson played seven offensive snaps, and guard Trevor Keegan appeared off the bench.

Loveland caught 7-of-9 targets for 65 yards against Seattle on Monday Night Football. He led the Bears in receptions and finished second in receiving yards.

On the other sideline, Seattle tight end AJ Barner turned his lone catch into a 17-yard gain on three targets. Former Michigan linebacker Devin Bush also saw action for Chicago.

Turner recovered two fumbles and made three tackles as Cincinnati beat Tennessee, 43-36, in overtime. Unfortunately, Turner left the game in the fourth quarter due to injury, so hopefully he isn't out for long.

Fellow Bengals cornerback Daxton Hill made four solo tackles, defensive tackle Kris Jenkins added one, and William Wagner handled long-snapping duties.

Ben Bredeson started at guard in Tampa Bay's 16-0 win over Atlanta.

Josh Uche had four solo tackles and a sack, and Kenneth Grant added two tackles, in Miami's 24-19 loss to New England.

Rashan Gary made two tackles and Jaishawn Barham added a solo stop in Dallas' 33-30 overtime loss to Arizona.

Mason Graham made three tackles in Cleveland's 27-6 loss to Pittsburgh.

Jourdan Lewis had two tackles in Jacksonville's 42-7 win over Indianapolis.

Kwity Paye had two tackles in the Raiders' 38-33 win over the Jets.

Mike Sainristil made a special-teams tackle in Washington's 27-10 win over Philadelphia.

#2707. 2. Bundesliga: Keller strikes late to secure important Fürth victory over Kiel

With the contest seemingly heading towards a goalless draw, Keller struck in the 87th minute to settle a closely fought encounter and give Heiko Vogel's side a much-needed victory.

Fürth started the contest brightly, enjoying the majority of possession during the opening stages, although clear-cut opportunities were initially difficult to come by. Holstein Kiel threatened first through Giorgi Kvilitaia, who was found inside the penalty area following a cross from the right, but the Georgian forward was quickly crowded out before he could get a clean shot away.

The visitors gradually grew into the game, with Hiroki Sekine missing a good opportunity in the 25th minute after getting on the end of a delivery from Leon Parduzi. The Japanese defender found himself unmarked inside the penalty area but could only direct his header over Florian Hellstern's crossbar. Jonas Therkelsen also went close shortly beforehand, seeing his effort from the edge of the box drift narrowly wide.

Fürth struggled to create much in the final third, although Felix Klaus fired wide after a promising counter-attacking opportunity. The hosts came closest to breaking the deadlock just before half-time when Gian-Luca Itter intercepted a misplaced pass and released Omar Sillah through on goal. However, the forward lost his footing while attempting to control the ball, allowing Timon Weiner to avoid being tested. The sides subsequently went into the interval goalless.

Holstein Kiel introduced John Tolkin and Gyan de Regt at the interval, replacing Leon Parduzi and Jonas Therkelsen respectively, but the visitors almost immediately found themselves under pressure. Fürth worked the ball through Ole Pohlmann and Shinta Appelkamp before Klaus fired narrowly over from distance.

Kiel responded with a dangerous counter-attack of their own in the 53rd minute. De Regt picked out Adrian Kaprálik, with an excellent diagonal pass, allowing the winger to race into the penalty area. His effort towards the near post was well saved by Hellstern, who pushed the ball behind for a corner.

The visitors continued to threaten, with Phil Harres denied by Hellstern in the 64th minute after a defensive error from Fürth's Hendry Blank inadvertently played the ball into his path. The goalkeeper reacted well to block the striker's close-range effort and keep the scores level.

Kiel were arguably the more dangerous side as the second half progressed, prompting Fürth to introduce Aaron Keller in place of Pohlmann in the 66th minute. Jordan and Faton Ademi also entered the contest as Vogel looked to inject fresh energy into his attacking options.

With neither side able to find a breakthrough, the match appeared destined to finish without a goal. However, Keller had other ideas, with the substitute finding the back of the net in the 87th minute to hand Fürth a crucial late advantage.

The hosts subsequently held on to their narrow lead to secure a 1-0 victory, ensuring another disappointing afternoon for Tim Walter's side and claiming three important points in their battle to move away from the bottom end of the 2. Bundesliga table.

#2706. Q&A with Hall of Famer Mitch Richmond, talking Yaxel Lendeborg, LeBron, Jokic, Game Pulse

Mitch Richmond is NBA history personified: NBA champion, Rookie of the Year, five-time All-NBA, six-time All-Star and Hall of Famer. For many fans, he is best remembered as part of the legendary Run TMC era of the Golden State Warriors, with Tim Hardaway and Chris Mullin.

Before sitting down for an interview with NBC Sports, Richmond was interacting with fans on the NBA App through Game Pulse. For those unfamiliar, Game Pulse combines a live court visualization with highlights and advanced statistics, including shot charts, in a live-updating experience that also features commentary and perspectives from NBA legends such as Muggsy Bogues, Carlos Boozer, Gary Payton, Joakim Noah and more.Here is our conversation with Richmond (edited for length and clarity).

NBC Sports: You've been on this Game Pulse NBA app experience with the fans. How has that been for you?

Richmond: It's been great. You know, that's my first time being on the Pulse. I always watch the association, and sometimes I already catch everything on NBA TV. But it was my first time, so it was a good experience.

Q: It seems like it's a good experience for the fans. They get real interaction not just with the studio people, but with people like yourself, who happen to be Hall of Famers.

Richmond: Yeah, no question about it. It's just the fan engagement. The fans want to be as close as they can, and sometimes they want to hear from other players watching the game. So it gives me an opportunity to kind of reach out to them, and especially since I played so long ago, so they don't know me. But it's a time to start Googling me. You know what I mean?

Q: I think people underestimate, though, like how great and how impactful Run TMC was, and that era of Warriors basketball. As you look at the league now. Is there a player that kind of reminds you of Tim Hardaway?

Richmond: That's a good question. Oh man, who reminds me of Little Tim? Oh man, I don't, it's hard. He had such power when he dribbles the ball, he gives you that shoulder as he goes by that you can't get back in front of him. Yeah, man, that's hard to do.

Q: It might be even harder with Chris Mullin in some ways.

Richmond: Oh man, let's see who Mully would be. I mean, Mully was not the fastest guy, but it is back to what I say: It's how you use your body, and how you use your skills, and how you move. We see it now in today's game, it's all about getting guys in angles when they pick-and-roll. They want you on their back and they want to make sure that you never get back in front of them. Mully had the tendency, if you get on the side of him, he has a way that you never get back around him. And so he was really, really methodical of how he's going to move and take his little steps, and might do a little bird flip. So yeah, he was very tough to guard.

Q: You're close to the Warriors still to this day. They've been fun to watch at the start of the season. What's impressed you about Yaxel Lendeborg as a rookie, just coming in like this?

Richmond: Coming in with that attitude, man, like I belong. And truly, truly, they need a spark like that. We don't know how long Curry is gonna Curry is gonna give us, but they need a young star to come in and kind of help some of that load for Curry right now. I think he's the guy. He has the temperament, and I like him. I like how he came in with Luka, arguing a little bit, but hey, I think that you need that. You need that spark. You need that spice.

Q: I like that [Warriors coach Steve] Kerr trusted him enough to give him that assignment in his first NBA game.

Richmond: I'm pretty sure he wanted it, and I think that's what great players do at times, man. It's for greatness. I want to guard the best player. You know what I mean. I have no problem. I want to guard the best player. We haven't seen that in a while.

Q: What other rookies have stood out to you?

Richmond: I mean, you look at Caleb. Man, he's going to be a star down in Chicago. Caleb Williams. I like AJ [Dybantsa of the Wizards]. AJ is good. Even the young [Cameron] Boozer. Hopefully, he can start to get his game rolling. But I think it's a lot of good young talent that we have, and I just love watching the games, to tell you the truth.

Q: Houston is off to a fast start. Dallas has knocked off two undefeated teams. What are you liking about those teams? What have you seen from them that's making them look kind of dangerous early?

Richmond: I spent a little time with them in Macau when the Rockets played the Dallas Mavericks over there [preseason], and so they looked like just a fun team. And actually, both teams was personable, and I think they get along with one another. One, and they got two good coaches that's coaching them right now. So, man, I thought Houston had a little bit more than Dallas, but Dallas has been playing excellent this year.

Q: Houston, I like the way they're built. I think they can be really dangerous in a West that feels a little more open right now.

Richmond: No question about it. I think the West is wide open. I think someone... can Portland come out of there? You know Portland is looking pretty good right now. I think the West, like you say, the West is wide open. Lakers are even looking pretty good.

Q: You mentioned Portland. Is there anybody else who's just like, wow! When they're on, I kind of want to watch them. I want to watch those players.

Richmond: I'm loving watching the Knicks, tell you the truth. I love watching the Knicks and how they play. Then I just start going for players to see how they're doing. I go and pop over at Denver and see what [Nikola] Jokic is doing. I'm always on the channel with Golden State. I'm always turning the channel to Dallas. I mean, the Lakers, because the Lakers can actually do something as well. We didn't expect that, but the center that they got from Utah?

Richmond: I mean, no one ever saw this, buried in Utah, and now seeing him, and he was hurt as well. But to see what he's been doing and the numbers he's been putting up, you know, they needed a big man like that to run the floor and catch it at the rim.

Q: On the other side, the Heat have just not gelled yet. It hasn't come together consistently. When you see them, what's missing?

Richmond: I think just a little bit more time together. You know what I mean? I think sometimes, teams mesh very well. Look at Philly. You know, how LeBron [James] just came and and haven't missed the beat over there. They're just playing real fluid ball as well. I think Boston is playing pretty good as well. I think sometimes you need just a little bit more time to gel. We haven't seen that yet, so hopefully they can they can catch a groove and start winning some games.

Q: Philadelphia has gelled really quickly, but is that just LeBron bringing his own culture and that's a team where guys seem willing to sacrifice, and they're kind of in the right place to make plays.

Richmond: I think the sacrifice is a little different when you have a star player coming in that is a volume shooter. LeBron kind of plays every part of the game, so he doesn't need those 40-point nights. You know, he might have one this year, but he has enough guns around him. And I think the guys, you have your shooting hands ready to shoot the ball when you have a guy that is a willing passer, and LeBron has been more of a willing passer, especially when he knows that he got young guns at his beck and call anywhere he goes. These guys can really shoot the ball. Look at Embiid. Embiid is in better shape. The guys are bringing enthusiasm. They had some enthusiasm over there. Let's see if they can keep it the whole year, because at some point in time, teams are going to start figuring them out, and see how it happens. But I do like the start of them; they look like a team to be reckoned with later.

Q: You mentioned Jokic's passing and a couple other guys. There are some great passers in the league right now. Who are some of the guys you want to tune in to watch because they see the court differently?

Richmond: Jokic is that guy. You know, if I played with him, man, I'd be coming off screens all day, going back door because he truly, truly finds guys. We have to put LeBron, he's still there. LeBron still knows how to get passes to the right guys. It's a few others out there, but I just love how guys like that move the ball, share it, and it looks wonderful.

#2705. Giants are betting favorite to win NFC East, and have John Harbaugh to thank

The New York Giants are now the betting favorite to win the NFC East, per FanDuel Sportsbook. The 4-2-1 division-leading Giants are -134 to win their first division title since 2011. The Dallas Cowboys are +220, the Washington Commanders +400, and the Philadelphia Eagles +1600.

The struggles of the division's other three underachieving teams have opened the door for the Giants. Head coach John Harbaugh, though, deserves most of the credit. Harbaugh, the $100 million coach the Giants successfully courted after the Baltimore Ravens fired him following 18 seasons, made his team believe it could do what it has done so far.

Harbaugh, 63, gave a huge hint of what was to come at his introductory press conference in January. Asked if he considered taking a year off from coaching after the Ravens let him go, Harbaugh scoffed at the idea.

"I figured I didn't have enough time to take time off," Harbaugh said. "There's no time for that, so just couldn't wait to get back to work. That was never a question."

There is something else Harbaugh doesn't have time for. Rebuilding, or accepting that circumstances — like major injuries at crucial positions — will derail hopes of a good season.

"We have an opportunity to go win, and I like these players, man," Harbaugh said at that introductory press conference. "I know they want to be successful and they want to go to work, so absolutely we can do that, and that's our plan to do that. The plan is to win every game. I mean, one game at a time. You go into every game planning to win that game. That's our expectation."

Harbaugh has driven the Giants to have the best, most productive day possible every day. Harbaugh's Giants put in as many hours and practice as hard as the rules will allow.

"You do the best you can with it every single day. Well, that means a lot when you really think about what that means," Harbaugh said. "Are we really doing our best? Are we really putting everything we have into it for this day? Are we really attacking the day with an enthusiasm unknown to mankind? Another level? Is that possible? Is that something that we can accomplish? Can we have the best meeting and the best practice in the history of the National Football League? Can we? When you do that day by day, you build something, you take it onto the field, and you let the chips fly, and you go play some ball."

So far, a lot of the chips have fallen in the Giants' favor.

In 18 seasons in Baltimore, Harbaugh's teams made the playoffs 12 times, had just three losing seasons, and won a Super Bowl. He did not have to convince anyone he knew what he was doing.

"It started from day one in the spring. Coach (John Harbaugh) came in here and just the details, the messaging, the leadership. His record speaks for itself as a head coach. The guy has won a lot of games," GM Joe Schoen said during the bye week. "The players were eager to buy in. We have a good, young nucleus of players here that just want to win. Just want to win, whatever it takes. Coach Harbaugh and his staff have done a very good job of laying out the plan. This is what it looks like. This is how you practice. This is how you approach OTA's. This is how you approach the offseason program. This is how you train in training camp. This is how you prepare in-season, week to week."

If Harbaugh were building instead of trying to win as often as possible, he probably wouldn't have brought so many ex-Ravens with him.

Giving 33-year-old Odell Beckham a chance, even though it didn't work out, was about trying to field the best team Harbaugh could right now.

Trading for J.J. McCarthy after Jaxson Dart's Week 2 season-ending injury was a clear sign that Harbaugh wasn't tossing in the towel on the season, despite whatever long-term quarterback drama that move eventually brings with it.

Going after Jeffery Simmons and Jonathan Taylor on the trade market is about capitalizing on the opportunity the Giants have, not building for a better tomorrow.

None of the Giants' NFC East challengers have had the seasons they imagined. I asked the lead writers from Blogging the Boys (Cowboys), Bleeding Green Nation (Eagles), and Hogs Haven (Commanders) for thoughts on whether they felt their teams could challenge for the crown, and who would eventually win the division.

At 3-5, Dallas is in second place. The Cowboys already have a loss to the Giants. They have losses to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Arizona Cardinals. They haven't fixed their defensive issues, with young defensive coordinator Christian Parker looking like he might not be ready for the job. Owner Jerry Jones is being asked about head coach Brian Schottenheimer's future.

Despite that, R.J. Ochoa of Blogging the Boys is still a believer that the Cowboys will pull themselves together and win the division.

"The Dallas Cowboys will in the most basic, bare bones, literal way possible.

"I say this because of the non-Giants teams in the division; the Cowboys might be the least fallible. On paper, the Cowboys have pieces that comprise contending/challenging teams, but they have not been anything close to their on-paper version so far this season.

"They deserve no benefit of the doubt right now. Everyone keeps believing they will put together a little run to make "challenging" a thing, but they are losing to hapless teams like the Buccaneers and Cardinals.

"Congratulations to the Giants on a successful start to the John Harbaugh era.

The Eagles, entering Sunday's game with the Giants, have lost a stunning six games in a row. They have lost an immense amount of talent, including quarterback Jalen Hurts to injury. They have traded away players like A.J. Brown and Cam Jurgens, and watched right tackle Lane Johnson retire during the season.

Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation is taking the Cowboys to emerge as champs.

"The Eagles are arguably the worst team in the NFL. It's hard to see how things are going to get better for them this season.

"The Giants certainly have a good energy going for them as they currently sit atop the division. But quarterback uncertainty remains. The Cowboys could eventually wake up; they have the NFL's sixth-easiest remaining schedule. I'll take Dallas to very narrowly edge the Giants."

The 2-4-1 Commanders lost quarterback Jayden Daniels for two games, and have been beset by clock management issues. It is hard to count them out, though.

Scott Bair of Hogs Haven isn't quite sure what to expect from the Commanders.

"The Commanders have the most talented quarterback in the division. Notice the word choice there. I said most talented. I did not say best. Not while he's learning a new scheme and seemingly a bit hesitant to let it rip.The rest of the team is not strong enough to contend with the Giants unless he's Superman, and Daniels isn't currently wearing the cape.

"So, to answer your question, I can't quite answer it yet.

"That Thursday night game against the Giants in Week 10 will tell us everything. If Daniels becomes JD5 and flashes the logo on his chest on that night, he'll answer the question for you.

"If he's hot, Washington goes on a heater and Big Blue is in trouble. Their defensive players have nearly (but not quite) figured this new blitz-heavy scheme out. If he remains timid or slightly out of sync, then the Giants cruise.

As the Giants return from their bye, they have games against the Eagles and Commanders in five days. Harbaugh knows what they mean.

"The two most important games of the season will be coming up after we come back from the bye, which will set the direction for the rest of the season really," Harbaugh said after the Week 7 victory over the Houston Texans.

Can the Giants pull this off? Maybe, maybe not. Watching it unfold, though, will certainly be better than already being knee-deep in draft talk.

#2703. Lions roar, Sooners stunned: East Texas A&M upsets Oklahoma 68-64 on opening night

NORMAN, Okla. — East Texas A&M coach Jaret von Rosenberg told fans to get excited about his team entering the 2026-27 season.

East Texas A&M, formerly known as Texas A&M-Commerce and with a basketball program that finished near the bottom in the Southland Conference the last two seasons, shocked Oklahoma with a 68-64 season-opening victory Monday night for its first win against a power conference opponent.

"I told people to get excited," said von Rosenberg, who has coached the program since 2017. "I think this basically solidifies that."

Bo Aldridge led East Texas A&M with 22 points on 8-for-12 shooting in the season opener for both teams. Mohamed Diakite and Alonzo Dodd each scored 15 points for the Lions, who entered the game as 30 1/2-point underdogs, according to one oddsmaker, and never trailed after taking a 13-12 lead with 12:59 remaining before halftime.

Oklahoma tied it at 58-all and 60-all with 2:51 to go but never took the lead. Aldridge made two free throws with 3 seconds left to play to seal it.

"You're always trying to get buy-in as fast as you can in the season," von Rosenberg said, "and you have a plan, and sometimes when the plan doesn't work it's hard to get guys to see it. The best thing from this whole situation is they can see what works and what's successful and what doesn't. So hopefully we can just build off this."

Pop Isaacs scored 15 points, and Derrion Reid scored 14 and grabbed 10 rebounds for the Sooners.

It was East Texas A&M's first win in the three-game series between the two teams. Oklahoma beat the Lions 84-56 on Nov. 21, 2024, and 87-59 on Dec. 1, 1970.

Oklahoma has an Southeastern Conference-most five players on the roster who have appeared in 100 or more games: Tae Davis (134), Duke Brennan (133), B.J. Edwards (110), Xzayvier Brown (104) and Isaacs (100). Brown didn't play on Monday because of a lower-body injury.

East Texas A&M, located about an hour east of Dallas, joined the Southland Conference in 2022 after long competing in Division II. Nine of the 15 players listed on the Lions' roster are freshmen.

"The only thing I know to do is apologize to the fanbase and get better," Oklahoma coach Porter Moser said after the loss. "I apologize to every single person that came in. The things you do in a game like this in basketball that gets you beat, we did. We had 15 turnovers, 15 missed free throws and (were) plus-18 from the 3-point line. Those are things that get you beat in this game. ... They got us on our heels, and we stayed on our heels."

Oklahoma entered having won 22 of its past 23 season openers, with the lone defeat during the stretch coming in 2022-23 to Sam Houston, 52-51, in Norman.

The Sooners also entered the 2026-27 season with 30 consecutive nonconference wins at Lloyd Noble Center.

East Texas A&M: Heads to Houston to play Rice on Thursday.

Oklahoma: Hosts Mississippi Valley State on Friday.

#2702. Bucks Reacts Survey: Are the Milwaukee Bucks too nice?

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NBA. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bucks fans and fans across the country.

This Milwaukee Bucks season was never going to be pretty and, so far, well, the Bucks could crack mirrors. There's still plenty to be excited about, of course—namely, the team's three youngest players—but to this point these Bucks aren't exactly the dawgs we hoped they'd be. Porous on the perimeter and feeble inside, are these Bucks simply too nice?

After seven games, the Bucks have shown promise on the glass—even if there are some warning signs—in an attempt to win the possession game and maximise their opportunities to keep the scoreboard ticking over and the games close. But there is more than one way to skin a cat, and the Bucks aren't doing much to make life difficult for their opponents—certainly not from a disruption point of view. So far, the Bucks sit dead last in steals per game (5.6 SPG), nearly half a steal worse than their nearest opponent (the Memphis Grizzlies, who average 6.0 SPG). They're also dead last in opponent turnovers, forcing just 12.7 per game (nearly a full turnover fewer than the New York Knicks and Utah Jazz, who force 13.6 turnovers a night). All this means that Milwaukee isn't generating extra looks through its defence.

Compounding the issue, the Bucks are mediocre at best when it comes to turning back shot attempts. Myles Turner and (sometimes) Kel'el Ware aside, these Bucks simply do not block shots, averaging just 4.6 BPG thus far, "good" for 18th in the league. But the Bucks' rim troubles don't stop there. They're currently 23rd in the league in defending the paint, conceding 50.9 points in the paint per night, while also allowing 27.6 free throw attempts per night (22nd in the league). It should come as no surprise then that they rank 21st in the league in opponent effective field goal percentage (at 54.8%).

Realistically, these numbers shouldn't be too surprising. While Turner blocks shots, he's never been an elite defender or physical presence—and he's the Buck with the best defensive reputation. Kyle Kuzma and Jaime Jaquez Jr. compete, but they don't have the physical gifts or explosive athleticism to be more than useful team defenders. In the backcourt, Tyler Herro has long been a defensive liability—or at least regarded as such. And none of these guys have any "nasty" in 'em.

Ryan Rollins, on the other hand, has the length, and has shown the capacity to lock down at times. He's also got some of that defensive stink to him (see his battles with Tyrese Haliburton). But in the early season, Rollins has seemed more intent on getting his shot off in a completely understandable bid to (1) prove himself worthy of the expectations placed on him prior to the season and (2) prove himself worthy of a new, lucrative contract—from Milwaukee or someone else—next offseason. Forest for the trees type stuff.

Of course, it's also worth noting that, despite their limitations, the starting group prior to last night's change-up has actually been a real positive for the Bucks. This group—the team's most frequent five-man lineup with 75 minutes of playing time—has a +21.6 net rating (per Basketball-Reference). Comparatively, just four of the team's 19 other five-man lineups have fared better, but each of these have played fewer than seven minutes together. In fact, besides the starting group, no other five-man lineup has played more than 17 minutes of action thus far, making it difficult to truly determine which combinations are working and which aren't.

Another factor to consider is the team's bench. Outside of AJ Green, the core reserves are all very young, meaning they're simultaneously learning the NBA game and trying to establish themselves in the league. This is not a new combination, but it's not an easy one either—and certainly not one that typically leads to winning basketball. Youth aside, the Bucks' bench also lacks any true defensive aces—at least at this stage—despite their effort (see Kasparas Jakučionis, Brayden Burries, and Nate Ament) or gifts (see Kel'el Ware). All of this is to say that, like the players themselves, Jon Horst has more work to do.

On a bigger scale, could the Bucks' struggles to disrupt opposing offences in part boil down to a mantra malfunction? Their new motto, "Compete. Together. Get better," sure is wholesome, but is it all a bit too Brady Bunch? And is Jenkins leaning too much into relationship-building with his new herd of fawns? His decision to bench Rollins suggests not. The likely answer, then, is that this is simply a case of culture first, results later. Build rapport—nurture the youth—then let the metamorphoses begin.

Regardless, for the Bucks to start doing more than show glimpses between the cracks, they might have to find a way to get a little meaner.

What do you think? Are these Bucks too squeaky clean? Let us know your thoughts by voting below—and don't forget to explain your reasons in the comments.

#2699. 'We don't have enough time to recover:' Is the NBA game outpacing the players?

Standing near half-court with a towel draped over his shoulders, Thunder center Isaiah Hartenstein attempted to drum up encouragement for his rookie deputy Aday Mara as he approached the bench. Teammates Micah Peavy and Bennett Stirtz waited to do the same, while occasionally tilting their heads back at the jumbotron, which flashed a deficit of nearly 20 points. Veteran guard Alex Caruso, dressed in street clothes, could only clap his hands in hopes of bringing a jolt of energy that simply would not come in a 119-98 loss to the Rockets — an unimaginable, disheartening new normal.

The 2026-27 season kicked off a fortnight ago, but Oklahoma City has already endured a campaign's worth of misfortune. Jalen Williams, lost to a fractured left fibula and a dislocated ankle. Cason Wallace, lost to a torn left labrum. Chet Holmgren, lost to a right patellar tendon tear. A tight-knit group that has always preached the importance of being where their feet are now is struggling to find its footing. A team that stood atop basketball's pinnacle less than 18 months ago now is dealing with questions about ever seriously challenging again, despite still boasting the reigning MVP and a former Coach of the Year. It's a unique type of hoops purgatory the organization hasn't experienced before.

"The morale's been pretty good all things considered," coach Mark Daigneault said on Saturday. "A week ago, the circumstances were a lot different than they are today. We understand that. We try to have an approach that can transcend these circumstances and the guys have done a great job. Obviously, the challenge is a little different now than it was prior to those injuries, but we have to recalibrate to what the challenge is and attack it a day and a game at a time."

While injuries have always been a part of the game, especially when competing at the highest level of the sport, the widespread volume and degree of ailments is troubling. One team being suddenly down 60% of its projected starting lineup is one thing, albeit a needle-in-a-haystack type probability. But the list of unavailables — Anthony Edwards, Tyrese Haliburton, Ja Morant, Ben Simmons, Jaren Jackson Jr., Paolo Banchero, Jalen Duren, Kawhi Leonard, Jalen Suggs and others — is growing, with various timelines ranging from multiple weeks to multiple months. Stars and teams are also being cautious with back-to-backs, whether due to early load management or having returned from long-term injuries. (The Pacers had 10 players out against the Hawks on Monday night, the second night of a back-to-back, citing a combination of rest and injury management.)

But the games aren't slowing down for anyone. The season has become streamlined to some degree, with the shortening of training camp/preseason (the typical ramp-up period) and the insertion of the NBA Cup. It's clearly taken a toll on the players, which in turn takes a toll on the overall product. And there doesn't seem to be an immediate fix for cramming 82 games into a six-month schedule.

Rockets guard Marcus Smart, who's dealt with serious injuries over his 12-year career, had an honest take on the growing epidemic.

"The level of basketball has become so extreme on the human body and we don't have enough time to recover like we used to," Smart said. "When I first came in the league, training camp and preseason were damn near three weeks, multiple games to get your body ready for an 82-game season. Now, depending on how far you go in the playoffs, you might get two months off? It's tough on the body.

"People don't understand; you're flying, your body's inflamed, you're landing in different time zones, go to sleep late and gotta be up early. Run as hard as you can, jump as high and fast as you can and be as physical as you can. All you're doing is asking yourself for injuries. But we signed up for it, and have to figure out a way to minimize it. Some of our best players are getting hurt and it's very unfortunate. We all want to be out here doing what we love."

There is a long list of sports scientists, doctors, data analysts and professionals who will attempt to dissect such a rapid rise of injuries in a short amount of time. But simply watching every night, the games look more rigorous, more demanding and more taxing.

Possessions are up, with the Chicago Bulls topping out at 110.2 a night, up from 107 courtesy of the 2025-26 Miami Heat. League average pace from the previous campaign is now hovering over the bottom third. The game has also become more aggressive. Last season's Pistons team, thought to be one of the more physical units around, committed 22 fouls per game. That same figure would rank 18th today. More teams are comfortable sending bodies to the offensive glass, with the Milwaukee Bucks' 33 chances per night a whopping 10 marks higher than last season's No. 1. On the defensive end, no team averaged double digits in contested rebound rate last season — there are eight such teams now. Average team speed and distance are up, too.

"There's not just one straightforward answer," said Jeff Stotts, injury analyst and owner of InStreetClothes.com. "I think you're seeing younger players get injured with a higher frequency because they're likely to have more miles on their legs before they get to the NBA. … I think the game has outpaced the player. And now you're asking your bigger, stronger athletes to also cover more ground, not only work on accelerators but also their brakes. Asking our big guys to stretch their games all the way out to the 3-point line. All those things increase the chances and likelihood of injuries occurring along the way."

Last season, only three players averaged more than 36 minutes a night — Amen Thompson, Kevin Durant and Luka Dončić. That list has since nearly tripled in size. The aforementioned list of injured stars sans Haliburton also has another thing in common: all of their usage rates were lower than the previous season. What that means is while you may be on the ball less, you're off the ball more — relocating, cutting, changing direction and using your body in other ways that still can accumulate pressure and load.

A good indicator of injury prevention is measuring an athlete's workload against their overall fitness level. Essentially the more they're asked to do physically, the more time they need to recover.

"We're in this constant back and forth between rest and acute-to-chronic load ratio, where we're trying to minimize spikes," Stotts said. "Sudden increases in load on the body in relationship to the overall conditioning of the athlete. The teams that have found success have found ways to quantify the data in a way that helps buy-in. Some teams won't rest players; others will build it in. There's no great cure."

Is such a spike in absences this early into the season enough to warrant an alternative look at scheduling or the larger umbrella of how the sport is played altogether? No magic wand can guarantee a clean bill of health, but the games, pace and aggression are increasing in frequency — and the players, whom the entire business model and ecosystem revolves around, are suffering because of it.

#2698. Malachi Toney vs. Leonard Moore is the showdown within the Miami vs. Notre Dame showdown

CORAL GABLES, Fla. (AP) — There's a subplot to No. 1 Miami vs. No. 4 Notre Dame this weekend.

And that matchup might be just as noteworthy to college football fans as the Hurricanes and Fighting Irish squaring off with huge College Football Playoff implications.

Toney is the star wide receiver and dazzling Heisman Trophy candidate for the top-ranked Hurricanes (8-0), the go-to guy for the nation's best offense. Moore is the lockdown cornerback and quite possibly the top defensive player on a Fighting Irish (7-1) team that happens to have the top-ranked defense in the country. The teams meet Saturday night at Notre Dame Stadium.

"I think if you ask both kids, they're looking forward to playing against elite talent," Miami offensive coordinator Shannon Dawson said. "I think guys like that appreciate people that master their craft the way the other one does. I don't know Leonard like I obviously know Mali, but there's a very humble approach to this game. He's an elite player but he also appreciates elite competitiveness. ... You're going to get people's respect when you're that level player."

The mutual admiration from both sides was evident this week.

"He's as good as there is out there," Dawson said of Moore.

Added Notre Dame coach Marcus Freeman, when asked about Toney: "He's one of one."

Toney's college debut came last season against Notre Dame in a 27-24 Miami victory that ultimately decided which team got the last at-large spot in the CFP field three months later. Toney had six catches for 82 yards and a touchdown — the one that opened the scoring.

Freeman didn't know much about Toney going into that game, other than he was still just 17 and should have been going into his senior year of high school. Toney reclassified to enter college a year early.

"Then you see him live, in person, and you go 'Oh my gosh, he is the real deal,'" Freeman said. "And he wasn't known on a college level — but after that game he was. He's athletic, he's fast, he runs good routes, he is competitive. And as you've watched him, he has even improved this year."

Entering this week, nobody in college football has more catches than Toney's 182 since the start of last season. His next catch will give him outright possession of the No. 2 spot on Miami's all-time list; he's currently tied there with Mike Harvey, 18 catches behind school record-holder Xavier Restrepo's 200.

Toney isn't making much of the potential 1-on-1 matchup.

"It's an opportunity to get better," he said Tuesday. "That's what it is."

Toney wears jersey No. 1; Moore wears jersey No. 15. The real story is No. 1 vs. No. 4, but 1 vs. 15 carries plenty of weight.

How much is Miami quarterback Darian Mensah looking forward to the matchup?

"Massively," Mensah said. "It's a huge opportunity for 1 to go out and put on a show. I think he's done it all year. Obviously, 15 is a great player and he's going to win some plays."

Moore was a unanimous All-American selection last season and has done nothing to suggest he won't be one again in 2026. He has seven interceptions and 23 pass breakups in his career; on the surface, they might not seem like huge numbers, but they become exceptional when considering that teams rarely try to test him.

"He is as gifted in his toolbox as I've been around," Freeman said. "His toolbox is extremely large. He has a skill set to be able to play corner and play nickel, and I truly believe he could play safety. That's the type of player he is. Mentally he can handle it, and physically. And that's why he's considered — if not the top — one of the top players in the country."

#2694. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

Dawn Staley's squad held on, but Mack still walked away as only the fifth player ever to drop 35 on them.

Scoring on a Dawn Staley defense is hard enough, but putting up 35 against them is almost unheard of.

Since Dawn Staley has been at the helm at South Carolina (2008) only 15 players have ever scored 30 on South Carolina. Only 4 had ever scored 35.

Maryland sophomore Addi Mack joins Caitlin Clark (Iowa), Alissa Pili (Utah), Chennedy Carter (Texas A&M), & Maci Morris (Kentucky) as the only players to score 35+ on Dawn's South Carolina.

Addi Mack has been a scorer for years. The Minnesota native was a four-star recruit who racked up over 4,600 high school points, even shattering Jalen Suggs' school scoring mark.

#2691. Major League Baseball proposes delaying salary cap implementation to 2028 in talks with players

NEW YORK (AP) — Major League Baseball proposed delaying the start of a salary cap until 2028, saying teams have too many commitments for next season that wouldn't allow them to reduce spending quickly enough.

A day after the start of free agent negotiations for the 2026-27 offseason, owners on Tuesday proposed to players that the sport adopt a hard cap of $258.2 million for 2028 and a mandatory floor of $180.2 million, using luxury tax payrolls with average annual values.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits, including earlier free agency, a $1 million minimum salary, a 30% increase to the pre-arbitration bonus pool and transactional reform that will reduce roster churn."

#2688. 2. Bundesliga: Hannover come from behind to claim first win under Sandro Wagner

Nicolai Rapp had given the visitors an early advantage, but second-half goals from Husseyn Chakroun and Marcel Hartel turned the contest around, before Dynamo's afternoon deteriorated further when Friedrich Müller was sent off.

Dresden made the brighter start and almost took the lead inside the opening ten minutes when Jonas Sterner delivered a low ball into the penalty area for Christoph Daferner, whose effort towards the near post was kept out by Leo Weinkauf.

However, the visitors would not have to wait much longer to break the deadlock. In the 11th minute, Alexander Rossipal delivered a corner from the right which was flicked on by Friedrich Müller, allowing Rapp to collect the loose ball at the far post before calmly finishing from close range to put Thomas Stamm's side ahead.

Hannover struggled to find a response despite enjoying the majority of possession, with efforts from Stefan Thordarson, Hayate Matsuda and Boris Tomiak failing to seriously trouble Lennart Grill. At the other end, Sterner forced another important save from Weinkauf in the 41st minute, while a late delivery from Husseyn Chakroun almost resulted in an unfortunate own goal from Müller.

The hosts headed into the interval trailing by a goal, having struggled to turn their possession into meaningful attacking opportunities, prompting Wagner to make two changes at half-time, introducing Franz Roggow and Waniss Taïbi for Thordarson and Kolja Oudenne.

The substitutions appeared to have an immediate impact as Hannover returned with considerably more attacking intent. Benjamin Källman and Hartel both threatened shortly after the restart, before the hosts finally found their equaliser in the 54th minute.

Chakroun was the man to restore parity, bringing Hannover back into the contest and giving the home supporters renewed belief. However, Dresden almost responded immediately when Rossipal struck the post just a minute later, missing a golden opportunity to restore the visitors' advantage.

Instead, the momentum remained with Hannover, who completed their turnaround in the 61st minute. Following an error from Dresden in possession, the hosts were awarded a penalty, with Hartel stepping up to confidently convert from the spot and put Wagner's side 2-1 ahead.

Dresden's hopes of finding a response suffered another major setback in the 65th minute when Müller received his second yellow card following a foul, leaving the visitors with ten men for the remainder of the contest.

Hannover looked to take advantage of their numerical superiority and thought they had extended their lead in the 76th minute when Källman found the net. However, following a VAR review, the goal was ruled out, ensuring the visitors remained within touching distance.

Despite the disallowed goal, Hannover managed the closing stages well to secure a valuable three points and end their winless run under Wagner.

The result represents a significant boost for Hannover, who move away from the foot of the table, while Dresden slip to the bottom following another disappointing away performance.

#2685. Micah Parsons and Dan Orlovsky engage in brutal back-and-forth over ‘most clutch quarterback’ in NFL

NFL player Micah Parsons and analyst Dan Orlovsky have taken their debate about Bo Nix being the most clutch quarterback online.

After the Denver Broncos' 28-24 win against the Kansas City Chiefs, it was Dan Orlovsky who stated that Nix was the most clutch quarterback in the NFL. He had a reason to make this statement, as the Broncos QB had made two big plays in the fourth quarter of the game against the Chiefs to help his team get the win.

The Broncos were down by 11 points entering the fourth quarter and needed a huge response from their team. First, their defence got the stop, and then it was time for the offence to show up. In typical Nix fashion, the 23-year-old helped the team get a touchdown on the first drive of the fourth quarter. They also scored on the conversion, which reduced the deficit to just three points.

On the next offensive drive, Nix once again made a huge play, as he connected with rookie running back Jonah Coleman, who gained 51 yards and then went on to score a touchdown to help the Broncos take the lead.

Nix created history as he recorded his 15th game-winning drive, the most for a quarterback in the NFL. Despite the stats, the Green Bay Packers star defensive lineman did not agree with the title Orlovsky had given Nix.

As Orlovsky's clip started making rounds on the internet, Parsons decided to push back on the analyst and wrote: "@danorlovsky7, I'm starting to see a pattern here!"

The former NFL player replied to Parsons by asking, "What's that?" The five-time Pro Bowler then accused Orlovsky of having favourites.

Having played as a quarterback in the NFL for over a decade, Orlovsky definitely knows a lot about the position and claimed that he had previously been critical of Nix.

This stands true as the 43-year-old had a lot to say about Nix's game after the Broncos' loss to the San Francisco 49ers. However, in this situation, Orlovsky wanted to go with facts.

"Most clutch in the NFL?" was the question Parsons asked during the back-and-forth. Orlovsky replied by saying: "He's 25-3 since the start of last year when trailing He's flawed but when it's on the line—he's the best right now production wise."

Parsons has been very vocal as the season has progressed. His analysis of the game has not been well received by people in the NFL, with analysts calling out Parsons after his comments about the Kansas City Chiefs.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- Since the 2026 playoffs began, we've been using words like "relentless" and "inevitable" when it comes to the Milwaukee Brewers. As they finished their coronation in Game 5 with a 4-1 victory over the Rays to take the series and win their first title in franchise history, it's pretty clear that the Brewers were the team of destiny from early in the season.

Game 5 on Wednesday never really felt like the Rays' night. Their pitching situation was dire after needing to use Nick Martinez in Game 4. The offense was dealing with Jacob Misiorowski and a full Brewers bullpen of studs. Junior Caminero was compromised and Yandy Díaz would join him. It just never felt like it was going to be their night and it wasn't, because of course it wasn't. It was the Brewers' night. The Brewers' series. The Brewers' season.

It took some longer than others to see it, myself admittedly included. They struggled in two different spans in April, with a six-game losing streak and later a four-game losing streak. That was about it, though. After a loss on May 4 dropped them to 18-16, the Brewers went absolutely bonkers the rest of the season: 85-43. And now they've completed an 11-2 playoff run against stacked competition. That means they finished 96-45. Holy smokes.

It's a misnomer to act like this is some ragtag bunch; a motley crew, island of the misfit toys collection of big-league players. The Brewers have stars. They have a former MVP in Christian Yelich and, though he's past his prime, he was a quality contributor in the playoffs. Jacob Misiorowski is going to win the National League Cy Young. Jackson Chourio is an emerging superstar. William Contreras is an All-Star catcher. Brice Turang is arguably the best second baseman in baseball.

The Brewers are such a well-rounded bunch and the front office thrives on winning on the margins, which is why some might slap inappropriate labels on them, such as the little engine that could. That doesn't begin to cover it. They are, in fact, a team of destiny getting contributions from all over the place.

There are more examples, of course. It was just a team full of winners. No matter what obstacle popped up for the Brewers this season, and especially in the playoffs, they reacted by winning. For crying out loud, they scored eight runs with two outs in the World Series. That was off-the-charts outrageous in Game 3.

Then there were the injuries. Yelich and Chourio missed time. Quinn Priester was lost for the season in spring training. Brandon Woodruff missed most of the year before making the World Series roster. With these injuries, in addition to the trade of Peralta, the door was open for players like Drohan, Gasser and Logan Henderson to make the most of their opportunities.

That's just what happens with teams of destiny. It's that ol' "next man up" mentality. The Brewers have been practicing this for years, trading away established veterans before they reach free agency and immediately replacing them with inexperienced players or even retreads like Jake Bauers who are ready to step in. For every player out the door, there's someone else ready to shine.

The Brewers just won 11 playoff games and came from behind to win six times. That's beyond ridiculous. Overall, teams scoring first in the playoffs were 27-13. Milwaukee accounted for six of the losses in there, bludgeoning its opponents even after falling behind.

The "destiny" thumbprints were all over this series. Even in their Game 4 loss, they just kept coming. And they responded to that loss by getting ace-level work from Misiorowski in Game 5 and putting up run-scoring rallies in three of the first six innings. They didn't need any home runs. They strung together winning plays on singles and doubles and sacrifice flies. They can win on home runs, too, as they've done a few times this postseason. They just find ways to win, almost every time. Their starters, bullpen, defense and clutch hitting are just too good. That's what it takes to win, and the Brewers won it all.

I mentioned the early struggles at the start of the season. They closed in opposite fashion. Including the playoffs, the Brewers were 26-5 after Sept. 6. They had established themselves as the best team in baseball from May 4 until early September, and then went into overdrive. How is it even possible for a 103-win team to level up and get better?

Relentless. Inevitable. The team of destiny. Milwaukee Brewers, World Series champions.

#2682. How Oregon State turned a raw athlete into a starting linebacker

CORVALLIS — Two years ago, Jarrel Comer was a freshman at Tallahassee Community College and had not played competitive football since middle school. Now he's a starting outside linebacker at Oregon State.

Comer played basketball at Eastside High School in Gainesville, Florida, but began college as a regular student. He looked for opportunities to play sports again and football became the opportunity at Citrus College in California.

He boarded a plane for the first time to take a cross-country flight to play football for the first time in more than four years.

"I was willing to take that chance to get to where I am today," Comer said.

He had 58 tackles (8.5 for loss), including six sacks at the California junior college and got on the radar of linebackers coach Cort Dennison, then at Idaho. Dennison kept pursuing Comer at OSU, where he signed in January and arrived during the spring.

Justin Joyner wins first game as Oregon State coach in blowout

Atkinson, Legree join Nike's Blue Ribbon Elite as OSU extends apparel deal

Pac-12 confirms play clock error led to penalty on Oregon State in its loss to Fresno State

At 6-foot-4 and 245 pounds, Comer was dominating in junior college from his athleticism alone. He didn't know the finer points of playing football. Hand placement, setting the edge in the run game and pass coverage were not in his repertoire. Comer was there to pin his ears back and attack the quarterback, regardless of the down and distance.

"They didn't ask much of me," Comer said. "They told me just do what I do, use my athleticism, get to the quarterback."

What Comer lacks in experience, he makes up for in ability. He consistently ranks among OSU's fastest players in practice, which was invaluable to a team seeking more pass rush.

"His athleticism is off the charts," defensive coordinator Mike MacIntyre said. "We see him grow leaps and bounds. Playing a lot more (against Montana), he will grow leaps and bounds going into this Saturday because now he's seen it, it slows down, he understands the different things."

RELATED: Experts release Oregon State vs. UTEP predictions, best bets, and preview for Week 4

Comer has 10 tackles thus far, including four in each of the past two games, and is already more than a situational pass rusher for the Beavers. He credits MacIntyre and edge coaches Joe Seumalo and George Frazier with helping him learn the game, particularly pass coverage.

Ideally, pairing Comer with Takari Hickle will allow OSU to generate more pressure as teams won't be able to focus all their offensive line on one side.

"Teams have to respect his speed," Hickle said. "If they don't, then he'll run right by them. He is definitely a threat in coverage and in the pass game."
