#2680. What's next for the Rays? Three questions after World Series loss, including payroll and Junior Caminero

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Tampa Bay Rays' 2026 season is over. Coming off a 98-win regular season, the American League East title, and their third-ever pennant, the Rays were eliminated in five games from the 2026 World Series by the juggernaut Milwaukee Brewers. There's pride to be taken in the Rays' overall body of work this year, but the prevailing reality is that they failed to achieve their ultimate goal. While the Brewers are celebrating their first World Series title, the Rays remain on the list of franchises that have never hoisted the trophy.

This all means that the Rays now turn their attention to 2027 and whether they're likely to make another run at relevance, contention, and perhaps another bite at the championship apple. Let's explore that now by exploring three questions that will define the Rays' coming offseason and their 2027 campaign.

The Rays, across so much of their history, have reliably punched above their weight. The foundation of that has been a level of support and investment from club ownership that's been entirely lacking. The present ownership group, led by Jacksonville real estate something or other Patrick Zalupski, took over in September of 2025, so this is almost wholly an indictment of former owner Stuart Sternberg.

Since the Rays' current run of contention began with their 90-win campaign in 2018, the club has never ranked higher than 24th in Opening Day active roster payroll and never higher than 22nd in luxury tax payroll (basically 40-man roster payroll based on average annual value of contracts). Twice in that span, the Rays have ranked last in year-end 40-man payroll. Given that the current revenue-sharing structure gives small-market teams more than enough to cover cash payrolls, this is all a plain dereliction of duties on the part of Sternberg. One of the canniest front offices in all of sports and the rosters they have assembled deserve more buy-in from ownership.

Maybe now that Zalupski's group is in charge and the Rays finally appear to have a new ballpark – heavily funded by tax dollars – across the finish line, things will change on this front. It'd be a fine time for that, given that the Rays right now are self-evidently capable of vying for a title. This winter, they have a number of key contributors due for arbitration raises, including Shane McClanahan, Jonathan Aranda, Griffin Jax, and Bryan Baker. Yandy Díaz in August triggered a $13 million vesting option for 2027, which, based on prior organizational behavior, might make him a trade candidate. There are also a number of investments needed in the rotation, which we'll get into below.

There's also the matter of what the next collective bargaining agreement will look like once one is agreed to and the forthcoming lockout ends. Signs point to the next CBA being of benefit to teams like the Rays, and that may inform some of their offseason behavior before that owner-implemented lockout likely begins on the night of Dec. 1.

The need for better stewardship from owners will be acutely critical to the makeup of the 2027 rotation. McClanahan's incoming arb raise – which will likely give him the highest salary of any Rays arb-eligible player this offseason — makes him a trade candidate. Freddy Peralta, their stabilizer after he was acquired leading up to the trade deadline, is a free agent. Drew Rasmussen has an $8 million option/$500,000 buyout for 2027. It should be a no-brainer to exercise said option, but, well, you know. There's also Nick Martinez, who has a $20 million mutual option for next season. That likely means he's headed for free agency, but the Rays should still pick up their end of it on principle. That's 80% of the rotation, at least as it was constituted after the trade deadline and before McClanahan's forearm injury. In all, that quartet of starters combined for a 3.03 ERA during the regular season and 42 of the team's 54 quality starts. They also combined for a WAR of 11.2, and that's despite getting just 10 starts from Peralta.

The Rays will need to do a lot of retention work on this front if they're going to again be the best team in the American League next season. As it stands right now, the rotation is the biggest unknown going into the offseason.

The 23-year-old third baseman and emerging superstar is the lineup fulcrum for Tampa Bay. Since his rookie season of 2024, Caminero has improved his OPS+ from 105 to 130 to 144 this past season. His WAR has swollen from 0.7 in 43 games as a rookie to 4.3 in 2025 to 5.7 in 2026.

He hits the ball exceptionally hard, and he has the fastest bat speed in the game. Additionally, Caminero in 2026 made impressive strides in terms of his plate discipline. Prospects these days, thanks to developmental and training advances at the lower levels, are arriving more ready than ever, and some start off at their peak. Caminero, though, has shown improvement on a number of forward-looking fronts, and that raises the compelling possibility that he still has some growth in him. Is a 50-homer season and an MVP award in the offing? That seems quite possible, and given the unbalanced nature of the Rays' lineup, they could use even more from their best player.

#2679. 10 takeaways from Oregon State’s loss at Fresno State

FRESNO, Calif. — Oregon State lost to Fresno State 38-22 Saturday night at Valley Children's Stadium.

Here are 10 takeaways as the Beavers prepare to host Texas State.

Two things can be true. Oregon State can still be ahead of schedule and on its way to a legitimately surprising season amid a massive rebuild, complete with a potent offense. Much of its success thus far came by pounding less talented teams and several of the worst defenses in the country. And where OSU was vulnerable was there to be exploited by teams like Fresno State, which has talent and good coaching.

The Beavers are not a College Football Playoff team. That dose of reality doesn't diminish what's being accomplished this season. They're simply not one of the two most talented teams in the Pac-12 right now.

JaMarcus Shephard and his staff were outcoached for definitely the first time in conference play and arguably for the first time this season.

Matt Entz laid out in detail what Fresno State picked up from studying Braden Atkinson from his time at Mercer and Oregon State's tendencies. Bye weeks also include self-scouting. Fresno State was more prepared for what OSU showed and particularly offensively the Beavers did not have an effective counter.

Winning on the road against a team with at least comparable (if not better) talent and coaching is a difficult task to begin with. It becomes a whole lot harder with six presnap penalties and allowing five sacks with two leading to fumbles. OSU absolutely could have led by multiple scores early if not for a false start negating Jake Reichle's would-be touchdown, if Aeryn Hampton's foot was in bounds and if multiple other penalties didn't occur.

That doesn't even get into defensive miscues from missed tackles or over-pursuits.

Houston was more physically dominating than Fresno State, but that's to be expected. Oregon State's offensive line had a brutal showing nearly across the board, with sacks allowed by multiple players in one-on-one matchups. OSU's rushing stats are skewed by the sacks and not nearly as poor as the final box score, but the bottom line is Fresno State won the line of scrimmage and it's not a particularly stout group.

Fresno State's 6-foot-4 receiver had a big night with two touchdowns. Freeman had a massive advantage against Isaiah Houi and performed accordingly. If there's one piece OSU's receiving corps is missing it is a target with the size and length of Freeman, which the Beavers are leaning on via their tight ends. But an outside target like him is hard to beat and he showed why.

OSU showed a vulnerability early, but against Houston and Texas Tech it was understandable in terms of talent and timing on the schedule.

Tackling improved over the prior five games, but opponents' speed also dropped. Against legitimate athletic threats, the Beavers showed their tackling fundamentals, speed, strength and angles are still areas of weakness.

Entz detailed Atkinson's reliance on his first read and susceptibility to being impacted by pass rush when it's not there. Of course, a defense has to have the talent and ability to do something about it. Atkinson's ceiling is high provided he develops in his reading of progressions, grows more comfortable checking into run plays and finds effective counters to the better defenses OSU faces.

Ojeda's three field goals should not get lost to the box score, particularly with a 54-yarder.

At 14-9, if OSU manages to make a stop and gain momentum, the game could have changed and the importance of Ojeda's kicks becomes paramount to the game.

As the sample size for OSU's kickoffs grows, so too does the success opponents continue to have. To allow a 44-yard kickoff return following a 14-play drive that spanned more than five minutes is inexcusable. OSU would literally have been better off kicking out of bounds, which has been enough of an issue as well.

The Beavers rank 114th in average kickoff return yards allowed and 126th on a per game basis.

Without belaboring a point that's been stated on nearly a weekly basis, the matchup disadvantage at No. 2 corner remains the Achilles' heel for the defense.

Against bigger receivers like Freeman it's simply a matter of when, not if, they will haul in big catches.

#2676. Brewers win the 2026 World Series: Where the Brew Crew ranks among the best recent MLB champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG -- The Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions. There's so much weight in such a statement on its own, but let's consider for a second all the context behind it.

The 2026 Brewers won 103 games in the regular season and then, more impressively, went a ridiculous 11-2 in the playoffs, never facing elimination, never even trailing in a series. They were one loss away Not only that, but they came so close to being the first team ever to go 8-0 in the League Championship Series and World Series. The 1976 Reds were the only team to sweep both the LCS and World Series, but that only got them to 7-0 because the LCS was five games until 1985. The best playoff record in the era of multiple wild cards was the 2022 Astros at 11-2, and the Brewers have tied that. The 2005 White Sox went 11-1 and so did the 1999 Yankees. We're already up in rarefied air. But there's more.

Think about how hot the Brewers closed. They finished the regular season by winning 15 of their last 18 games. This means they went 26-5 after Sept. 6. Further, look at who they decimated in the playoffs. The Padres were riding a run of 19 wins in 22 games, including a two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series. The Brewers went 3-1 in that NLDS. The Dodgers were the two-time defending champions who swept the Brewers in the NLCS last year. They won 100 games in 2026. The Brewers swept them in four games. The Rays won 98 games in the regular season and were 7-2 thus far in the playoffs. The Brewers took them down in five with their only loss coming in 12 innings.

Remember the Bob Uecker line from "Major League?" There's nothing left but a vapor trail.

That's the Brewers' path to the championship. They just became an absolute killing machine down the stretch, pulverizing everything in their path.

Statistically, they can't touch the 1998 Yankees (114 wins, +309 run differential, 11-2 playoff record including World Series sweep) and certainly can't get to the 1927 Yankees (110-44, +376 run differential, swept World Series). But what about more recently?

Such an exercise is subjective, but let's figure out where these Brewers rank in recent memory. Probably really close to the top, if not all the way up. This wasn't a team loaded with future Hall of Famers, as the Dodgers were last season, for example, but the numbers say these Brewers take a back seat to very few, if any, teams in the past couple of decades.

In fact, let's sort through it. I'll go with the multiple-wild card era, so we're starting in 2012. Let's narrow it down to teams that won at least 100 games and also won the World Series. Yes, the World Series title is a requirement, so we can safely say goodbye to the 2021 Giants and 2022 Dodgers.

We'll compare the teams via regular-season record, run differential, playoff record and how they fared in the World Series. As you'll see, the Brewers will have the most impressive resume here.

An absolute juggernaut in the regular season outside of a wretched stretch before the All-Star break, the Cubs finally broke the faux curse and won it all. They had the regular-season MVP and two Cy Young candidates, in addition to the Cy Young winner from the previous year. On the downside of this argument, they trailed in both the NLCS and World Series (three games to one). Coming back is impressive, but the most dominant teams didn't fall behind.

The first World Series title in franchise history came with a young and (at least it felt like it at the time) fun team. They had the MVP and a former Cy Young winner and also traded for future Hall of Famer Justin Verlander. They needed seven games in both the ALCS and World Series.

The highest win total on the list is right here. They also never faced elimination in the playoffs, though they did trail 1-0 in the ALCS. The MVP of the league was again on the champs and they also had three Cy Young winners (Chris Sale hadn't won his yet, but he was the undisputed ace).

After a 106-win regular season, the Astros steamrolled through the American League side of the bracket, going 7-0. They did lose Games 1 and 3, though, to fall behind 2-1 in the World Series after seeing the Phillies club them for a bunch of home runs in a 7-0 Game 3 win. The Astros righted the ship thereafter, though, and won the next three games, including two nail-biters.

Though the regular seasons are pretty comparable in that chart above, the Brewers were easily the top dog in the postseason. They lost one game between the NLCS and World Series.

We should probably loop in the 2013 Red Sox, the 2015 Royals and the repeat champion 2024-25 Dodgers as well.

If I had to rank them, I think the Mount Rushmore in this era would be:

The 2025 Dodgers were a tough omission, but they didn't even earn a bye due to a relatively low regular-season win total.

I'm willing to hear arguments for the Brewers over that Red Sox team, too. After all, the Red Sox did lose a whole three playoff games, even though they never faced elimination.

The bottom line is that the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers are one of the best, if not the greatest, champions in recent history.

#2675. 2. Bundesliga: Clinical Nürnberg punish wasteful St. Pauli at the Millerntor

An unfortunate early own goal from Eric Smith gave Miroslav Klose's side the lead, but despite St. Pauli dominating large spells of the contest, the hosts struggled to make their opportunities count. Abdoulie Ceesay eventually restored parity in the second half, only for substitute Sigurd Haugen to put Nürnberg back in front before 17-year-old Marc Kornwachs Barjuan sealed the victory in the closing stages.

Nürnberg found themselves under pressure from the opening exchanges, with St. Pauli looking to make their home advantage count. Abdoulie Ceesay came close to opening the scoring inside two minutes, failing to make sufficient contact with a cross from the left, before Joel Chima Fujita sent an effort narrowly over the crossbar shortly afterwards.

Despite the hosts' promising start, it was Nürnberg who took the lead in the seventh minute through an unfortunate own goal. Julian Justvan drove towards the byline on the right before attempting to cut the ball back into the penalty area, where Eric Smith inadvertently diverted the delivery into his own net.

St. Pauli responded positively and came agonisingly close to equalising in the 17th minute when Louis Oppie struck the crossbar with a powerful effort following a corner. The hosts continued to dominate, with Connor Metcalfe wasting a particularly good opportunity in the 31st minute after finding himself through on goal, only to drag his low finish narrowly wide.

Branimir Hrgota and Ceesay also threatened as the half progressed, but Nürnberg goalkeeper Jan Reichert proved an important figure for the visitors. His best contribution came in stoppage time when he produced an excellent save to deny Ceesay from close range, ensuring Nürnberg maintained their fortunate advantage heading into the break.

St. Pauli continued where they left off after the interval, although Nürnberg initially looked more organised defensively. However, the hosts eventually found the breakthrough they deserved in the 58th minute. After winning possession high up the pitch, it was Arkadiusz Pyrka who collected the ball on the right before delivering a precise low cross into the six-yard box, where Ceesay was on hand to turn home and level the game at 1-1.

Despite the equaliser, it was Klose's substitutions that would ultimately prove decisive. Having introduced Sigurd Haugen in the 65th minute, the Nürnberg forward needed just six minutes to make his mark. A poor backpass from Oppie allowed Haugen to race through on goal and round Voll, before finishing from an incredibly tight angle to restore the visitors' advantage in the 71st minute.

St. Pauli attempted to respond but struggled to find a way through Nürnberg's increasingly organised defence. The visitors continued to frustrate the hosts, with several bookings arriving during a heated closing period as St. Pauli searched for another equaliser.

Nürnberg then put the result beyond doubt in the 90th minute when another substitute Marc Kornwachs Barjuan found the net via a stunning strike to make it 3-1, completing an excellent afternoon for Klose's side.

The final whistle confirmed a valuable away victory for Nürnberg, ending their four-match winless run in all competitions and strengthening their position in the promotion race. For St. Pauli, meanwhile, the defeat brought an end to their six-game unbeaten run, with their inability to convert a number of excellent first-half opportunities ultimately proving costly.

#2673. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

For the first time in franchise history, the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions, and All-Star catcher William Contreras was named World Series MVP. Contreras also went 10 for 14 in ABS challenges behind the plate and 4 for 9 throwing out basestealers.

#2669. MLB Lockout 101: Everything to know about baseball's likely upcoming work stoppage

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 Major League Baseball season is over, and the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions for the first time. The Brewers finished off the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night in Game 5 of the 2026 World Series. MLB Opening Day for 2027 is scheduled for March 24. But whether fans are watching baseball again or not in less than five months is very much up in the air.

Major League Baseball's players and owners are in the process of negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement, or CBA. The CBA is the accord that governs the working relationship between the players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, and the clubs. It covers pretty much every aspect of that relationship that you can imagine, all the way from the overarching salary and payroll structure to daily meal money and days off during the season.

Not surprisingly, it's the economic platform of the game that's the toughest to negotiate because that is always, in essence, a fight over money, or how the league's substantial revenues will be divided up between teams and players. That's keenly relevant right now because players and owners are sparring over whether or not MLB will have a cap on salaries moving forward. The owners have renewed their push for a salary cap after not aggressively (or at least not this aggressively) pursuing one since the 1994-95 players' strike.

Matters are such that the owners are expected to implement a lockout of the players after the current CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year.

There are two kinds of labor stoppages in MLB: the strike and the lockout. A strike is when the labor side – players as represented by their union, in this instance – puts a halt to operations. A lockout is when the management side – team owners and the commissioner's office doing their bidding, in this instance – initiates the stoppage. In plainspoken terms, a strike is a refusal to work, and a lockout is a refusal to permit work to be done. For those on the outside, the result is the same, in that there's no Major League Baseball during a lockout or strike.

When a lockout is in force in MLB, as is expected to be the case after this CBA expires, nothing happens on the major-league front. And we do mean nothing.

There's an almost literal element to a lockout in that anyone on the 40-man roster of any MLB club will be locked out of any team facility for the duration of the stoppage. That also means no access to team trainers or team physicians or members of the coaching staff. Beyond that, there's a transaction freeze in place starting the moment the lockout begins (more on that in a moment).

Additionally, MLB is expected to remove player images and videos from the league's official website, MLB.com, and player images and even names would be removed from articles on MLB.com. A league memo acquired by The Athletic also forbids contact between players and anyone on the club side, at least to the greatest extent possible. The latter extends all the way down to a recommendation against sending holiday cards to players who have been locked out.

Bottom line: A lockout means the sport at the highest level is on hold across all fronts until further notice. "Further notice" almost certainly means when a new CBA is agreed to in principle and then ratified by both sides.

As just noted, a lockout means a transaction freeze, which means no players on any 40-man rosters can be traded and no major-league free agents can be signed for as long as the lockout lasts. Free agency, however, begins on Monday (Nov. 2), so there is roughly one month available for those looking to make trades or signings (once the five-day exclusive negotiating window closes and qualifying offers are extended) before the freeze sets in.

It's worth noting that in the run-up to the last lockout of 2021-22, we saw a swarm of free agent signings just before the lockout began. We could see that flurry of moves again, particularly in light of proposed changes to contract structures that would limit lengths and dollar amounts. Would players like Tarik Skubal, who are eyeing mid-nine-figure contracts, want to get their deals done quickly and hope they're grandfathered in?

That said, there's a lot more uncertainty about what the game's financial structure will look like after this CBA negotiation concludes, at least relative to the last time we did this. That may have a chilling effect on the trade and free agent markets leading up to the lockout date. Clubs don't like mass uncertainty when it comes to making major roster decisions, and they may prefer to see what the league's salary and revenue sharing systems will look like for the next half-decade (the term of each CBA these days) before committing to signings and trades.

If the lockout spans a meaningful amount of time, then that means a great deal of usual winter business will be put on hold. The MLB Winter Meetings and the major-league portion of Rule 5 Draft are typically held in the first half of December, so those could be imperiled. Last time out, the major-league portion of the Rule 5 Draft was indeed canceled, although the November Rule 5 protection deadline had already passed. If the lockout stretches into January, then the exchange of arbitration figures between eligible players and their teams will be delayed. Get well into late January and early February without an agreement, and arbitration hearings and the spring training schedule could be shortened or imperiled altogether. Needless to say, local businesses and elected officials in Florida and Arizona would very much not like that. That, though, could be the least of our worries.

It very well might. It's too soon to say, but there's the real potential for disruption and, perish the thought, maybe even cancellation of the 2027 season. The latter is of course the worst-case scenario, and there's no reason to think there's a strong threat of that possibility, at least this far out. During the last lockout, though, the two sides weren't fighting over quite as much territory, and we very nearly lost games from the regular-season schedule. Lest anyone forget, the last time the owners vigorously pushed for a salary cap, we wound up losing the World Series.

There is a wrinkle of note that may make a worst-case scenario less likely. If the lockout drags on long enough to cancel 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the fallout could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives.

Just players on the 40-player roster will be affected by the lockout, as mentioned. While that includes some minor leaguers, the vast majority of minor-league players are not on the 40 and thus will not be impacted. Minor leaguers now have their own CBA independent of MLB players, and that CBA is still in force. Thus, they're not being locked out. The minor-league season will proceed as normal, albeit minus those prospects on their respective 40s, just as it did during the 2021-22 lockout. So, yes, there will be affiliated professional baseball going on even if the lockout stretches into the 2027 regular season.

To hear commissioner Rob Manfred tell it, the lockout is designed to hasten negotiations between the two sides and speed up the process of forging a new CBA that, assuming it arrives in time, will cover the 2027-31 MLB seasons. Manfred cited this very reason leading up to the lockout of 2021-22, and during the drumbeat phase of this approaching lockout, he said this:

"In a bizarre way, it's actually a positive. There is leverage associated with an offseason lockout, and the process of collective bargaining under the NLRA (National Labor Relations Act) works based on leverage. The great thing about offseason lockouts is the leverage that exists gets applied between the bargaining parties."

After implementing the 2021-22 lockout, Manfred said the drastic decision was designed to "jumpstart the negotiations and get us to an agreement that will allow the season to start on time."

Actions, though, hold sway over words, and after locking out the players, MLB owners didn't make their first CBA proposal to the players for another six weeks or so. In reality, the purpose of a lockout is to preempt a strike. The union can time a strike so as to exert maximum leverage and apply maximum pressure on ownership, say, during the stretch drive or soon after Opening Day or just in advance of the playoffs. From a fan and observer standpoint, though, at least this gets the clock started before games hang directly in the balance.

Yes. The forthcoming lockout will be the 10th labor stoppage in modern MLB history – five strikes and, soon, five lockouts. Here's a quick look at the nine lockouts and strikes that have already happened:

As you can see, there are occasions in which the stoppage is lengthy and disruptive, and in other instances they barely register. Given the complex nature of the current negotiation, the expectation is that the upcoming lockout won't be resolved quickly. There is, though, some runway between "immediate resolution" and "2027 season greatly harmed."

It's the salary cap, first and foremost. MLB has coveted a capped system for decades, but for the MLBPA, the strongest union in sports, a cap is a complete nonstarter. If the stoppage turns into a war, then it will be because owners continue pushing for a cap and players continue to resist. Let it be known that despite the public narrative, the main advantage of a salary cap for owners is not that it will promote competitive balance, but rather that a payroll cap figures to increase franchise values.

Otherwise, changes to the way the league shares local revenues are also up for negotiation. MLB already shares local revenues at significant levels, but Manfred and owners want to share them more equally among teams, perhaps similar to what the NFL does. The good news is that the union has already shown a willingness to discuss such changes and indeed has proposed something similar. That's common ground on a negotiation that figures to need as much of that as possible. As well, increasing the sharing of local revenues, especially local broadcast revenues, would help achieve what the league claims a cap would achieve and do so without a 1994-95 scale of work stoppage.

Given the all-encompassing nature of the CBA, many other issues will need to be sorted out. Those may include the length of the regular season, postseason format, the minimum salary, any changes to free agency and salary arbitration, the implementation of an international draft, retention of the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, draft bonus pools and eligibility, and -- if retained -- the structure of the Competitive Balance Tax system. That's not an exhaustive list, and all of it has to be hammered out, at least in terms broadly agreeable to both sides, for the lockout to end. For now, though, the league hasn't moved off its demand for a cap, and until that changes -- or until the union acquiesces (highly unlikely) -- that issue will determine how long the lockout lasts.

Yes, there is. Once we get into spring training and beyond, any continued shutdown costs clubs and players money. MLB owners have a significantly larger war chest than the players do, but neither side relishes missed broadcast and gate revenues or paychecks. As detailed above, there's heavy incentive to get this resolved before the 60-game mark of the regular season because of broadcast contracts. Along similar lines, with attendance continuing to rise and revenues also increasing each year, the game is in a relatively healthy spot. Pace-of-play initiatives are broadly popular among paying customers, as is the implementation of the ABS challenge system. Expansion to 32 teams is probably also on the horizon. All of that adds up to a potentially lucrative glut of national broadcast contracts, and a lockout that cuts the 2027 season to ribbons would do great harm to what may be MLB's most important business-side objective of all right now. The 1994-95 strike also still provides a roadmap to how much damage the "nuclear" outcome can do to the sport.

Every labor stoppage is a skirmish over money, but the prospect of losing a hunk of the money they're fighting over can reveal shared interests and the foundations of compromise. Therein lies the hope for those of us on the outside.

The San Francisco 49ers have the day off on Tuesday, but they usually have a group of players in for workouts or tryouts. According to Aaron Wilson, the Niners worked out defensive tackle Dominic Bailey.

We'll have the full list of players the 49ers worked out around 2 pm PT when the NFL's transaction wire is released.

The 49ers lost defensive tackle Naquan Jones from the practice squad. The only other defensive tackle remaining is McKinnley Jackson. So, perhaps the team is looking for another big body like Jones. CJ West is still on the injured reserve. Maybe this is the team saying West is still a week or more away from returning by working out Bailey.

But Bailey isn't the same body type as a traditional nose tackle, like Jones and West. The sixth-year senior out of Tennessee is listed at 6'3″, 270 pounds. He went undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft. Bailey started all 12 games for the Vols.

Per Sumer Sports, Bailey played 109 snaps in the preseason for the Houston Texans at defensive tackle. He had five solo tackles and three pressures. He has not played a regular-season snap.

#2665. MLB proposes delaying salary cap and floor until 2028 season so free agency can proceed as normal

MLB doesn't want free agency to come to a grinding halt with a lockout on the horizon. Because of that, the league altered one of its biggest demands as it engages in collective-bargaining agreement (CBA) negotiations with the players' union.

In order to ensure players can sign with teams now, MLB proposed to push its implementation of a salary cap and salary floor to the 2028 season. That move would make it easier for teams to negotiate and sign free agents now, before a new CBA is put into place.

Additionally, MLB tweaked its figures for both a salary cap and a floor. Under the new proposal, the league would cap teams at a payroll of $258.2 million. The salary floor would be $180.2 million.

Those figures are up from MLB's previous proposal, which called for a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor.

#2664. Key MLB offseason dates: When does free agency start? What else will happen before potential lockout?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 MLB season is complete and the Brewers are World Series champions. They defeated the Rays to clinch the first title in franchise history. We were assured a first-time champion this season and the Brewers won it. The Rays will try again for their first title next year. With the World Series now complete, the 2026-27 offseason has officially begun, and several significant events are right around the corner.

Of course, this all comes with a disclaimer. When the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. That could take days, weeks, months, who knows? It may affect spring training and even the 2027 regular season, or they may find labor peace before the spring. Regardless, the likely lockout will all but certainly affect some of the calendar. MLB free agency will still begin in early November, but transactions will all come to a halt the minute there is a lockout.

Here now are the important dates and deadlines for the coming weeks and months.

As of 9 a.m. ET, eligible players (i.e. those with at least six years of service time) are free agents. Free agents cannot sign with a new team just yet. They have to wait five days for that. The first five days of the offseason are an exclusive negotiating period during which free agents can only talk money with their most recent team. Very few players re-sign during the exclusive negotiating period. Edwin Díaz returning to the Mets four years ago is by far the most notable in recent memory. Once players get this close to free agency, they typically test the market. Also, trades involving 40-man roster players resume on this day for the first time since the summer's trade deadline.

This year's Gold Glove winners will be announced during an ESPN broadcast at 8:30 p.m. ET. The Cubs and Blue Jays lead the way with five Gold Glove finalists each. In addition to the nine individual positions in each league, there is also a utility Gold Glove and a team Gold Glove.

Most contract option decisions are due on this date. Some contracts specify a different date (the Yankees had to make a decision on Zack Britton's 2022 club option in November 2020, for example), but the vast majority have to be made within five days of the end of the World Series. Club options are controlled by the team, player options and opt-outs are controlled by the player, and mutual options are kind of pointless. They're a way to shift money to the next year's payroll more than anything.

Some option decisions are no-brainers, like the Braves picking up their $17 million club option on Ronald Acuña Jr. or Luis Severino picking up his $22 million player option with the Athletics. This offseason's notable contract option decisions include Michael King (can opt out of two years and $58 million with Padres), Bo Bichette (can opt out of two years and $84 million with Mets), and Luis Robert Jr. (Orioles hold $20 million club option).

The qualifying offer is a one-year contract worth the average of the top 125 salaries, or $23.15 million this offseason, according to the New York Post. To be eligible for the qualifying offer, a free agent must have spent the entire 2026 season with one team and have never received the QO previously. The Mariners can make Randy Arozarena the QO, but the Dodgers cannot do the same with Tarik Skubal because he was traded during the season.

The five-day exclusive negotiating period ends and free agents are truly free. They can negotiate and sign with any team as of 5 p.m. ET on this date. That said, much like the regular season, MLB's free agency is a marathon, not a sprint. We (probably) won't see a rush of signings on Day 1 because MLB is not a salary-capped league (not yet, anyway), and free agents aren't worried about getting left out in the cold when cap space runs out.

Rookies of the Year on Monday, Managers of the Year on Tuesday, Cy Youngs on Wednesday, and MVPs on Thursday. The awards will be announced during an MLB Network broadcast at 7 p.m. ET each day. Awards finalists will be announced Nov. 2. The All-MLB Team, Comeback Players of the Year, and Relievers of the Year will also be announced on Nov. 11.

Generally speaking, the GM Meetings are used to handle off-the-field matters like rule changes, but when you put all 30 GMs in one place, deals inevitably get discussed and sometimes completed. The Angels signed Travis d'Arnaud and the Braves traded Nick Allen to the Astros at last year's GM Meetings, for example. Also, the groundwork is often laid this week for deals that are completed at a later date.

If Silver Sluggers are your thing, this is the date for you. Four years ago, a utility player Silver Slugger was added, then three years ago, MLB and Louisville debuted a team Silver Slugger. Finalists will be announced Nov. 2.

The deadline for free agents to accept or reject the QO is 4 p.m. ET.  Players who accept the QO sign that one-year, $23.15 million contract and remain with their team (and cannot be traded until June 15 without their consent). Free agents who reject the QO are attached to draft pick compensation. Their former team receives a draft pick if they sign elsewhere, and their new team has to forfeit a draft pick(s) and, in some cases, international bonus money. Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are among the free agents who will surely reject the QO and sign more lucrative contracts this offseason.

That is a fancy way of saying this is the deadline for teams to add eligible minor leaguers to the 40-man roster to protect them from the Rule 5 Draft. Generally speaking, college players drafted no later than 2023 and high school players drafted no later than 2022 are Rule 5 Draft eligible this winter, as are players signed internationally no later than 2022. Among the notable Rule 5 Draft-eligible prospects this offseason are Dodgers righty Christian Zazueta and Nationals righty Travis Sykora. Those two and many others will be added to the 40-man roster on this date. The deadline is 6 p.m. ET, specifically.

It should be noted that there are usually several minor trades in the days leading up to the Rule 5 Draft protection deadline as teams get their 40-man roster in order. Four years ago, the Rays traded Xavier Edwards to the Marlins in the 40-man roster management move at the Rule 5 Draft protection deadline.

The now triannual owners meetings cover big-picture business matters and are rarely a source of hot stove news or rumors. Three years ago, the owners voted on and approved the Athletics' proposed relocation to Las Vegas at their November meetings. With the collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1 and talks with the MLB Players Association ongoing, the owners will likely use this week as one last strategy session.

This is the deadline for teams to offer contracts to their pre-arbitration and arbitration-eligible players for 2027. Contracts do not have to be signed yet. An offer just has to be extended. Players who do not receive a contract offer before the deadline are considered "non-tendered" and immediately become free agents. Notable players are non-tendered every offseason as teams determine that their salary outweighs their performance and the trade market turns up nothing worthwhile. Adolis García and Nathaniel Lowe were among the players non-tendered last offseason.

Specifically, the CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET, and it is very likely the owners will lock out the players at that time. It is possible MLB and the MLBPA will agree to a new CBA before this date, sure, but it would be a major surprise. All major league transactions get put on hold during the lockout. There will be no trades or free agent signings involving 40-man roster players, or even any negotiations. Here is our timeline of CBA talks and proposals. Because a potential lockout would bring so much uncertainty, any events and deadlines listed after this date are subject to change. We'll put asterisks as a reminder.

These are the extra draft picks given each year to teams that fall in the bottom 10 in revenue and/or market size. There is overlap between the two groups, so there are typically 14-15 competitive balance picks awarded each year, not 20. Competitive balance picks are MLB's only tradeable draft picks. Last offseason, picks were included in the Shane Baz, Brendan Donovan, and Caleb Durbin/Kyle Harrison trades. Five years ago, the assignment of competitive balance picks was pushed back until after the lockout.

Voting results for the Hall of Fame's Contemporary Baseball Committee for Managers, Executives, and Umpires will be announced during an MLB Network broadcast. The Hall of Fame has restructured its veteran committee three times in the last 14 years, and this year's Contemporary Baseball Committee will consider "candidates whose primary contribution to the game came since 1980." The 16-person committee will consider eight candidates on the ballot. This has nothing to do with the CBA and the announcement will take place as scheduled.

This is typically when all hot stove hell breaks loose. The Winter Meetings are the busiest period of the offseason and feature plenty of trades, free agent signings, and rumors. It is three-plus days of nonstop hot stove action. Historically, the biggest moves of the offseason are completed at the Winter Meetings. GMs can talk face-to-face with agents and other GMs to get things done. Last year, Pete Alonso, Edwin Díaz, and Kyle Schwarber signed during the Winter Meetings while Jose A. Ferrer and Harry Ford were among those traded. The Winter Meetings were canceled during the last lockout. It seems likely they would be canceled again during a potential lockout this offseason.

In an effort to curb tanking, MLB and the MLBPA agreed to a lottery to determine the top six picks of the annual amateur draft as part of the current CBA. The 18 non-playoff teams each have a shot at the No. 1 pick, though the worst teams have the highest odds. Here are this year's odds for the No. 1 selection in the 2027 Draft (via Baseball America):

Teams that pay into revenue sharing cannot pick in the lottery in back-to-back years, so the Giants (No. 4 pick in 2026) are not eligible for the lottery this year. The Pirates, meanwhile, cannot get a lottery pick this year because teams that receive revenue sharing can not pick in the lottery in three consecutive years. They had the No. 6 pick in 2025 and the No. 5 pick in 2026. The Giants and Pirates cannot pick higher than No. 10 overall in 2027.

The lottery determines the top six draft picks. Picks 7-18 are the remaining non-playoff teams in reverse order of the standings. Picks 19-30 are the 12 postseason teams ordered by their finish, with the Wild Card Series losers coming first and the World Series winner picking last. The draft lottery was not yet a thing during the last lockout. It's unclear how MLB would handle it during a potential lockout this offseason.

By rule, players selected in the Rule 5 Draft must remain on their new team's MLB roster all season in 2027; otherwise, they must go through waivers and be offered back to their original team. Teams don't often find difference-makers in the Rule 5 Draft. They usually look for middle relievers, platoon bats, and lottery tickets. Most Rule 5 Draft picks don't stick and wind up back with their original team. Last offseason's notable Rule 5 Draft selection was Blue Jays righty Spencer Miles, who gave them 95 ⅔ innings with a 2.63 ERA. The Rule 5 Draft was canceled and not held during the last lockout. There is a minor-league phase that still took place, however, because that phase does not involve 40-man roster players.

This is the deadline for teams and arbitration-eligible players to submit salary figures for 2027. The player files what he believes he should be paid while the team files what it believes the player should be paid. This date is only the filing deadline, and the two sides can still agree to a contract of any size even after filing salary figures. The vast majority of arbitration-eligible players agree to a contract before the filing deadline and avoid this headache. MLB Trade Rumors released their 2027 salary arbitration projections a few weeks ago. The entire arbitration process (submit filing figures, hearings, etc.) was pushed back until after the lockout five years ago.

The 2027 international amateur signing period opens at 9 a.m. ET. The annual signing period used to run from July 2 to June 25, though MLB and the MLBPA agreed to push the start of the 2020-21 and 2021-22 signing periods back to the following January because of the pandemic, and now the January start is permanent and the signing period is neatly confined to a single calendar year. These are non-40-man roster players and the international signing period opened as scheduled during the last lockout.

The 2027 Hall of Fame class will be announced during a live MLB Network broadcast. The Hall of Fame ballot will be revealed on Nov. 16, votes are compiled over the following weeks, then the results are announced in January. Newcomers to this year's ballot include Jon Lester and Buster Posey. This is Omar Vizquel's tenth and final year of eligibility. This is also Year 6 on the ballot for Alex Rodriguez and Year 4 for Chase Utley. Among holdovers, Utley was closest to getting in without actually getting in last year. He received 59.1% of the vote, well short of the 75% needed for induction, but he's made huge gains in his three years on the ballot and is trending toward induction.

Inevitably, a few arbitration-eligible players and their teams will be unable to come to terms on a contract, and wind up in front of an arbitration panel. Each side states their case -- hearings can be contentious because the team will outline the player's shortcomings and explain why he deserves a lower salary than he believes -- and the three-person panel picks either the salary the player filed or the salary the team filed on Jan. 8. Nothing in between. Again, teams and players can work out a contract of any size prior to a hearing, even after filing salary figures. Skubal and Kyle Bradish were among the players to go to an arbitration hearing before the 2026 season. Hearings were pushed back until after the lockout five years ago, and in some cases they took place during the season.

Spring training camps open across Arizona and Florida in the middle of February. Each team sets its own reporting dates for pitchers and catchers and then position players, though they'll all be up and running by the second full week of February. All 30 teams are scheduled to play their first exhibition game on Feb. 19. If the lockout extends into February, the start of spring training will be delayed. During the lockout five years ago, MLB announced spring delays one week at a time, piece by piece.

March 24 is the exclusive Opening Night game on Netflix (teams TBA). The other 28 teams will begin their seasons one day later. There's Rivalry Weekend, a special series in Las Vegas and more. Of course, if the lockout extends in March, Opening Day and other games will be pushed back. Five years ago, the regular season started a week late and teams picked up the existing schedule. A new schedule was not drawn up. Missed games were made up with doubleheaders and on mutual off-days throughout the year, with a few extra days tacked on to the end of the season as well.

At this point, everyone knows the conflict between Troy Aikman and Joe Buck, and the tensions might've boiled over on the small screen during their latest NFL Monday Night Football (MNF) broadcast on ESPN.

A clip from their broadcast on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, went viral. Buck is introducing himself and the rest of the crew, including Aikman, who barely smiles when his name is called.

Maybe it was just an off moment for Aikman, but the recent reports of his unhappiness with the network and fight with Buck suggest otherwise.

Aikman and Buck had a heated confrontation before the MNF game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Buffalo Bills a few weeks back.

It stemmed from the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback being unhappy that his partner signed a five-year, $108-million contract extension with ESPN.

After all, they have been a duo for over two decades. They jumped ship from FOX to join ESPN in 2022. Aikman didn't appear happy that his broadcasting partner negotiated a new deal without him.

This led to their confrontation before MNF a few weeks ago. Aikman was asked about it afterward and appeared to indicate that he was set to become a "free agent" after this season. This means his longtime partnership with Buck might be ending after 22 years.

They still have about half of the regular season to go together. Aikman and Buck are also set to call the Super Bowl, which marks the first time ESPN has broadcast the game. That historic night will bring an end to their fifth season on ESPN. Buck's new deal will keep him around until at least ESPN's next Super Bowl in a few years.

#2656. Jacob Misiorowski wraps breakout Brewers year with World Series title and a reminder that best is yet to come

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- When the Brewers took the field for Game 5 of the World Series, they did so with their ace on regular rest. All that stood between them and their first World Series championship was a win with the best possible formula that they could draw up on the lineup card.

If there was any question, it was if Misiorowski could channel some of his early season magic. In the playoffs, he hadn't been bad, but hadn't been nearly as dominant as in the regular season. He also hadn't gone more than five innings in a start.

He stepped up, as championship-caliber athletes do. He was forced to leave the game late in the sixth inning due to calf cramp, but the Brewers already had a 4-0 lead (the eventual final score) and handed things off to their elite bullpen on cruise control. Misiorowski came through with 5 ⅔ innings of scoreless ball, allowing only two hits. He stifled the Rays until the game felt like it was elementary. Only two pitchers have ever recorded a scoreless start of 5+ innings with two or fewer hits allowed in a potential World Series clincher: Misiorowski and some guy named Tom Glavine in 1995.

And behind their ace, the inevitable Brewers are World Series champions.

"It's awesome," Misiorowski said on the field after the Brewers clinched. "It's awesome for this team, it's awesome for the city of Milwaukee. I just made it work. It didn't matter how we won tonight, just that we won."

There were questions in the aftermath of Game 4 about whether Brewers manager Pat Murphy should have brought Misiorowski in for the bottom of the 12th to close things out. There shouldn't have been. It wasn't Game 7. The Brewers were up 3-0 in the series. Losing Game 4 meant they had full-strength Misiorowski waiting to close the door in Game 5. Unsurprisingly, he did exactly that, despite likely being on fumes from his 2026 workload.

In 2025, Misiorowski only worked 141 ⅓ innings between the minors, majors and playoffs. That was a career high in his professional career. In 2026, he finishes with 193 ⅔. It's a monster leap, and it's why the Brewers held his workloads in check down the stretch. They needed something left in the tank to achieve the ultimate goal. That was the plan all along: for him to do exactly what he did in Game 5.

And we're only scratching the proverbial surface here. Remember what a phenom Misiorowski was in the regular season, especially early in the year? He was the must-see player in the sport. Even with his workload monitored, he finished the season with a ridiculous 1.80 ERA (leading the majors) and 252 strikeouts (again, leading the majors) in 174 ⅔ innings. He also led the majors in WHIP, strikeout rate and had the lowest hit rate.

Between his rookie season and this year, "The Miz" ratcheted up his strikeout rate, plummeted his walk rate, improved his efficiency and, early in the year before workload became a concern, worked much deeper into games. As a rookie, he was a talent to dream on. As a sophomore, he was the dream. He's already as decorated as any pitcher the Brewers have ever had (with the Brewers, that is).

Now, let's keep a few things in mind. Misiorowski is:

After the Brewers swept the Dodgers in the NLCS, Murphy remarked on how they don't have a bunch of Hall of Famers, an indirect shot at Los Angeles' star-studded lineup, but there's an argument that Misiorowski has a strong foundation right now (so does Jackson Chourio, by the way).

Given the improvements that Misiorowski made from Year 1 to Year 2 in the majors, there's every reason to expect that next year he'll be just as good, only he'll have built up more stamina for late in the season.

Could he go 200 innings in the regular season next year and lead the Brewers to back-to-back championships while winning a second Cy Young? I don't see why not. That would have sounded like a pipe dream to Brewers fans if we got in a time machine to the aftermath of last year's sweep at the hands of those dastardly, mega-payroll Dodgers. But, you see, Misiorowski just had a dream season. With a guy with his level of talent, the only answer is to dream bigger.

#2655. Thomas Haugh’s 19 points and 10 rebounds lead No. 1 Florida past No. 14 Miami, 77-67

TAMPA, Fla. — Thomas Haugh had 19 points and 10 rebounds to lead No. 1 Florida to a 77-67 win over No. 14 Miami on Monday night in the season opener for both programs.

Rueben Chinyelu added six points and 14 rebounds for the Gators, who left Benchmark International Arena with a loss the last time they played there to Iowa in the second round of the NCAA Tournament on March 22.

Acaden Lewis, a transfer from Villanova, had 24 in his first game for the Hurricanes.

Haugh, the preseason Southeastern Conference Player of the Year who would have likely been a lottery pick had he left for the NBA, was dominant from start to finish. The 6-foot-9 senior chipped in five offensive boards, four assists, two steals and a block. He didn't commit a turnover and hit 4 of 8 from 3-point range.

Miami kept within striking distance, scoring the first eight points of the second half. The Hurricanes sliced Florida's lead to 53-51 when Somto Cyril followed a missed free throw with a dunk.

But the Gators answered with defense, holding the Hurricanes without a field goal over a five-minute stretch. When Urban Klavzar made a 3-pointer, Florida led 66-55.

When Haugh didn't connect, his teammates picked him up. Late in the first half, Isaiah Brown followed Haugh's miss with a putback dunk to give Florida a 44-32 advantage.

Stuck in a tight battle over the game's first eight minutes, Florida used a 9-0 run to take command and didn't trail again.

Florida, which has managed to retain its roster nucleus over multiple years, won with muscle and effort. A physical matchup between instate rivals, the contest included two technicals and three fouls that were upgraded to flagrants.

Florida: Hosts Jacksonville on Thursday night.

#2652. Ranking the last 10 World Series: Where does Brewers vs. Rays 2026 showdown land in the last decade?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- Another World Series is in the books. Two close, fun games in Milwaukee both went the Brewers' way before they decided to fully stomp on the collective necks of the overwhelmed Rays in Game 3. They dropped Game 4, but it took 12 innings before the Rays could beat them. Then the Brewers closed things down in Game 5. The Senior Circuit claims its third straight World Series championship and, for the first time ever, the Brewers are World Series champions.

As I do annually, I'll now rank the last 10 World Series.

What makes a truly great Fall Classic? Well, the best ones go all seven games and have an epic finish in Game 7. Close games in the rest of the series help, along with some back-and-forth and memorable moments.

To be clear, every World Series is amazing, so anything that doesn't rank highly was still good; it's just on a relative scale here.

Specifically, we're judging this from a "no horse in the race" perspective. That is to say that the 2026 World Series for long-time Brewers fans was the best ever and they wouldn't change anything. Likewise for Rangers fans in 2023. This is all subjective and done by one person who just loves baseball and wants every World Series to go seven games.

Let's get to it! The last 10 World Series, ranked:

I often say that every World Series is amazing. But maybe this one doesn't count the same because nothing was the same in that godforsaken year. The 2020 Fall Classic just doesn't bring back any fond memories for me.

I was truly happy that we had a season at all that year, even if it was only 60 games with no fans in attendance. We needed something fresh to watch and it was a good product. There were good games in this series too, notably the Rays' huge comeback in Game 4 and when the Dodgers stormed back to win Game 6 after Blake Snell was famously pulled.

Major League Baseball did its best here, but it's never going to feel the same. I can't watch these highlights back without getting annoyed. The lack of full ballparks with home fans going crazy really puts a damper on that, even if it was the right decision.

I'll be shocked if I ever rank this one anywhere but last, and it's not due to the quality of play. Even a sweep in a normal series is better.

Game 1 was one for the ages. The Rangers jumped out to a 2-0 lead in the first inning, the Diamondbacks got three in the third and the Rangers immediately tied it. The D-backs tacked on two more, though, and headed to the ninth with a 5-3 lead. Then Corey Seager hit a game-tying, two-run blast and let out a roar right after connecting. In the 11th, Adolis García hit a walk-off home run. What a game.

There were plenty of fun moments the rest of the series, but a ninth-inning Rangers rally to put Game 5 away meant there were no other hotly contested games in this one. It was only 3-1 in Game 3 when the D-backs got the tying run to the plate, but a double play ended that threat.

Still, the Rangers winning their first-ever World Series championship is notable and gains some bonus points. Between that and Game 1, this series wasn't a complete dud.

It might be recency bias to put this one above 2023, but Games 1, 2 and 4 delivered in a huge way. Game 4 ended up being one of the most exciting extra-innings games ever. Plus, this was much more of a heavyweight battle, given that it pitted both No. 1 seeds with 103 and 98 wins, respectively. That 2023 series was 90 wins vs. 84.

The Brewers really had to sweat out Game 1, especially after a review wiped out what looked like the game-ending double play. And how about Game 2? The Rays jumped out to a 4-0 lead in the top of the first, but what has defined this Brewers group all season was bouncing back. They got two runs across in the bottom of the first and chipped away until they won, 5-4, with the Rays stranding the tying run at third base. The games in Milwaukee were hotly contested and all kinds of fun.

Game 3 in St. Pete ceased to be fun for anyone aside from Brewers fans in the fifth inning, but it was historic to watch them score eight runs with two outs. Even just typing it out sounds absurd. There were two outs in the inning and no runs had scored. Then they up an eight spot. Ridiculous.

Game 4 saw the Rays take a lead twice only to see the Brewers come back to tie it. That's just what the '26 Brewers did. A 2-2 score lasted until the 12th inning when Cooper Pratt hit a solo shot to take the lead for the Crew. An error to start the bottom of the 12th opened the door for the Rays, though, and they got singles from Liam Hicks, Jonny DeLuca, Chandler Simpson and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson to win it.

Game 5 gave us Jacob Misiorowski putting the finishing touches on a dream season both individually and for the Brewers as a whole. Pratt continued his hot streak with a two-hit, two-RBI night and William Contreras had an RBI double in the inning that put the thing away.

It was probably as good of a series as a five-gamer can be, but it never felt like the Brewers were losing this thing, making it all feel inevitable.

The Red Sox won 108 games in the regular season and never faced elimination in the playoffs. Game 1 was a great illustration of Boston's offensive dominance as they jumped out to a lead in the first inning and answered right back every time the Dodgers scored, including with five runs on seven hits in four innings against Clayton Kershaw. Game 2 was pretty good with two middle-innings lead changes. Game 3 was the marathon 18-inning affair that ended on a Dodgers' walk-off home run by Max Muncy. Game 4 was 0-0 through 5 ½ innings. The Dodgers then scored four, but the Red Sox scored nine in the final three innings, including a game-tying homer by Steve Pearce -- off Kenley Jansen -- and later a three-RBI double by Pearce. The Red Sox hit four home runs in a 5-1 win in Game 5 to clinch it.

It was a tough call in picking this one over 2018 for the best five-game series of the last decade. I'll go with 2024 because we saw the first-ever walk-off grand slam, which came in extra innings after the Yankees had already taken a lead over the Dodgers. Freddie Freeman hit that slam and homered again in Game 2 ... and in the first inning of Game 3. Oh, and in the first inning of Game 4 too. The Yankees responded in that game, though, to avoid the sweep. After seeing home runs early from Aaron Judge, Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Giancarlo Stanton in Game 5, it looked like the Yankees were sending the series back to L.A., but then they had a total meltdown in the fifth inning. The Yankees took the lead back in the sixth, but the Dodgers wouldn't be denied and scored two in the eighth to finish things off.

Jorge Soler led off the series with a home run and the Braves built a 5-0 lead through three innings. The Astros answered with a comfortable win of their own in Game 2. Game 3 was very low-scoring and finished 2-0, though it wasn't a pitcher's duel for the ages or anything. Game 4 was outstanding. The Astros held a 2-0 lead going into the sixth and the Braves got one run. In the seventh, Dansby Swanson hit a home run to tie it and then Soler followed with the go-ahead shot. With a 3-1 series lead, the Braves got an Adam Duvall grand slam in the first inning of Game 5 and it looked like that game would just be a coronation, but the Astros battled and battled, recording nine runs on 12 hits despite zero home runs. That did not happen in Game 6. It was a dud. Soler's three-run homer in the third essentially ended it and the Braves won, 7-0.

There were some good games and great moments, but it falls a bit shy of a classic.

It was quite a start. There were fireworks early as the Astros grabbed a 5-0 lead through three thanks to two Kyle Tucker home runs. The Phillies got five runs between the fourth and fifth innings to tie it up and then won in 10 innings thanks to a J.T. Realmuto home run. Game 2 wasn't quite as fun, but the Astros evened the series up. Game 3 wasn't close, but it was party central in Citizens Bank Park with the Phillies hitting five home runs, including a few majestic blasts from Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber. The next night, the Astros threw the second no-hitter in World Series history. Sure, it was a combined effort, but that's still history. Game 5 was tremendous theater. The Astros scored in the first, but then Schwarber hit a leadoff bomb to tie it. Jeremy Peña later homered for the Astros and it was 3-1 in the eighth when the Phillies cut it to one and put two runners on for Schwarber. The inning ended on a nice play from the little-used Trey Mancini at first base. Then there was an amazing play from Chas McCormick in center in the ninth to prevent the tying run from reaching scoring position.

Game 6 was scoreless through five and this was a duel, with frontline starters Zack Wheeler and Framber Valdez putting up zeroes. Schwarber broke the tie in the sixth with a home run and it looked like this series might stretch to seven games. The Astros got two runners on with one out in the seventh, however, and then lefty José Alvarado came in to face lefty Yordan Alvarez. Alvarez hit a booming home run to dead center that paved the way for the Astros' second World Series title.

For not going seven games, this was a damn good series. It was the best that didn't go seven in the last 10 years. But we need that Game 7 for an all-time great World Series. And we've seen three in the last decade.

I know we've seen these teams a bunch at this point, but at the time, it was a fresh matchup. The Astros had never won a World Series and the Dodgers hadn't been to the Fall Classic since 1988.

Game 1 was a classic from an all-time great. Clayton Kershaw, in 103-degree weather, allowed just one run on three hits in seven innings while striking out 11. The Dodgers won 3-1 that game and had a 3-1 lead heading to the eighth in Game 2. They got one in the eighth off Jansen before Marwin Gonzalez hit a game-tying homer. The Astros hit back-to-back home runs to start the 10th, but the Dodgers answered and tied the game in the bottom of the 10th. George Springer hit a two-run homer in the 11th and the Dodgers got one back, but it wasn't enough. The Astros rode a big early inning to a Game 3 win, but it was close. Game 4 was tied 1-1 heading into the ninth and then the Dodgers scored five in the ninth to win it and even the series. Game 5 remains the most ridiculous (in a good way) game I've ever seen in person. In 10 innings, the two teams combined for 25 runs on 28 hits, including seven home runs. Four of the home runs either tied the game or took the lead. The Dodgers trailed Game 6, facing elimination, 1-0 heading to the sixth, but got two runs that inning and one in the seventh to force a Game 7. The finale, unfortunately, wasn't very good.

There's an argument for this series to sit above our No. 2 pick here, but it was demoted for two reasons. First off, yes, getting to Game 7 is paramount to having a highly ranked series, but we needed a truly great Game 7 here and didn't get it, while the top two in the rankings did. Further, the sign-stealing scandal definitely casts a pall over this thing in hindsight. I still loved every minute of it at the time.

The Washington Nationals had never won the World Series before and started the season 19-31. They were on the ropes in the Wild Card Game, but just never quit.

Juan Soto starred in a 5-4 Nationals win in Game 1. Game 2 ended up as a blowout Nats win, but it was tied heading into the seventh before they scored 10 in the final three frames. The Astros responded by winning Games 3-5 in D.C., and while none of them were especially memorable, we now had the quirk of every road team winning in the series.

The Nats closed with wins in Games 6 and 7. Game 6 was close until late and Game 7 was awesome. First off, the pitching matchup of Zack Greinke vs. Max Scherzer, who had been dealing with a back issue, was a battle between two likely Hall of Famers. The Astros had a 2-0 lead going into the seventh inning. Anthony Rendon homered and Soto drew a walk. The Astros went to the bullpen and then Will Harris gave up a Howie Kendrick two-run home run off the foul pole in right field. It was one of the most dramatic plays in World Series history. The Nats actually tacked on enough that the game wasn't particularly close in the ninth, but it was still a classic based purely on the Kendrick homer.

As established, I think the best-ever World Series discussion requires an all-time great Game 7 in addition to a good series leading up to it. We got that and then some with this one. It was so absurd that we ranked the seven most crazy/amazing moments and had a few others to spare.

I think we also have to consider that the Blue Jays hadn't been to a World Series since Joe Carter's historic walk-off homer in Game 6 in 1993 and that the Dodgers were the first MLB repeat champion since 2000. There was good history behind this.

What did we see in this one that set it apart even before that insane Game 7? A lot.

This list doesn't include everything, of course. It was a great series that had so many notable moments. It wasn't a difficult choice to rank this as the best World Series of the last 10 years. It's one of the best of all time. My hunch is this occupies the top spot until it falls off the list based on the passage of time.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.
